The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father, nor the father suffer for the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself.

God repeats the principle and makes it run both ways. Neither generation carries the other's guilt. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself.

There is one great exception, and it is the heart of the gospel. The righteousness of one man has been placed on others, and the sin of others has been placed on him. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21). This is not the unfairness of the sour grapes proverb. It is the free, willing exchange of grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — Is My Way Not Just?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If a wicked person turns from all his sins, None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him (vv. 21-22). Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live? (v. 23). But if a righteous person turns to wickedness, his former righteousness will not save him (v. 24). The people say the Lord's way is not just; God answers that it is their ways that are unjust (vv. 25-29).
verseByVerse.theology: God judges each person by the direction of his life, and he delights not in death but in repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if a wicked person turns away from all his sins that he has committed and keeps all my statutes and does what is just and right, he shall surely live; he shall not die. None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him; for the righteousness that he has done he shall live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But if a wicked person turns away from all his sins that he has committed and keeps all my statutes and does what is just and right, he shall surely live; he shall not die.

Now the chapter moves from generations to individual lives. What matters is not only what family you come from, but which way you are facing now. A wicked person can turn. And if he does, he shall surely live; he shall not die.

None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered against him; for the righteousness that he has done he shall live.

Here is astonishing grace. None of the transgressions... shall be remembered against him. Not some. None. God does not keep a file open in case the repentant sinner slips. I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins (Isa 43:25). I will remember their sins no more (Heb 8:12).

Zacchaeus was a thief and a traitor. When he turned, Jesus said, Today salvation has come to this house (Luke 19:9). There is no past so dark that it cannot be forgotten by God when a sinner turns to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?

This verse is the heart of the chapter, and it shows the heart of God. The question expects the answer no. God takes no pleasure in anyone's death. What he wants is that he should turn from his way and live.

Many people imagine God as eager to condemn. Ezekiel, the prophet of judgment, says the opposite. God judges because he is just, but he delights in mercy. Paul says God desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim 2:4). Peter says he is not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Pet 3:9). And Jesus said, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance (Luke 15:7).

If you are far from God, this is his heart toward you. He is not waiting to crush you. He is waiting for you to turn.

verseByVerse.quote: But when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice and does the same abominations that the wicked person does, shall he live? None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered; for the treachery of which he is guilty and the sin he has committed, for them he shall die. "Yet you say, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' Hear now, O house of Israel: Is my way not just? Is it not your ways that are not just? When a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice, he shall die for it; for the injustice that he has done he shall die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice and does the same abominations that the wicked person does, shall he live? None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered; for the treachery of which he is guilty and the sin he has committed, for them he shall die.

The same principle works the other way. A person who has lived rightly and then turns away to wickedness cannot lean on his past. None of the righteous deeds that he has done shall be remembered. God judges the direction of a life, not a ledger of old credits.

As in 3:20, this is not saying that God's true children can be snatched out of his hand. It is saying that a life of apparent righteousness that ends in apostasy shows that the heart was never truly turned to God: They went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). And it is a real warning that God uses to keep his people: the one who endures to the end will be saved (Matt 24:13). No one can rest on a past spiritual experience while living in present rebellion.

"Yet you say, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' Hear now, O house of Israel: Is my way not just? Is it not your ways that are not just?

And the people complain: The way of the Lord is not just. It is not fair, they say, that a wicked man can turn and be forgiven, or that a righteous man can turn and be lost.

God throws the charge back. Is it not your ways that are not just? What would be unjust is to punish a son for his father, or to refuse mercy to the repentant. God's way is the only truly just way. The problem is not his justice but their unwillingness to face their own guilt. Is there injustice on God's part? By no means! (Rom 9:14).

When a righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice, he shall die for it; for the injustice that he has done he shall die.

verseByVerse.quote: Again, when a wicked person turns away from the wickedness he has committed and does what is just and right, he shall save his life. Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die. Yet the house of Israel says, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' O house of Israel, are my ways not just? Is it not your ways that are not just?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again, when a wicked person turns away from the wickedness he has committed and does what is just and right, he shall save his life.

Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die.

Notice the two steps: he considered and turned. Repentance begins with thinking — stopping, looking honestly at your life, weighing where it is going. Then it acts: turned away from all the transgressions. The prodigal son came to himself and then arose and went to his father (Luke 15:17-18).

Many people never repent because they never stop to consider. Life is too busy and too noisy. One of the most important things a person can do is to sit still long enough to ask: where is my life going, and what does God say about it?

Yet the house of Israel says, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' O house of Israel, are my ways not just? Is it not your ways that are not just?

The same complaint, the same answer. When people keep accusing God of unfairness, it is usually because they would rather argue than repent.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will judge each one by his ways: Repent and turn from all your transgressions, lest iniquity be your ruin (v. 30). Cast away from you all the transgressions that you have committed, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel? (v. 31). For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who commands a new heart pleads with sinners to turn and live, and in Christ he gives what he commands.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, declares the Lord GOD. Repent and turn from all your transgressions, lest iniquity be your ruin. Cast away from you all the transgressions that you have committed, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, declares the Lord GOD. Repent and turn from all your transgressions, lest iniquity be your ruin.

Now the chapter becomes an appeal. I will judge you... every one according to his ways. Each person. We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Cor 5:10). And therefore: Repent and turn. (The ESV notes that the last phrase may be rendered "lest iniquity be your stumbling block".)

Cast away from you all the transgressions that you have committed, and make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?

Cast away — like throwing off filthy clothes. And then a command that seems impossible: make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit!

How can anyone make himself a new heart? In 11:19 and again in 36:26, God promises, I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. So which is it? Both. God commands what he alone can give, so that we will stop trusting ourselves and ask him for it. The command shows us our duty and our inability; the promise shows us his grace. Paul holds both together: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Phil 2:12-13).

And then a moving question: Why will you die, O house of Israel? God is not describing an inevitable fate. He is pleading. As if to say: you do not have to die. Why would you choose it?

verseByVerse.quote: For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live."

The chapter ends with four words that sum up the whole gospel invitation: so turn, and live.

I have no pleasure in the death of anyone. Not anyone. God's heart toward sinners is not hostile but pleading. The door is open.

Jesus said to religious people who knew the Scriptures well, you refuse to come to me that you may have life (John 5:40). The tragedy of lost people is not that God refused them, but that they refused him. And the Bible's last invitation echoes this one: let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price (Rev 22:17).

Whatever your family, whatever your past, whatever you have done, God's word to you today is the same: turn, and live.

18.title: Turn, and Live
18.overview:
The exiles repeat a proverb blaming their suffering on their parents' sins: the fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge. God forbids the proverb. All souls belong to him, and the soul who sins shall die (vv. 1-4).

God gives three generations as examples. A righteous man, who avoids idolatry and adultery, does not oppress, returns pledges, feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, does not profit from the poor, and acts justly and faithfully, shall live. His violent son, who does all these sins, shall die, and his blood is on his own head. That son's son, who sees his father's sins and does not copy them, shall live and not die for his father's iniquity. The soul who sins shall die; neither father nor son bears the other's guilt (vv. 5-20).

If a wicked person turns from his sins, he will live, and none of his transgressions will be remembered against him, for God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked but wants him to turn and live. If a righteous person turns to wickedness, his past righteousness will not save him. When the people say the Lord's way is not just, God answers that it is their ways that are not just (vv. 21-29).

God will judge each by his ways. He calls them to repent, cast away their transgressions and make themselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why will you die? I have no pleasure in the death of anyone; so turn, and live (vv. 30-32).
18.theology:
Every soul belongs to God and is personally accountable to him; no one may hide behind the sins of parents or society (vv. 2-4, 20; Deut 24:16; Jer 31:29-30).

True righteousness is specific: pure worship, sexual faithfulness, justice, mercy to the poor and honesty with money (vv. 5-9; Isa 58:7; Matt 25:35-36).

The righteous live by faith, and faith shows itself in a changed life; yet no one but Christ fully meets this standard, and he died for the unrighteous (v. 9; Hab 2:4; Jas 2:18; Rom 3:10; 1 Pet 3:18).

A godly family cannot save an ungodly child, and an ungodly family cannot doom a child who turns to God (vv. 10-18).

The only transfer of righteousness and guilt is the gracious exchange of the cross (2 Cor 5:21).

God forgets the sins of the repentant and does not credit past righteousness to the apostate (vv. 21-26; Isa 43:25; 1 John 2:19; Matt 24:13).

God takes no pleasure in the death of anyone; he pleads with sinners to turn and live (vv. 23, 32; 1 Tim 2:4; 2 Pet 3:9; Luke 15:7).

God commands a new heart and promises to give it, so that repentance is both our duty and his gift (v. 31; 11:19; 36:26; Phil 2:12-13).
18.examples:
Your father ate the sour grapes and your teeth ache.

A cloak given back before the sun goes down.

A son who saw everything his father did, and did not do likewise.

A file of sins that God does not keep.

Stopping long enough to consider.

A God who asks: why will you die?

Four words: so turn, and live.

19.text: <sup>1</sup>And you, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel,<sup>2</sup>and say: What was your mother? A lioness! Among lions she crouched; in the midst of young lions she reared her cubs.<sup>3</sup>And she brought up one of her cubs; he became a young lion, and he learned to catch prey; he devoured men.<sup>4</sup>The nations heard about him; he was caught in their pit, and they brought him with hooks to the land of Egypt.<sup>5</sup>When she saw that she waited in vain, that her hope was lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a young lion.<sup>6</sup>He prowled among the lions; he became a young lion, and he learned to catch prey; he devoured men,<sup>7</sup>and seized their widows. He laid waste their cities, and the land was appalled and all who were in it at the sound of his roaring.<sup>8</sup>Then the nations set against him from provinces on every side; they spread their net over him; he was taken in their pit.<sup>9</sup>With hooks they put him in a cage and brought him to the king of Babylon; they brought him into custody, that his voice should no more be heard on the mountains of Israel.<sup>10</sup>Your mother was like a vine in a vineyard planted by the water, fruitful and full of branches by reason of abundant water.<sup>11</sup>Its strong stems became rulers' scepters; it towered aloft among the thick boughs; it was seen in its height with the mass of its branches.<sup>12</sup>But the vine was plucked up in fury, cast down to the ground; the east wind dried up its fruit; they were stripped off and withered. As for its strong stem, fire consumed it.<sup>13</sup>Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land.<sup>14</sup>And fire has gone out from the stem of its shoots, has consumed its fruit, so that there remains in it no strong stem, no scepter for ruling. This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Lioness and Her Cubs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel is to lament for Israel's princes (v. 1). Their mother was a lioness who raised her cubs among lions (v. 2). One cub grew into a young lion that devoured men, but the nations caught him in a pit and dragged him with hooks to Egypt (vv. 3-4). She raised another, who prowled, devoured and laid waste the land with his roaring (vv. 5-7), until the nations netted him, caged him and brought him to the king of Babylon, that his voice should no more be heard on the mountains of Israel (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Kings who rule like predators end as captives, and the royal house that bred them mourns.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel, and say: What was your mother? A lioness! Among lions she crouched; in the midst of young lions she reared her cubs. And she brought up one of her cubs; he became a young lion, and he learned to catch prey; he devoured men. The nations heard about him; he was caught in their pit, and they brought him with hooks to the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel,

A lamentation was a funeral song. Ezekiel is told to sing a dirge for Judah's kings — and to sing it while Zedekiah was still on the throne. It is like playing a funeral march for a man who has not yet died. The message is unmistakable: the royal house is already as good as dead.

and say: What was your mother? A lioness! Among lions she crouched; in the midst of young lions she reared her cubs.

The mother is Judah and its royal house. And the lion was Judah's own emblem. On his deathbed Jacob had said, Judah is a lion's cub... he crouched as a lion and as a lioness; who dares rouse him? and The scepter shall not depart from Judah (Gen 49:9-10). Judah was the tribe of kings, and its kings were meant to be lions — strong, courageous protectors.

Among lions she crouched. But she raised her cubs among the lions of the nations, and they learned the ways of the nations.

And she brought up one of her cubs; he became a young lion, and he learned to catch prey; he devoured men.

The nations heard about him; he was caught in their pit, and they brought him with hooks to the land of Egypt.

The first cub is taken to Egypt. That identifies him as Jehoahaz, who reigned three months in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 23:31) before Pharaoh Neco put him in bonds and he came to Egypt and died there (2 Kgs 23:34).

And notice what he learned: he learned to catch prey; he devoured men. A king was supposed to be a shepherd who protected his people. These kings became predators who fed on them. Power used to devour instead of to serve always ends in a pit.

verseByVerse.quote: When she saw that she waited in vain, that her hope was lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a young lion. He prowled among the lions; he became a young lion, and he learned to catch prey; he devoured men, and seized their widows. He laid waste their cities, and the land was appalled and all who were in it at the sound of his roaring. Then the nations set against him from provinces on every side; they spread their net over him; he was taken in their pit. With hooks they put him in a cage and brought him to the king of Babylon; they brought him into custody, that his voice should no more be heard on the mountains of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When she saw that she waited in vain, that her hope was lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a young lion.

The mother's hope that her first cub would come back is gone. So she pins her hopes on another. That is the story of Judah's last years: one king after another, each one expected to save the nation, each one failing.

He prowled among the lions; he became a young lion, and he learned to catch prey; he devoured men,

and seized their widows. He laid waste their cities, and the land was appalled and all who were in it at the sound of his roaring.

The second cub is even more violent — seizing widows, laying waste cities, terrifying the land with his roar. (The ESV notes that seized is literally "knew".) This one is carried off to Babylon. Most likely it is Jehoiachin, whom Nebuchadnezzar took prisoner and carried away... to Babylon (2 Kgs 24:12, 15); some think it points to Zedekiah, whose capture was still to come. Either way, the pattern is the same.

Then the nations set against him from provinces on every side; they spread their net over him; he was taken in their pit.

With hooks they put him in a cage and brought him to the king of Babylon; they brought him into custody, that his voice should no more be heard on the mountains of Israel.

A caged lion. (The ESV notes that in a cage may be "in a wooden collar".) And the sad line: that his voice should no more be heard on the mountains of Israel. The roar that once terrified the land falls silent.

Set this against the true Lion of Judah. John wept because no one could open the scroll, and an elder said, Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered. But when John turned to look, he saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain (Rev 5:5-6). Judah's lions devoured men. The true Lion of Judah was slain for men. His power is the power of self-giving love, and his voice will never be silenced.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Their mother was also a fruitful vine by abundant water, whose strong stems became rulers' scepters (vv. 10-11). But it was plucked up in fury, dried by the east wind and burned (v. 12). Now it is planted in a dry wilderness (v. 13), and fire has come out of its own stem, so that there remains in it no strong stem, no scepter for ruling. This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The line of David's kings seemed to end in fire and exile, but God's promise of a coming King did not die.

verseByVerse.quote: Your mother was like a vine in a vineyard planted by the water, fruitful and full of branches by reason of abundant water. Its strong stems became rulers' scepters; it towered aloft among the thick boughs; it was seen in its height with the mass of its branches. But the vine was plucked up in fury, cast down to the ground; the east wind dried up its fruit; they were stripped off and withered. As for its strong stem, fire consumed it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your mother was like a vine in a vineyard planted by the water, fruitful and full of branches by reason of abundant water.

A second picture of the same mother. Now she is a vine, planted by the water, lush and fruitful. (The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read "in your blood" instead of in a vineyard.) This is Judah in its days of blessing, with every advantage God could give.

Its strong stems became rulers' scepters; it towered aloft among the thick boughs; it was seen in its height with the mass of its branches.

Its strong branches became royal scepters — kings grew from this vine. It towered high (the ESV notes, perhaps "among the clouds"), impressive and admired. The house of David at its height under Solomon was exactly that.

But the vine was plucked up in fury, cast down to the ground; the east wind dried up its fruit; they were stripped off and withered. As for its strong stem, fire consumed it.

And then, all at once: plucked up in fury. Thrown to the ground, dried by the east wind from Babylon, its fruit stripped, its strongest branch burned. Height is no protection when God uproots.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land. And fire has gone out from the stem of its shoots, has consumed its fruit, so that there remains in it no strong stem, no scepter for ruling. This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land.

The vine that grew beside abundant water is now in a dry and thirsty land — exile in Babylon. It is not quite dead, but it is far from its source.

Many believers know what it feels like to be transplanted from a well-watered place to a desert — a loss, an illness, a move, a season when God feels far. Even there, God can make things grow. The book of Ezekiel will end with a river flowing into the desert and making it live (47:8-9).

And fire has gone out from the stem of its shoots, has consumed its fruit, so that there remains in it no strong stem, no scepter for ruling. This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation.

Here is a tragic detail: fire has gone out from the stem of its shoots. The fire did not only come from outside. It came from within the royal line itself. Zedekiah's rebellion lit the fire that burned Jerusalem. The kings destroyed the kingdom.

No strong stem, no scepter for ruling. It looks like the end of David's dynasty. Jacob had said The scepter shall not depart from Judah... until tribute comes to him (Gen 49:10). Has the scepter departed?

Not forever. In the next chapters Ezekiel will hear God say of the crown, This also shall not be, until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs, and I will give it to him (21:27). And he has already heard the promise of a tender sprig planted by God himself (17:22). The scepter was laid down in the dust so that it could be picked up by the true King.

This is a lamentation and has become a lamentation. What began as a song about the future became history. Ezekiel's dirge came true. But the story of David's line did not end with a lament. It ended with an empty tomb.

19.title: A Lament for the Princes
19.overview:
Ezekiel is to sing a funeral lament for the princes of Israel. Their mother was a lioness who raised her cubs among lions. One cub became a young lion that devoured men, but the nations caught him and brought him with hooks to Egypt. She raised another cub, who also devoured men, seized widows and laid waste cities with his roaring, until the nations caught him in a net, put him in a cage and brought him to the king of Babylon, so that his voice was heard no more on the mountains of Israel (vv. 1-9).

Their mother was also like a fruitful vine planted by abundant water, whose strong stems became rulers' scepters and towered high. But it was plucked up in fury, dried by the east wind and burned. Now it is planted in a dry wilderness, and fire has come out from its own stem, leaving no strong stem and no scepter to rule. This is a lament, and it has become a lament (vv. 10-14).
19.theology:
Rulers are meant to be protectors; power used to devour others ends in captivity and silence (vv. 3-9).

Privilege and height are no protection when God uproots a proud house (vv. 10-12).

Judgment often comes from within: the royal line lit the fire that consumed it (v. 14).

God's promise of a King from Judah did not die with Judah's kings; the true Lion of Judah conquers as the slain Lamb (Gen 49:9-10; 21:27; Rev 5:5-6).
19.examples:
A funeral song for a king still on his throne.

Lion cubs who learn to hunt their own people.

A roar silenced in a cage.

A vine by the river, replanted in the desert.

A fire that started in the royal branch itself.

The Lion who turns out to be a slain Lamb.

20.text: <sup>1</sup>In the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, certain of the elders of Israel came to inquire of the LORD, and sat before me.<sup>2</sup>And the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>3</sup>"Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel, and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD, Is it to inquire of me that you come? As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you.<sup>4</sup>Will you judge them, son of man, will you judge them? Let them know the abominations of their fathers,<sup>5</sup>and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day when I chose Israel, I swore to the offspring of the house of Jacob, making myself known to them in the land of Egypt; I swore to them, saying, I am the LORD your God.<sup>6</sup>On that day I swore to them that I would bring them out of the land of Egypt into a land that I had searched out for them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the most glorious of all lands.<sup>7</sup>And I said to them, 'Cast away the detestable things your eyes feast on, every one of you, and do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt; I am the LORD your God.'<sup>8</sup>But they rebelled against me and were not willing to listen to me. None of them cast away the detestable things their eyes feasted on, nor did they forsake the idols of Egypt. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them and spend my anger against them in the midst of the land of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations among whom they lived, in whose sight I made myself known to them in bringing them out of the land of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>So I led them out of the land of Egypt and brought them into the wilderness.<sup>11</sup>I gave them my statutes and made known to them my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live.<sup>12</sup>Moreover, I gave them my Sabbaths, as a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them.<sup>13</sup>But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness. They did not walk in my statutes but rejected my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; and my Sabbaths they greatly profaned. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them in the wilderness, to make a full end of them.<sup>14</sup>But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out.<sup>15</sup>Moreover, I swore to them in the wilderness that I would not bring them into the land that I had given them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the most glorious of all lands,<sup>16</sup>because they rejected my rules and did not walk in my statutes, and profaned my Sabbaths; for their heart went after their idols.<sup>17</sup>Nevertheless, my eye spared them, and I did not destroy them or make a full end of them in the wilderness.<sup>18</sup>"And I said to their children in the wilderness, 'Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers, nor keep their rules, nor defile yourselves with their idols.<sup>19</sup>I am the LORD your God; walk in my statutes, and be careful to obey my rules,<sup>20</sup>and keep my Sabbaths holy that they may be a sign between me and you, that you may know that I am the LORD your God.'<sup>21</sup>But the children rebelled against me. They did not walk in my statutes and were not careful to obey my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; they profaned my Sabbaths. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them and spend my anger against them in the wilderness.<sup>22</sup>But I withheld my hand and acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out.<sup>23</sup>Moreover, I swore to them in the wilderness that I would scatter them among the nations and disperse them through the countries,<sup>24</sup>because they had not obeyed my rules, but had rejected my statutes and profaned my Sabbaths, and their eyes were set on their fathers' idols.<sup>25</sup>Moreover, I gave them statutes that were not good and rules by which they could not have life,<sup>26</sup>and I defiled them through their very gifts in their offering up all their firstborn, that I might devastate them. I did it that they might know that I am the LORD.<sup>27</sup>"Therefore, son of man, speak to the house of Israel and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: In this also your fathers blasphemed me, by dealing treacherously with me.<sup>28</sup>For when I had brought them into the land that I swore to give them, then wherever they saw any high hill or any leafy tree, there they offered their sacrifices and there they presented the provocation of their offering; there they sent up their pleasing aromas, and there they poured out their drink offerings.<sup>29</sup>(I said to them, 'What is the high place to which you go?' So its name is called Bamah to this day.)<sup>30</sup>"Therefore say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Will you defile yourselves after the manner of your fathers and go whoring after their detestable things?<sup>31</sup>When you present your gifts and offer up your children in fire, you defile yourselves with all your idols to this day. And shall I be inquired of by you, O house of Israel? As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you.<sup>32</sup>"What is in your mind shall never happen—the thought, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone.'<sup>33</sup>"As I live, declares the Lord GOD, surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you.<sup>34</sup>I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you out of the countries where you are scattered, with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out.<sup>35</sup>And I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face.<sup>36</sup>As I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will enter into judgment with you, declares the Lord GOD.<sup>37</sup>I will make you pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant.<sup>38</sup>I will purge out the rebels from among you, and those who transgress against me. I will bring them out of the land where they sojourn, but they shall not enter the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD.<sup>39</sup>"As for you, O house of Israel, thus says the Lord GOD: Go serve every one of you his idols, now and hereafter, if you will not listen to me; but my holy name you shall no more profane with your gifts and your idols.<sup>40</sup>"For on my holy mountain, the mountain height of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, there all the house of Israel, all of them, shall serve me in the land. There I will accept them, and there I will require your contributions and the choicest of your gifts, with all your sacred offerings.<sup>41</sup>As a pleasing aroma I will accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples and gather you out of the countries where you have been scattered. And I will manifest my holiness among you in the sight of the nations.<sup>42</sup>And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I bring you into the land of Israel, the country that I swore to give to your fathers.<sup>43</sup>And there you shall remember your ways and all your deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you shall loathe yourselves for all the evils that you have committed.<sup>44</sup>And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I deal with you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways, nor according to your corrupt deeds, O house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD."<sup>45</sup>And the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>46</sup>"Son of man, set your face toward the southland; preach against the south, and prophesy against the forest land in the Negeb.<sup>47</sup>Say to the forest of the Negeb, Hear the word of the LORD: Thus says the Lord GOD, Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall devour every green tree in you and every dry tree. The blazing flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from south to north shall be scorched by it.<sup>48</sup>All flesh shall see that I the LORD have kindled it; it shall not be quenched."<sup>49</sup>Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! They are saying of me, 'Is he not a maker of parables?'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — I Will Not Be Inquired Of
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the seventh year some elders come to inquire of the LORD (v. 1). God refuses: As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you (vv. 2-3). Instead Ezekiel is to confront them with the abominations of their fathers (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: God will not be consulted as an oracle by people who have not dealt with their idols.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, certain of the elders of Israel came to inquire of the LORD, and sat before me. And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel, and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD, Is it to inquire of me that you come? As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you. Will you judge them, son of man, will you judge them? Let them know the abominations of their fathers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, certain of the elders of Israel came to inquire of the LORD, and sat before me.

About eleven months after the temple vision (8:1), the elders are back at Ezekiel's door. They want to inquire of the LORD. They are not asking to repent. They want information — perhaps about when they will go home.

And the word of the LORD came to me:

"Son of man, speak to the elders of Israel, and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD, Is it to inquire of me that you come? As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you.

God refuses, with an oath. As in 14:3, they come with idols still in their hearts. God is not a fortune teller to be consulted by people who have no intention of obeying the answer.

That is a searching thought for anyone who prays for guidance. Do we want God's direction so that we can obey it, or only so that we can plan around it?

Will you judge them, son of man, will you judge them? Let them know the abominations of their fathers,

Instead of an answer, a history lesson. Let them know the abominations of their fathers. The elders want to talk about the future. God makes them face the past, because they are repeating it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–26 — Rebellion, and the Sake of His Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God recounts Israel's history. In Egypt he chose them and swore to bring them to a glorious land, and told them to cast away their idols, but they rebelled; yet he acted for the sake of my name (vv. 5-10). In the wilderness he gave them his statutes and Sabbaths, but they rebelled again; again he spared them for his name's sake (vv. 11-17). He warned their children, and they rebelled too (vv. 18-22). So he swore to scatter them, and gave them over to statutes that were not good, defiling them through their own offerings (vv. 23-26).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's whole history is a record of rebellion met by a patience grounded in God's concern for his own name.

verseByVerse.quote: and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day when I chose Israel, I swore to the offspring of the house of Jacob, making myself known to them in the land of Egypt; I swore to them, saying, I am the LORD your God. On that day I swore to them that I would bring them out of the land of Egypt into a land that I had searched out for them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the most glorious of all lands. And I said to them, 'Cast away the detestable things your eyes feast on, every one of you, and do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt; I am the LORD your God.' But they rebelled against me and were not willing to listen to me. None of them cast away the detestable things their eyes feasted on, nor did they forsake the idols of Egypt. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them and spend my anger against them in the midst of the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day when I chose Israel, I swore to the offspring of the house of Jacob, making myself known to them in the land of Egypt; I swore to them, saying, I am the LORD your God.

The story begins with grace. I chose Israel. I swore (the ESV notes, literally "I lifted my hand" — the gesture of an oath). I am the LORD your God. Before Israel did anything, God chose them and bound himself to them.

On that day I swore to them that I would bring them out of the land of Egypt into a land that I had searched out for them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the most glorious of all lands.

A land that I had searched out for them — God himself had scouted out the best place for his people. The most glorious of all lands. Every gift was prepared before they asked.

And I said to them, 'Cast away the detestable things your eyes feast on, every one of you, and do not defile yourselves with the idols of Egypt; I am the LORD your God.'

But they rebelled against me and were not willing to listen to me. None of them cast away the detestable things their eyes feasted on, nor did they forsake the idols of Egypt. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them and spend my anger against them in the midst of the land of Egypt.

This detail is not in the book of Exodus in so many words, but Joshua confirms it: Put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt (Josh 24:14). Israel carried Egypt's idols in their hearts even while God was bringing them out. The golden calf was not a sudden lapse; it was an old love.

Notice the phrase the detestable things your eyes feast on. Idolatry begins with the eyes, with what we keep looking at and longing for.

verseByVerse.quote: But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations among whom they lived, in whose sight I made myself known to them in bringing them out of the land of Egypt. So I led them out of the land of Egypt and brought them into the wilderness. I gave them my statutes and made known to them my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live. Moreover, I gave them my Sabbaths, as a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations among whom they lived, in whose sight I made myself known to them in bringing them out of the land of Egypt.

Here is the key phrase of the chapter, and it will come back four times: I acted for the sake of my name. Why did God not destroy Israel in Egypt? Not because they deserved mercy. Because his own name — his reputation, his glory among the nations — was at stake.

This is not vanity. God's name is his revealed character: faithful, gracious, true to his promises. If he had abandoned Israel, the nations would have concluded that he was weak or false. Moses argued exactly this on the mountain (Exod 32:12; Num 14:15-16). And it is the firmest ground of hope there is. Our salvation does not rest on our faithfulness, which fails, but on God's commitment to his own glory, which never does. For my name's sake I defer my anger... My glory I will not give to another (Isa 48:9, 11). Your sins are forgiven for his name's sake (1 John 2:12).

So I led them out of the land of Egypt and brought them into the wilderness.

Brought them into the wilderness. Freedom from Egypt did not lead straight into comfort. It led into a school. Moses told the next generation why: God led them in the wilderness that he might humble you, testing you to know what was in your heart, and to teach them that man does not live by bread alone (Deut 8:2-3). Many believers find that God brings them out of one bondage and then into a hard season. It is not abandonment. It is training.

I gave them my statutes and made known to them my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live.

At Sinai God gave his law, and it was a gift of life: if a person does them, he shall live (Lev 18:5). The law showed the way of life. But it also showed that no one walks that way perfectly. Paul quotes this very sentence to show that the law cannot save sinners: The one who does them shall live by them, but all who rely on works of the law are under a curse, and Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:10, 12-13). Christ is the one man who did them and lived, and he died for those who did not.

Moreover, I gave them my Sabbaths, as a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them.

The Sabbath was a weekly sign that Israel belonged to God and that he, not they, made them holy (Exod 31:13). Resting from work was a confession of dependence. And it pointed forward: there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, entered by those who rest from their own works (Heb 4:9-10).

Notice the purpose: that they might know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them. The Sabbath was not about earning holiness by resting correctly. It was a weekly reminder that God makes his people holy. For Christians, the Lord's Day carries the same gospel in a new form: we stop our work and gather, confessing that our standing with God rests on what Christ has finished.

verseByVerse.quote: But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness. They did not walk in my statutes but rejected my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; and my Sabbaths they greatly profaned. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them in the wilderness, to make a full end of them. But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out. Moreover, I swore to them in the wilderness that I would not bring them into the land that I had given them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the most glorious of all lands, because they rejected my rules and did not walk in my statutes, and profaned my Sabbaths; for their heart went after their idols. Nevertheless, my eye spared them, and I did not destroy them or make a full end of them in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the house of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness. They did not walk in my statutes but rejected my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; and my Sabbaths they greatly profaned. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them in the wilderness, to make a full end of them.

The second round. The same people who received the law at Sinai rejected it in the wilderness. They despised the very rules that would have given them life.

But I acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out.

Moreover, I swore to them in the wilderness that I would not bring them into the land that I had given them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the most glorious of all lands,

because they rejected my rules and did not walk in my statutes, and profaned my Sabbaths; for their heart went after their idols.

That generation did not enter the land; they died in the wilderness. And the root is named again: their heart went after their idols. Disobedience is always a matter of the heart's loves.

Nevertheless, my eye spared them, and I did not destroy them or make a full end of them in the wilderness.

Nevertheless. The judgment was real, but it was not total. God spared the nation, even as he disciplined a generation. Yet he saved them for his name's sake, that he might make known his mighty power (Ps 106:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "And I said to their children in the wilderness, 'Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers, nor keep their rules, nor defile yourselves with their idols. I am the LORD your God; walk in my statutes, and be careful to obey my rules, and keep my Sabbaths holy that they may be a sign between me and you, that you may know that I am the LORD your God.' But the children rebelled against me. They did not walk in my statutes and were not careful to obey my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; they profaned my Sabbaths. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them and spend my anger against them in the wilderness. But I withheld my hand and acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And I said to their children in the wilderness, 'Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers, nor keep their rules, nor defile yourselves with their idols.

I am the LORD your God; walk in my statutes, and be careful to obey my rules,

and keep my Sabbaths holy that they may be a sign between me and you, that you may know that I am the LORD your God.'

The third round: the next generation. God calls them to break with their parents — exactly the message of chapter 18. Do not walk in the statutes of your fathers. A new generation always has a chance to choose differently.

And notice what God calls the fathers' way of life: the statutes of your fathers and their rules. Human traditions can harden into a rival law. Jesus said to the religious leaders of his day, You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men (Mark 7:8). Every generation must test the customs it inherits against God's word.

But the children rebelled against me. They did not walk in my statutes and were not careful to obey my rules, by which, if a person does them, he shall live; they profaned my Sabbaths. "Then I said I would pour out my wrath upon them and spend my anger against them in the wilderness.

And they did not. At Baal of Peor, on the edge of the promised land, the people ate and bowed down to their gods (Num 25:2). Children repeated the sins of their parents.

But I withheld my hand and acted for the sake of my name, that it should not be profaned in the sight of the nations, in whose sight I had brought them out.

A third time: for the sake of my name. The pattern is relentless — rebellion, deserved wrath, mercy for his name's sake. If God's patience depended on Israel's goodness, there would have been no Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, I swore to them in the wilderness that I would scatter them among the nations and disperse them through the countries, because they had not obeyed my rules, but had rejected my statutes and profaned my Sabbaths, and their eyes were set on their fathers' idols. Moreover, I gave them statutes that were not good and rules by which they could not have life, and I defiled them through their very gifts in their offering up all their firstborn, that I might devastate them. I did it that they might know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moreover, I swore to them in the wilderness that I would scatter them among the nations and disperse them through the countries,

because they had not obeyed my rules, but had rejected my statutes and profaned my Sabbaths, and their eyes were set on their fathers' idols.

Already in the wilderness, God warned that persistent rebellion would end in scattering. The exile Ezekiel's hearers were living in had been announced centuries before.

Moreover, I gave them statutes that were not good and rules by which they could not have life,

and I defiled them through their very gifts in their offering up all their firstborn, that I might devastate them. I did it that they might know that I am the LORD.

These are hard verses, and they must be read with care. God is not saying that he commanded child sacrifice. Through Jeremiah he said of it, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind (Jer 7:31). He is saying that when his people rejected his good statutes, he handed them over to the evil customs they preferred.

This is judicial giving-over. So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels (Ps 81:12). God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven (Acts 7:42). God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts (Rom 1:24). It is a terrible judgment of God simply to let people have what they insist on. The statutes they chose instead of his were not good, and could not give life. They led to the horror of offering their own firstborn — and that horror itself became part of the judgment.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the land their fathers worshipped on every high hill (vv. 27-29). God asks the present generation whether they will do the same, still offering their children in fire (vv. 30-31). And he exposes their secret plan: Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone — it will never happen (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: God will not let his people dissolve into the world, even when they want to.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, son of man, speak to the house of Israel and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: In this also your fathers blasphemed me, by dealing treacherously with me. For when I had brought them into the land that I swore to give them, then wherever they saw any high hill or any leafy tree, there they offered their sacrifices and there they presented the provocation of their offering; there they sent up their pleasing aromas, and there they poured out their drink offerings. (I said to them, 'What is the high place to which you go?' So its name is called Bamah to this day.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore, son of man, speak to the house of Israel and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: In this also your fathers blasphemed me, by dealing treacherously with me.

For when I had brought them into the land that I swore to give them, then wherever they saw any high hill or any leafy tree, there they offered their sacrifices and there they presented the provocation of their offering; there they sent up their pleasing aromas, and there they poured out their drink offerings.

The fourth round is life in the land. God kept his oath and brought them in. And wherever they saw any high hill or any leafy tree, they worshipped there. Every beautiful place became a shrine to something other than God.

That is a picture of the human heart. We are worshippers by nature. If we do not worship the Creator, we will turn every good thing he made — beauty, pleasure, nature, success — into a god.

(I said to them, 'What is the high place to which you go?' So its name is called Bamah to this day.)

The ESV notes that Bamah means "high place". God asks a question that sounds almost weary: what is this high place you keep going to? The name stuck as a reminder of their unfaithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Will you defile yourselves after the manner of your fathers and go whoring after their detestable things? When you present your gifts and offer up your children in fire, you defile yourselves with all your idols to this day. And shall I be inquired of by you, O house of Israel? As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you. "What is in your mind shall never happen—the thought, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Will you defile yourselves after the manner of your fathers and go whoring after their detestable things?

Now the history lesson lands on the elders in the room. You have heard what your fathers did. Will you do the same?

When you present your gifts and offer up your children in fire, you defile yourselves with all your idols to this day. And shall I be inquired of by you, O house of Israel? As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I will not be inquired of by you.

To this day. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is "make your children pass through the fire". The same sins continue. And so the answer to their request is the same: I will not be inquired of by you.

"What is in your mind shall never happen—the thought, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone.'

Here is what was really in their hearts. Not repentance, but assimilation. Let us be like the nations. In exile, the easiest path was to blend in — adopt Babylon's gods, customs and values, and stop being different. It is the same wish Israel had when they demanded a king: that we also may be like all the nations (1 Sam 8:20).

And God says: What is in your mind shall never happen. He will not let his people dissolve into the world. That is both a rebuke and a mercy. Christians face the same pull. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Rom 12:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–44 — The Wilderness of the Peoples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you (v. 33). God will bring them out in a new exodus into the wilderness of the peoples and judge them face to face (vv. 34-36). He will make them pass under the rod, bring them into the covenant and purge the rebels (vv. 37-38). On his holy mountain all Israel will serve him, and he will accept them as a pleasing aroma (vv. 39-41). There they will remember their ways and loathe themselves, and know that he dealt with them for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways (vv. 42-44).
verseByVerse.theology: God's kingship will not let his people go; he purifies them and restores them by grace, not by their deserving.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I live, declares the Lord GOD, surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you. I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you out of the countries where you are scattered, with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out. And I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face. As I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will enter into judgment with you, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As I live, declares the Lord GOD, surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you.

Here is a striking sentence: I will be king over you. They wanted to be like the nations. God says: you are mine, and I will rule you, whether you like it or not.

With a mighty hand and an outstretched arm is the language of the exodus: I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment (Exod 6:6). But now added to it: with wrath poured out. God's kingship over his rebellious people will involve both rescue and discipline.

There is deep comfort here for anyone who belongs to God and is drifting. He will not let you go. His love is not a passive feeling. It is a King's determined claim.

I will bring you out from the peoples and gather you out of the countries where you are scattered, with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, and with wrath poured out.

And I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples, and there I will enter into judgment with you face to face.

As I entered into judgment with your fathers in the wilderness of the land of Egypt, so I will enter into judgment with you, declares the Lord GOD.

A new exodus. God will bring them out of the nations as he brought their fathers out of Egypt, and lead them into a new wilderness — the wilderness of the peoples — where he will meet them face to face, as at Sinai. The wilderness is a place of testing and sifting. Before the promised land, a reckoning.

Face to face. At Sinai the LORD spoke with you face to face at the mountain, out of the midst of the fire (Deut 5:4). Meeting God face to face is terrifying for rebels and glorious for the redeemed. For those in Christ, the promise is the second: now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face (1 Cor 13:12).

verseByVerse.quote: I will make you pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant. I will purge out the rebels from among you, and those who transgress against me. I will bring them out of the land where they sojourn, but they shall not enter the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will make you pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant.

A shepherd counted his sheep by making them pass one by one under his staff (Lev 27:32; Jer 33:13). God will do that with his people. Each one will be examined. Not one will be missed, and not one will slip through unexamined.

That is a picture of personal care as well as judgment. Jesus the Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out (John 10:3). And those who pass under his rod are brought into the bond of the covenant.

I will purge out the rebels from among you, and those who transgress against me. I will bring them out of the land where they sojourn, but they shall not enter the land of Israel. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

The rebels will be sifted out. They will leave Babylon, but they will not enter the land — just as the rebellious generation left Egypt and died in the wilderness. Being among God's people outwardly is not the same as belonging to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, O house of Israel, thus says the Lord GOD: Go serve every one of you his idols, now and hereafter, if you will not listen to me; but my holy name you shall no more profane with your gifts and your idols. "For on my holy mountain, the mountain height of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, there all the house of Israel, all of them, shall serve me in the land. There I will accept them, and there I will require your contributions and the choicest of your gifts, with all your sacred offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As for you, O house of Israel, thus says the Lord GOD: Go serve every one of you his idols, now and hereafter, if you will not listen to me; but my holy name you shall no more profane with your gifts and your idols.

A startling, ironic command: Go serve every one of you his idols. If you insist, go ahead — but stop pretending to worship me at the same time. What God hates most is a mixture: idols on Monday, the LORD's name on Sabbath. My holy name you shall no more profane.

Elijah put the same choice to Israel on Mount Carmel: How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him (1 Kgs 18:21). God would rather have honest rejection than a divided heart that uses his name as decoration. The worst place to stand is in between.

"For on my holy mountain, the mountain height of Israel, declares the Lord GOD, there all the house of Israel, all of them, shall serve me in the land. There I will accept them, and there I will require your contributions and the choicest of your gifts, with all your sacred offerings.

And then the promise. On my holy mountain... all the house of Israel, all of them, shall serve me. Not a divided worship, not a mixture, but whole-hearted service. There I will accept them. God, who refused to be inquired of at the start of the chapter, will accept his people's worship at the end.

All the house of Israel, all of them. The divided kingdoms of north and south will worship together again. Ezekiel will hear it more fully later: they shall be no longer two nations, and no longer divided into two kingdoms (37:22). God's restoration heals divisions among his people as well as their relationship with him.

verseByVerse.quote: As a pleasing aroma I will accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples and gather you out of the countries where you have been scattered. And I will manifest my holiness among you in the sight of the nations. And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I bring you into the land of Israel, the country that I swore to give to your fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As a pleasing aroma I will accept you, when I bring you out from the peoples and gather you out of the countries where you have been scattered. And I will manifest my holiness among you in the sight of the nations.

As a pleasing aroma I will accept you. Not only their offerings, but the people themselves, will be a fragrance to God. That is the language of acceptable sacrifice.

And I will manifest my holiness among you in the sight of the nations. The nations saw God's name profaned when Israel sinned and was scattered. They will see his holiness when he restores and purifies his people. The church's life is meant to do the same: let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven (Matt 5:16).

How can sinners become a pleasing aroma to God? Only through another. Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Eph 5:2). In him believers become the aroma of Christ to God (2 Cor 2:15), and offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Pet 2:5).

And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I bring you into the land of Israel, the country that I swore to give to your fathers.

I swore — again, literally "lifted my hand". The oath of verse 5 is kept. God's promises outlast every generation's rebellion.

verseByVerse.quote: And there you shall remember your ways and all your deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you shall loathe yourselves for all the evils that you have committed. And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I deal with you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways, nor according to your corrupt deeds, O house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there you shall remember your ways and all your deeds with which you have defiled yourselves, and you shall loathe yourselves for all the evils that you have committed.

Notice the order again. First God restores them; then they remember and loathe their sin. Repentance deepens after grace, not only before it. The more clearly a believer sees God's kindness, the more deeply he hates the sin that grace forgave.

And you shall know that I am the LORD, when I deal with you for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways, nor according to your corrupt deeds, O house of Israel, declares the Lord GOD."

And the chapter's refrain comes home: for my name's sake, not according to your evil ways. This is the gospel in one line. He does not deal with us according to our sins (Ps 103:10). For your name's sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt, for it is great (Ps 25:11). God saves sinners not because of anything in them but because of who he is.

If you are tempted to think your record is too bad for God, remember that his mercy has never been based on the record. It is based on his name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–49 — Fire in the Forest of the South
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel is told to preach against the forest of the south: God will kindle a fire that devours every green tree in you and every dry tree, and it will not be quenched (vv. 45-48). Ezekiel complains, They are saying of me, 'Is he not a maker of parables?' (v. 49).
verseByVerse.theology: God's judgment spares neither the green nor the dry, and dismissing the messenger as a storyteller does not stop the fire.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward the southland; preach against the south, and prophesy against the forest land in the Negeb. Say to the forest of the Negeb, Hear the word of the LORD: Thus says the Lord GOD, Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall devour every green tree in you and every dry tree. The blazing flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from south to north shall be scorched by it. All flesh shall see that I the LORD have kindled it; it shall not be quenched." Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! They are saying of me, 'Is he not a maker of parables?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the word of the LORD came to me:

The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible this begins chapter 21. It is a short parable that leads into the sword oracle that follows.

"Son of man, set your face toward the southland; preach against the south, and prophesy against the forest land in the Negeb.

Say to the forest of the Negeb, Hear the word of the LORD: Thus says the Lord GOD, Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it shall devour every green tree in you and every dry tree. The blazing flame shall not be quenched, and all faces from south to north shall be scorched by it.

All flesh shall see that I the LORD have kindled it; it shall not be quenched."

A forest fire that burns every green tree... and every dry tree. (The ESV notes that toward the southland may be "toward Teman".) Judgment will reach everyone — the living and flourishing as well as the withered. The fire will sweep through the whole land, from south to north.

Perhaps Jesus had this picture in mind when, carrying his cross, he told the weeping women of Jerusalem, if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry? (Luke 23:31). If the fire of God's judgment fell on him, the green and innocent tree, how much more will it fall on the dry and guilty — unless they shelter in him.

Then I said, "Ah, Lord GOD! They are saying of me, 'Is he not a maker of parables?'"

And Ezekiel's frustrated complaint. The people have found a way to dismiss him: he just tells stories. Entertaining, clever, not serious. They will say something similar later: you are to them like one who sings lustful songs with a beautiful voice (33:32).

That is still a way people avoid God's word. They enjoy the preacher, admire the illustrations, and go home unchanged. Jesus spoke in parables too (Matt 13:34), and many heard the stories and missed the King. The fire in the parable is no less real because it comes in a story.

20.title: For the Sake of My Name
20.overview:
In the seventh year some elders come to inquire of the LORD, and God refuses to be consulted by them. Instead Ezekiel is to make them face the abominations of their fathers (vv. 1-4).

God recounts Israel's history. In Egypt he chose them, swore to bring them to a glorious land and told them to throw away their idols, but they rebelled; yet he acted for the sake of his name. In the wilderness he gave them his life-giving statutes and his Sabbaths, but they rebelled again, and he spared them for his name's sake though that generation did not enter the land. He warned their children not to follow their fathers, but they rebelled too, and again he held back for his name's sake. He swore to scatter them and gave them over to statutes that were not good, defiling them through their own offerings (vv. 5-26).

In the land their fathers worshipped on every high hill. God asks the present generation whether they will do the same, and refuses to be inquired of by them. Their secret wish to be like the nations and worship wood and stone will never happen (vv. 27-32).

With a mighty hand and outstretched arm and wrath poured out, God will be king over them. He will bring them out of the nations into the wilderness of the peoples and judge them face to face, make them pass under the rod, bring them into the covenant and purge the rebels. On his holy mountain all Israel will serve him, and he will accept them as a pleasing aroma. There they will remember their ways and loathe themselves, and know that he dealt with them for his name's sake, not according to their evil ways (vv. 33-44).

Ezekiel is told to prophesy a fire that will burn every green and dry tree in the forest of the south, and he complains that people dismiss him as a maker of parables (vv. 45-49).
20.theology:
God will not be consulted as an oracle by people unwilling to give up their idols (vv. 3, 31).

Israel's history shows persistent rebellion from Egypt onward, rooted in hearts and eyes set on idols (vv. 7-8, 16, 24).

God's patience and mercy rest on the glory of his own name, which is the firmest ground of hope for sinners (vv. 9, 14, 22, 44; Isa 48:9-11; Ps 106:8; 1 John 2:12).

God's law is good and life-giving, but sinners cannot gain life by it; Christ bore its curse (vv. 11, 13, 21; Lev 18:5; Gal 3:10-13).

When people persistently reject God's ways, he may give them over to the destructive ways they prefer (vv. 25-26; Ps 81:11-12; Acts 7:42; Rom 1:24).

God will not let his people dissolve into the world; as King he sifts, purifies and restores them (vv. 32-38; Rom 12:2; John 10:3).

God accepts his people as a pleasing aroma through the sacrifice of Christ, and deals with them by grace, not by their deeds (vv. 41, 44; Eph 5:2; 2 Cor 2:15; Ps 103:10).

Repentance deepens after grace (v. 43).
20.examples:
Elders who wanted a forecast, and got a history lesson.

A land God scouted out in advance for his people.

Egypt's idols packed in the luggage of the exodus.

Mercy, four times over, for the sake of his name.

Let us be like the nations — and God says: never.

Sheep counted one by one under the shepherd's staff.

A preacher dismissed as a teller of stories.

21.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem and preach against the sanctuaries. Prophesy against the land of Israel<sup>3</sup>and say to the land of Israel, Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am against you and will draw my sword from its sheath and will cut off from you both righteous and wicked.<sup>4</sup>Because I will cut off from you both righteous and wicked, therefore my sword shall be drawn from its sheath against all flesh from south to north.<sup>5</sup>And all flesh shall know that I am the LORD. I have drawn my sword from its sheath; it shall not be sheathed again.<sup>6</sup>"As for you, son of man, groan; with breaking heart and bitter grief, groan before their eyes.<sup>7</sup>And when they say to you, 'Why do you groan?' you shall say, 'Because of the news that it is coming. Every heart will melt, and all hands will be feeble; every spirit will faint, and all knees will be weak as water. Behold, it is coming, and it will be fulfilled,'" declares the Lord GOD.<sup>8</sup>And the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>9</sup>"Son of man, prophesy and say, Thus says the Lord, say: "A sword, a sword is sharpened and also polished,<sup>10</sup>sharpened for slaughter, polished to flash like lightning! (Or shall we rejoice? You have despised the rod, my son, with everything of wood.)<sup>11</sup>So the sword is given to be polished, that it may be grasped in the hand. It is sharpened and polished to be given into the hand of the slayer.<sup>12</sup>Cry out and wail, son of man, for it is against my people. It is against all the princes of Israel. They are delivered over to the sword with my people. Strike therefore upon your thigh.<sup>13</sup>For it will not be a testing—what could it do if you despise the rod?" declares the Lord GOD.<sup>14</sup>"As for you, son of man, prophesy. Clap your hands and let the sword come down twice, yes, three times, the sword for those to be slain. It is the sword for the great slaughter, which surrounds them,<sup>15</sup>that their hearts may melt, and many stumble. At all their gates I have given the glittering sword. Ah, it is made like lightning; it is taken up for slaughter.<sup>16</sup>Cut sharply to the right; set yourself to the left, wherever your face is directed.<sup>17</sup>I also will clap my hands, and I will satisfy my fury; I the LORD have spoken."<sup>18</sup>The word of the LORD came to me again:<sup>19</sup>"As for you, son of man, mark two ways for the sword of the king of Babylon to come. Both of them shall come from the same land. And make a signpost; make it at the head of the way to a city.<sup>20</sup>Mark a way for the sword to come to Rabbah of the Ammonites and to Judah, into Jerusalem the fortified.<sup>21</sup>For the king of Babylon stands at the parting of the way, at the head of the two ways, to use divination. He shakes the arrows; he consults the teraphim; he looks at the liver.<sup>22</sup>Into his right hand comes the divination for Jerusalem, to set battering rams, to open the mouth with murder, to lift up the voice with shouting, to set battering rams against the gates, to cast up mounds, to build siege towers.<sup>23</sup>But to them it will seem like a false divination. They have sworn solemn oaths, but he brings their guilt to remembrance, that they may be taken.<sup>24</sup>"Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you have made your guilt to be remembered, in that your transgressions are uncovered, so that in all your deeds your sins appear—because you have come to remembrance, you shall be taken in hand.<sup>25</sup>And you, O profane wicked one, prince of Israel, whose day has come, the time of your final punishment,<sup>26</sup>thus says the Lord GOD: Remove the turban and take off the crown. Things shall not remain as they are. Exalt that which is low, and bring low that which is exalted.<sup>27</sup>A ruin, ruin, ruin I will make it. This also shall not be, until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs, and I will give it to him.<sup>28</sup>"And you, son of man, prophesy, and say, Thus says the Lord GOD concerning the Ammonites and concerning their reproach; say, A sword, a sword is drawn for the slaughter. It is polished to consume and to flash like lightning—<sup>29</sup>while they see for you false visions, while they divine lies for you—to place you on the necks of the profane wicked, whose day has come, the time of their final punishment.<sup>30</sup>Return it to its sheath. In the place where you were created, in the land of your origin, I will judge you.<sup>31</sup>And I will pour out my indignation upon you; I will blow upon you with the fire of my wrath, and I will deliver you into the hands of brutish men, skillful to destroy.<sup>32</sup>You shall be fuel for the fire. Your blood shall be in the midst of the land. You shall be no more remembered, for I the LORD have spoken."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel is to prophesy against Jerusalem and its sanctuaries (vv. 1-2): Behold, I am against you and will draw my sword from its sheath and will cut off from you both righteous and wicked (v. 3). The sword will not be sheathed again (vv. 4-5). Ezekiel must groan with a breaking heart before the people, and when they ask why, he must say that the news is coming and every heart will melt (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: When God's judgment falls on a nation, it touches everyone in it, and the messenger feels it first.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem and preach against the sanctuaries. Prophesy against the land of Israel and say to the land of Israel, Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am against you and will draw my sword from its sheath and will cut off from you both righteous and wicked. Because I will cut off from you both righteous and wicked, therefore my sword shall be drawn from its sheath against all flesh from south to north. And all flesh shall know that I am the LORD. I have drawn my sword from its sheath; it shall not be sheathed again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to me:

(The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible this is 21:6; the preceding parable of the forest fire opens the chapter there. The fire of 20:45-49 now becomes a sword.)

"Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem and preach against the sanctuaries. Prophesy against the land of Israel

and say to the land of Israel, Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am against you and will draw my sword from its sheath and will cut off from you both righteous and wicked.

The parable of the fire is decoded. The forest is Jerusalem; the fire is a sword; and the sword is God's own: my sword.

And a hard phrase: both righteous and wicked. Does that contradict chapter 18, where God said the righteous shall live? No. Chapter 18 speaks of each person's final standing before God.
