But righteous men shall pass judgment on them with the sentence of adulteresses, and with the sentence of women who shed blood, because they are adulteresses, and blood is on their hands.

Righteous men shall pass judgment. Even by ordinary standards of justice, the verdict is obvious: adultery and bloodshed. The sisters are condemned not only by God's holiness but by any honest court.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the Lord GOD: "Bring up a vast host against them, and make them an object of terror and a plunder. And the host shall stone them and cut them down with their swords. They shall kill their sons and their daughters, and burn up their houses. Thus will I put an end to lewdness in the land, that all women may take warning and not commit lewdness as you have done. And they shall return your lewdness upon you, and you shall bear the penalty for your sinful idolatry, and you shall know that I am the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For thus says the Lord GOD: "Bring up a vast host against them, and make them an object of terror and a plunder.

And the host shall stone them and cut them down with their swords. They shall kill their sons and their daughters, and burn up their houses.

The sentence for adultery and murder under the law was death. The allegory becomes history: armies, swords, burning houses.

Thus will I put an end to lewdness in the land, that all women may take warning and not commit lewdness as you have done.

That all women may take warning. In the allegory the women are nations and cities. Samaria and Jerusalem are meant to be a warning to every people. And the New Testament says their story was written for our instruction (1 Cor 10:11). The church, the bride of Christ, must learn from the sisters. John saw the final form of unfaithfulness in the great prostitute... with whom the kings of the earth have committed sexual immorality (Rev 17:1-2).

And they shall return your lewdness upon you, and you shall bear the penalty for your sinful idolatry, and you shall know that I am the Lord GOD."

And the chapter ends where the prophets always end: you shall know that I am the Lord GOD.

Ezekiel 23 is a hard chapter to read aloud. But it shows how seriously God takes spiritual faithfulness. His people are a bride, and he is a faithful husband. And the gospel shows how far that husband went: Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her... so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:25-27). The unfaithful sisters drank their cup. The faithful Bridegroom drank it for his bride.

23.title: Two Sisters
23.overview:
Ezekiel tells of two sisters who were unfaithful from their youth in Egypt: Oholah, who is Samaria, and Oholibah, who is Jerusalem. Both became God's and bore him children (vv. 1-4).

Oholah lusted after the splendid officers of Assyria, defiled herself with their idols and never left the unfaithfulness she began in Egypt. So God handed her over to the Assyrians, who stripped her, took her children, killed her and made her a byword (vv. 5-10).

Oholibah saw her sister's fate and became worse. She lusted after Assyria, then fell for painted images of Babylonian officers and sent for them. When they defiled her she turned from them in disgust, and God turned from her in disgust. Yet she returned to the lusts of her youth in Egypt (vv. 11-21).

So God will bring the lovers she rejected against her from every side. In his jealousy they will mutilate her, take her children, strip her and end her unfaithfulness. She will be handed to those she hates and drink her sister's cup of horror and desolation to the dregs, because she forgot God and cast him behind her back (vv. 22-35).

God declares the sisters' abominations: idolatry and bloodshed, even sacrificing their children and entering God's sanctuary on the same day. They dressed up for foreign envoys and set God's incense and oil before them. Righteous men will judge them as adulteresses and murderers; a host will stone them and burn their houses, as a warning to all, and they will know that he is the Lord GOD (vv. 36-49).
23.theology:
God's people were unfaithful from the beginning, yet he made them his own; their idolatry is a betrayal of grace (vv. 3-4; 20:7-8).

Political alliances and admiration for worldly power led to adopting the gods of the nations (vv. 5-7, 12-16; 2 Kgs 15:19; 16:7-8; 20:12-17).

Seeing God's judgment on others increases responsibility (v. 11; Jer 3:6-8).

Idols follow a cycle of attraction, indulgence and disgust, and the heart that will not turn to God goes back to older idols (vv. 17-21; 1 John 2:15-17).

The powers courted instead of God become the instruments of judgment (vv. 9, 22-24, 28).

Worship alongside idolatry and cruelty is profanation (vv. 38-39; Jer 7:9-10).

The cup of God's wrath passes from sister to sister, and Christ drank it for his bride (vv. 31-34; Isa 51:17, 22; Mark 14:36; Eph 5:25-27).
23.examples:
Two sisters who both became his.

Purple uniforms and fine horses.

Falling in love with a painting on a wall.

Watching your sister fall and walking the same road.

A child sacrificed in the morning, temple worship in the afternoon.

God's incense set on the table for foreign guests.

A cup drained to its broken pieces.

24.text: <sup>1</sup>In the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, write down the name of this day, this very day. The king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem this very day.<sup>3</sup>And utter a parable to the rebellious house and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Set on the pot, set it on; pour in water also;<sup>4</sup>put in it the pieces of meat, all the good pieces, the thigh and the shoulder; fill it with choice bones.<sup>5</sup>Take the choicest one of the flock; pile the logs under it; boil it well; seethe also its bones in it.<sup>6</sup>"Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose corrosion is in it, and whose corrosion has not gone out of it! Take out of it piece after piece, without making any choice.<sup>7</sup>For the blood she has shed is in her midst; she put it on the bare rock; she did not pour it out on the ground to cover it with dust.<sup>8</sup>To rouse my wrath, to take vengeance, I have set on the bare rock the blood she has shed, that it may not be covered.<sup>9</sup>Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Woe to the bloody city! I also will make the pile great.<sup>10</sup>Heap on the logs, kindle the fire, boil the meat well, mix in the spices, and let the bones be burned up.<sup>11</sup>Then set it empty upon the coals, that it may become hot, and its copper may burn, that its uncleanness may be melted in it, its corrosion consumed.<sup>12</sup>She has wearied herself with toil; its abundant corrosion does not go out of it. Into the fire with its corrosion!<sup>13</sup>On account of your unclean lewdness, because I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed from your uncleanness, you shall not be cleansed anymore till I have satisfied my fury upon you.<sup>14</sup>I am the LORD. I have spoken; it shall come to pass; I will do it. I will not go back; I will not spare; I will not relent; according to your ways and your deeds you will be judged, declares the Lord GOD."<sup>15</sup>The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>16</sup>"Son of man, behold, I am about to take the delight of your eyes away from you at a stroke; yet you shall not mourn or weep, nor shall your tears run down.<sup>17</sup>Sigh, but not aloud; make no mourning for the dead. Bind on your turban, and put your shoes on your feet; do not cover your lips, nor eat the bread of men."<sup>18</sup>So I spoke to the people in the morning, and at evening my wife died. And on the next morning I did as I was commanded.<sup>19</sup>And the people said to me, "Will you not tell us what these things mean for us, that you are acting thus?"<sup>20</sup>Then I said to them, "The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>21</sup>'Say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the delight of your eyes, and the yearning of your soul, and your sons and your daughters whom you left behind shall fall by the sword.<sup>22</sup>And you shall do as I have done; you shall not cover your lips, nor eat the bread of men.<sup>23</sup>Your turbans shall be on your heads and your shoes on your feet; you shall not mourn or weep, but you shall rot away in your iniquities and groan to one another.<sup>24</sup>Thus shall Ezekiel be to you a sign; according to all that he has done you shall do. When this comes, then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.'<sup>25</sup>"As for you, son of man, surely on the day when I take from them their stronghold, their joy and glory, the delight of their eyes and their soul's desire, and also their sons and daughters,<sup>26</sup>on that day a fugitive will come to you to report to you the news.<sup>27</sup>On that day your mouth will be opened to the fugitive, and you shall speak and be no longer mute. So you will be a sign to them, and they will know that I am the LORD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Pot on the Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Son of man, write down the name of this day, this very day. The king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem this very day (vv. 1-2). Ezekiel tells a parable: a pot full of the choicest meat, boiled hard (vv. 3-5). Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose corrosion is in it (v. 6). The blood she shed lies uncovered on bare rock, crying out (vv. 7-8). God will heap on logs until the meat is burned and the empty pot glows to burn out its corrosion (vv. 9-12). I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed; now God will not relent (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: When people refuse God's cleansing, his fire must do what his mercy was not allowed to do.

verseByVerse.quote: In the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, write down the name of this day, this very day. The king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem this very day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me:

"Son of man, write down the name of this day, this very day. The king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem this very day.

This is an extraordinary moment. Ezekiel is in Babylon, hundreds of miles from Jerusalem, with no news service. And God tells him: write down today's date. The king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem this very day.

And the historical record matches it exactly: in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with all his army against Jerusalem and laid siege to it (2 Kgs 25:1; Jer 52:4).

Why write it down? So that when the news finally arrived months later, the exiles would know that Ezekiel had known it on the day. The written date would be proof that his words came from God. For years they had doubted him. Now the siege he had acted out with a brick (4:1-3) had begun.

God knows what is happening in every place at every moment. Nothing takes him by surprise, and he can reveal it when he chooses.

verseByVerse.quote: And utter a parable to the rebellious house and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Set on the pot, set it on; pour in water also; put in it the pieces of meat, all the good pieces, the thigh and the shoulder; fill it with choice bones. Take the choicest one of the flock; pile the logs under it; boil it well; seethe also its bones in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And utter a parable to the rebellious house and say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Set on the pot, set it on; pour in water also;

put in it the pieces of meat, all the good pieces, the thigh and the shoulder; fill it with choice bones.

Take the choicest one of the flock; pile the logs under it; boil it well; seethe also its bones in it.

It sounds like a cooking song — set on the pot, add water, put in the best cuts, pile on the logs, boil it well. (The ESV notes that the logs follows verse 10; the Hebrew reads "the bones".)

Remember the proud slogan of Jerusalem's leaders: This city is the cauldron, and we are the meat (11:3). They thought the pot protected them. God takes their own picture and turns it. Yes, you are in the pot. And now the fire is lit.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose corrosion is in it, and whose corrosion has not gone out of it! Take out of it piece after piece, without making any choice. For the blood she has shed is in her midst; she put it on the bare rock; she did not pour it out on the ground to cover it with dust. To rouse my wrath, to take vengeance, I have set on the bare rock the blood she has shed, that it may not be covered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Woe to the bloody city, to the pot whose corrosion is in it, and whose corrosion has not gone out of it! Take out of it piece after piece, without making any choice.

Now the parable darkens. The pot is corroded, rusted through, and the rust has never been cleaned out. Jerusalem is the bloody city (22:2), and its corruption is baked in.

Take out of it piece after piece, without making any choice. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is "no lot has fallen upon it". No one is selected to be spared. The meat is pulled out piece by piece, without distinction. The choice cuts who thought they were safe are dumped out with the rest.

For the blood she has shed is in her midst; she put it on the bare rock; she did not pour it out on the ground to cover it with dust.

The law required that the blood of an animal killed for food be poured out and covered with earth (Lev 17:13). Blood left in the open cried out. The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground, God said to Cain (Gen 4:10). Jerusalem did not even try to hide her bloodshed. She left it on bare rock, in plain view.

To rouse my wrath, to take vengeance, I have set on the bare rock the blood she has shed, that it may not be covered.

And God says: then I will leave it there. That it may not be covered. Job cried, O earth, cover not my blood, and let my cry find no resting place (Job 16:18). Innocent blood that is not covered keeps crying for justice.

There is only one blood that can cover sin, and it cries out for something else. We have come to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Heb 12:24). Abel's blood cried for vengeance. Christ's blood cries for mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Woe to the bloody city! I also will make the pile great. Heap on the logs, kindle the fire, boil the meat well, mix in the spices, and let the bones be burned up. Then set it empty upon the coals, that it may become hot, and its copper may burn, that its uncleanness may be melted in it, its corrosion consumed. She has wearied herself with toil; its abundant corrosion does not go out of it. Into the fire with its corrosion!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Woe to the bloody city! I also will make the pile great.

Heap on the logs, kindle the fire, boil the meat well, mix in the spices, and let the bones be burned up.

I also will make the pile great. God himself stokes the fire. The meat is boiled until even the bones burn. (The ESV notes that mix in the spices may be read "empty out the broth".)

Then set it empty upon the coals, that it may become hot, and its copper may burn, that its uncleanness may be melted in it, its corrosion consumed.

And then the empty pot itself is set on the coals until the metal glows and the rust burns away. The city will be emptied of its people, and then the empty city will be burned to purge its corruption.

She has wearied herself with toil; its abundant corrosion does not go out of it. Into the fire with its corrosion!

She has wearied herself with toil (the ESV notes that the meaning is uncertain) — perhaps all the effort to scrub the pot has failed. The corrosion is too deep. Reforms had come and gone. Josiah had cleaned the temple. It had not lasted. Only fire could remove it.

verseByVerse.quote: On account of your unclean lewdness, because I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed from your uncleanness, you shall not be cleansed anymore till I have satisfied my fury upon you. I am the LORD. I have spoken; it shall come to pass; I will do it. I will not go back; I will not spare; I will not relent; according to your ways and your deeds you will be judged, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On account of your unclean lewdness, because I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed from your uncleanness, you shall not be cleansed anymore till I have satisfied my fury upon you.

Here is the heartbreaking sentence at the centre of the chapter: I would have cleansed you and you were not cleansed. God wanted to clean them. Through prophet after prophet he offered cleansing. They refused.

Jesus said the same over the same city: How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! (Matt 23:37). The tragedy of judgment is not that God was unwilling to save, but that people were unwilling to be saved.

I am the LORD. I have spoken; it shall come to pass; I will do it. I will not go back; I will not spare; I will not relent; according to your ways and your deeds you will be judged, declares the Lord GOD."

Six short sentences, like hammer blows: I have spoken... it shall come to pass... I will do it. I will not go back; I will not spare; I will not relent. There comes a point when the time for turning is over. Today, while God still offers to cleanse, is the time to let him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–27 — The Delight of Your Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Ezekiel he will take the delight of your eyes at a stroke, but he must not mourn publicly (vv. 15-17). So I spoke to the people in the morning, and at evening my wife died. And on the next morning I did as I was commanded (v. 18). When the people ask why, he explains: God will profane his sanctuary, the delight of their eyes, and their children will fall; they too will be too stunned to mourn (vv. 19-24). On that day a fugitive will bring the news, and Ezekiel's mouth will be opened (vv. 25-27).
verseByVerse.theology: Ezekiel's personal grief became a sign of the nation's loss, and his costly obedience points to the God who gave up the delight of his heart.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, behold, I am about to take the delight of your eyes away from you at a stroke; yet you shall not mourn or weep, nor shall your tears run down. Sigh, but not aloud; make no mourning for the dead. Bind on your turban, and put your shoes on your feet; do not cover your lips, nor eat the bread of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to me:

"Son of man, behold, I am about to take the delight of your eyes away from you at a stroke; yet you shall not mourn or weep, nor shall your tears run down.

Now come deeply personal words. The delight of your eyes — Ezekiel's wife. We learn almost nothing else about her, but this phrase tells us everything that matters: he loved her. She was the joy of his life. And God tells him she will die at a stroke, suddenly.

And he must not mourn. No weeping, no tears.

Sigh, but not aloud; make no mourning for the dead. Bind on your turban, and put your shoes on your feet; do not cover your lips, nor eat the bread of men."

The mourning customs of the day — taking off the turban, going barefoot, covering the lips, eating the meal that neighbours brought — are all forbidden. He may sigh, but not aloud. He must grieve silently, inwardly, and go about as normal.

We should be careful here. This does not teach that Christians must not grieve. Jesus wept at the grave of his friend (John 11:35). Paul does not tell believers not to grieve, but not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess 4:13). Ezekiel's case was unique. His silent grief was to be a sign.

verseByVerse.quote: So I spoke to the people in the morning, and at evening my wife died. And on the next morning I did as I was commanded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I spoke to the people in the morning, and at evening my wife died. And on the next morning I did as I was commanded.

Read this verse slowly. It is deeply moving, and it is told with almost no emotion at all.

In the morning Ezekiel preached. At evening my wife died. On the next morning I did as I was commanded.

He did not argue. He did not walk away from his calling. With his heart broken, he got up the next morning, put on his turban and his shoes, and obeyed. This is what it cost to be God's messenger to a rebellious people.

Few of us will ever be asked for anything like this. But every servant of Christ is called to love him more than even the dearest things in life: Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matt 10:37). Ezekiel's obedience was not coldness. It was love for God that held firm when everything in him was breaking.

And his loss points beyond himself. There was a Father who gave up the delight of his eyes. This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased (Matt 3:17), and He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom 8:32). God knows from the inside what it is to lose the one he loves.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people said to me, "Will you not tell us what these things mean for us, that you are acting thus?" Then I said to them, "The word of the LORD came to me: 'Say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the delight of your eyes, and the yearning of your soul, and your sons and your daughters whom you left behind shall fall by the sword. And you shall do as I have done; you shall not cover your lips, nor eat the bread of men. Your turbans shall be on your heads and your shoes on your feet; you shall not mourn or weep, but you shall rot away in your iniquities and groan to one another. Thus shall Ezekiel be to you a sign; according to all that he has done you shall do. When this comes, then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the people said to me, "Will you not tell us what these things mean for us, that you are acting thus?"

The people are puzzled. His wife has died, and he is not mourning. What these things mean for us. They sense that his strange behaviour is a message.

Then I said to them, "The word of the LORD came to me:

'Say to the house of Israel, Thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the delight of your eyes, and the yearning of your soul, and your sons and your daughters whom you left behind shall fall by the sword.

Now the meaning. The temple is the delight of your eyes — the very same phrase used of Ezekiel's wife. What his wife was to him, the temple was to them. God will take it, and their children left behind in Jerusalem will die.

There is a warning here too. The people loved the temple — the pride of your power — more than the God of the temple. It had become their security and their idol. A psalmist could say, One thing have I asked of the LORD... that I may dwell in the house of the LORD... to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD (Ps 27:4). It was the LORD's beauty he sought, not the building's. When a sacred place becomes the delight of our eyes instead of God himself, he may take it away.

And you shall do as I have done; you shall not cover your lips, nor eat the bread of men.

Your turbans shall be on your heads and your shoes on your feet; you shall not mourn or weep, but you shall rot away in your iniquities and groan to one another.

Why will they not mourn? Because the disaster will be so overwhelming that ordinary mourning will be impossible. They will be numb, stunned, beyond ritual. They will simply rot away in your iniquities and groan to one another.

Thus shall Ezekiel be to you a sign; according to all that he has done you shall do. When this comes, then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.'

Ezekiel... a sign. His marriage, his loss and his silence all became the message. The prophet's life and the prophet's word were one.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, son of man, surely on the day when I take from them their stronghold, their joy and glory, the delight of their eyes and their soul's desire, and also their sons and daughters, on that day a fugitive will come to you to report to you the news. On that day your mouth will be opened to the fugitive, and you shall speak and be no longer mute. So you will be a sign to them, and they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As for you, son of man, surely on the day when I take from them their stronghold, their joy and glory, the delight of their eyes and their soul's desire, and also their sons and daughters,

on that day a fugitive will come to you to report to you the news.

On that day your mouth will be opened to the fugitive, and you shall speak and be no longer mute. So you will be a sign to them, and they will know that I am the LORD."

Their stronghold, joy and glory, delight, desire, their children — all will go. And when the news reaches Babylon, Ezekiel's long muteness (3:26) will end.

It happened just as God said: a fugitive from Jerusalem came to me and said, "The city has been struck down", and my mouth was opened, and I was no longer mute (33:21-22).

This chapter is a turning point in the book. Chapters 1-24 have been almost entirely judgment on Jerusalem. The next chapters turn to the nations, and then, once the city has fallen, Ezekiel's opened mouth will speak words of astonishing hope: a new shepherd, a new heart, dry bones living, a new temple. The silence of grief gives way to the voice of restoration.

24.title: The Delight of Your Eyes
24.overview:
On the day the king of Babylon began the siege of Jerusalem, God tells Ezekiel in Babylon to write down the date. Then Ezekiel tells a parable: a pot full of the choicest meat, boiled hard. Woe to the bloody city, the corroded pot. The meat will be taken out without distinction. Her bloodshed lies uncovered on bare rock, crying out, and God leaves it uncovered to rouse his wrath. He will heap on the logs until the bones burn, and then set the empty pot on the coals to burn away its corrosion. God would have cleansed her, but she was not cleansed; now he will not relent, and she will be judged by her ways (vv. 1-14).

God tells Ezekiel that he will take away the delight of his eyes at a stroke, and that he must not mourn aloud or follow the customs of grief. Ezekiel preaches in the morning; in the evening his wife dies; and the next morning he obeys. When the people ask what this means, he tells them that God will profane his sanctuary, the delight of their eyes, and their children will die; they too will be too overwhelmed to mourn, and will waste away in their sins. Ezekiel is a sign to them. On the day the city falls a fugitive will bring the news, and Ezekiel's mouth will be opened (vv. 15-27).
24.theology:
God knows and can reveal events far away at the moment they happen; his word is proven by its fulfilment (vv. 1-2; 2 Kgs 25:1).

False security in a privileged place gives no protection when God judges (vv. 3-6; 11:3).

Blood shed unjustly cries out to God; only the blood of Christ speaks a better word (vv. 7-8; Gen 4:10; Heb 12:24).

God offers cleansing, and judgment falls when it is refused (v. 13; Matt 23:37).

God may call his servants to costly obedience, and their lives can become a message (vv. 15-18, 24; Matt 10:37).

Grief is not condemned, but believers do not grieve without hope (John 11:35; 1 Thess 4:13).

Sacred places can become idols; God may take away what we love more than him (vv. 21, 25; Ps 27:4).

The prophet's loss points to the Father who gave up his beloved Son (Matt 3:17; Rom 8:32).
24.examples:
A date written down in Babylon on the day the siege began.

A rusty pot that no scrubbing could clean.

Blood left on bare rock, still crying.

I would have cleansed you.

A sermon in the morning, a death at evening, obedience the next day.

A turban tied on over a broken heart.

A mouth that will open when the news arrives.

And I will cut you off from the peoples and will make you perish out of the countries; I will destroy you. Then they will know that I am the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"Thus says the Lord GOD: Because Edom acted revengefully against the house of Judah and has grievously offended in taking vengeance on them,<sup>13</sup>therefore thus says the Lord GOD, I will stretch out my hand against Edom and cut off from it man and beast. And I will make it desolate; from Teman even to Dedan they shall fall by the sword.<sup>14</sup>And I will lay my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel, and they shall do in Edom according to my anger and according to my wrath, and they shall know my vengeance, declares the Lord GOD.<sup>15</sup>"Thus says the Lord GOD: Because the Philistines acted revengefully and took vengeance with malice of soul to destroy in never-ending enmity,<sup>16</sup>therefore thus says the Lord GOD, Behold, I will stretch out my hand against the Philistines, and I will cut off the Cherethites and destroy the rest of the seacoast.<sup>17</sup>I will execute great vengeance on them with wrathful rebukes. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I lay my vengeance upon them."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ammon said Aha! when God's sanctuary was profaned, the land made desolate and Judah exiled (vv. 1-3), and clapped and stamped with malice (v. 6). So God will hand Ammon to the people of the East, make Rabbah a pasture for camels, and cut Ammon off (vv. 4-5, 7).
verseByVerse.theology: To gloat over the judgment of God's people is to invite God's judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward the Ammonites and prophesy against them. Say to the Ammonites, Hear the word of the Lord GOD: Thus says the Lord GOD, Because you said, 'Aha!' over my sanctuary when it was profaned, and over the land of Israel when it was made desolate, and over the house of Judah when they went into exile, therefore behold, I am handing you over to the people of the East for a possession, and they shall set their encampments among you and make their dwellings in your midst. They shall eat your fruit, and they shall drink your milk. I will make Rabbah a pasture for camels and Ammon a fold for flocks. Then you will know that I am the LORD. For thus says the Lord GOD: Because you have clapped your hands and stamped your feet and rejoiced with all the malice within your soul against the land of Israel, therefore, behold, I have stretched out my hand against you, and will hand you over as plunder to the nations. And I will cut you off from the peoples and will make you perish out of the countries; I will destroy you. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With chapter 25 the book turns. For twenty-four chapters Ezekiel has spoken against Jerusalem. The siege has now begun (24:1-2), and the prophet's mouth is closed toward his own people until the city falls. In the meantime God speaks about the nations around Israel. The message is plain: the God who judges his own people does not ignore the sins of their neighbours. And judgment on the nations is also a promise to Israel — her enemies will not have the last word.

Say to the Ammonites, Hear the word of the Lord GOD: Thus says the Lord GOD, Because you said, 'Aha!' over my sanctuary when it was profaned, and over the land of Israel when it was made desolate, and over the house of Judah when they went into exile,

Ammon's sin was one word: Aha! A sneer of satisfaction at someone else's ruin. When Jerusalem's temple was desecrated and its people marched away, Ammon cheered.

Notice what God calls the temple: my sanctuary. He had judged it himself. But that did not give anyone else the right to rejoice. Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the LORD see it and be displeased (Prov 24:17-18). God's discipline of his people is his business, and those who enjoy it will face him.

therefore behold, I am handing you over to the people of the East for a possession... I will make Rabbah a pasture for camels and Ammon a fold for flocks. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

Rabbah, the capital, will become grazing ground for desert tribes' camels. The mocker will be mocked.

For thus says the Lord GOD: Because you have clapped your hands and stamped your feet and rejoiced with all the malice within your soul against the land of Israel, therefore, behold, I have stretched out my hand against you... I will destroy you. Then you will know that I am the LORD.

Clapped your hands and stamped your feet. The same gestures Ezekiel had made in grief (6:11), Ammon made in glee. And the root is named: all the malice within your soul.

This is a warning for anyone who enjoys the downfall of others — a rival's scandal, an opponent's failure, the collapse of a church we disagreed with. God promised Abraham, him who dishonors you I will curse (Gen 12:3). Christians are called to weep with those who weep, even when those who weep brought it on themselves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — Moab: Like All the Other Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab (with Seir) said, Behold, the house of Judah is like all the other nations (v. 8). God will open Moab's frontier cities to invaders and judge it, Then they will know that I am the LORD (vv. 9-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who deny that God's people are his will learn that he is the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: Because Moab and Seir said, 'Behold, the house of Judah is like all the other nations,' therefore I will lay open the flank of Moab from the cities, from its cities on its frontier, the glory of the country, Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim. I will give it along with the Ammonites to the people of the East as a possession, that the Ammonites may be remembered no more among the nations, and I will execute judgments upon Moab. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the Lord GOD: Because Moab and Seir said, 'Behold, the house of Judah is like all the other nations,'

Moab's sin was different. (The ESV notes that the Septuagint lacks and Seir.) Moab said: Judah is nothing special. Like all the other nations. Its God is no different from our gods; its fall proves it.

That was an attack on God's name, not only on Judah. Israel's whole identity was that the LORD had chosen them. To say they were just like everyone else was to say the LORD was just like every other god.

therefore I will lay open the flank of Moab from the cities, from its cities on its frontier, the glory of the country, Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim.

I will give it along with the Ammonites to the people of the East as a possession, that the Ammonites may be remembered no more among the nations, and I will execute judgments upon Moab. Then they will know that I am the LORD.

Moab's proud frontier towns — the glory of the country — will be opened like a wound in the side. And Moab will learn the very thing it denied: that I am the LORD.

Yet God's dealings with Moab are not only judgment. Long before, a Moabite widow named Ruth had said to an Israelite, your God my God, and she became the great-grandmother of King David, named in the family line of Jesus: Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth (Matt 1:5). God's grace reached into Moab, and Christ came from that line. Nations under judgment are never beyond the reach of his mercy for those who turn to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom acted revengefully against the house of Judah (v. 12), so God will make it desolate from Teman to Dedan and lay his vengeance on it through Israel (vv. 13-14). The Philistines took vengeance with malice of soul to destroy in never-ending enmity (v. 15); God will cut them off and execute great vengeance on them (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Vengeance belongs to God, and those who take it into their own hands against his people will meet his.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: Because Edom acted revengefully against the house of Judah and has grievously offended in taking vengeance on them, therefore thus says the Lord GOD, I will stretch out my hand against Edom and cut off from it man and beast. And I will make it desolate; from Teman even to Dedan they shall fall by the sword. And I will lay my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel, and they shall do in Edom according to my anger and according to my wrath, and they shall know my vengeance, declares the Lord GOD. "Thus says the Lord GOD: Because the Philistines acted revengefully and took vengeance with malice of soul to destroy in never-ending enmity, therefore thus says the Lord GOD, Behold, I will stretch out my hand against the Philistines, and I will cut off the Cherethites and destroy the rest of the seacoast. I will execute great vengeance on them with wrathful rebukes. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I lay my vengeance upon them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the Lord GOD: Because Edom acted revengefully against the house of Judah and has grievously offended in taking vengeance on them,

Edom, descended from Esau, was Israel's brother nation, and it nursed an ancient grudge. When Jerusalem fell, Edom took its revenge. A psalm remembers it: Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, "Lay it bare, lay it bare" (Ps 137:7). Obadiah pleaded, do not gloat over the day of your brother (Obad 12).

therefore thus says the Lord GOD, I will stretch out my hand against Edom and cut off from it man and beast. And I will make it desolate; from Teman even to Dedan they shall fall by the sword. And I will lay my vengeance upon Edom by the hand of my people Israel... and they shall know my vengeance, declares the Lord GOD.

Notice the contrast: Edom's vengeance and God's vengeance. Edom took vengeance into its own hands. God says: vengeance is mine. That is exactly the principle Paul gives to Christians: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord" (Rom 12:19). Personal revenge is not only wrong; it is taking God's place.

"Thus says the Lord GOD: Because the Philistines acted revengefully and took vengeance with malice of soul to destroy in never-ending enmity,

Never-ending enmity. The Philistines had fought Israel since the days of the judges. Their hostility was generations old and would not let go.

Hatred that is nursed for generations poisons whole peoples. Many conflicts in our world are driven by exactly this: never-ending enmity, handed down from parents to children. Only the gospel, which makes enemies into brothers in Christ, can break it.

therefore thus says the Lord GOD, Behold, I will stretch out my hand against the Philistines, and I will cut off the Cherethites and destroy the rest of the seacoast. I will execute great vengeance on them with wrathful rebukes. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I lay my vengeance upon them."

The Cherethites were a coastal people linked with the Philistines (1 Sam 30:14). And every oracle in the chapter ends the same way: Then they will know that I am the LORD. Mockery, contempt, revenge and hatred all end in the same place — face to face with the God they despised.

25.title: Against the Neighbours
25.overview: The book turns from Jerusalem to its neighbours. Ammon said Aha! when God's sanctuary was profaned and Judah went into exile, and rejoiced with malice; God will hand Ammon over to the people of the East and destroy it (vv. 1-7). Moab said Judah was like all the other nations; God will open its frontier cities to invaders and judge it (vv. 8-11). Edom took revenge on Judah; God will make Edom desolate and lay his vengeance on it through Israel (vv. 12-14). The Philistines took vengeance with never-ending enmity; God will cut them off. Each oracle ends with the nations knowing that he is the LORD (vv. 15-17).
25.theology:
The God who judges his own people also judges the nations; judgment on Israel's enemies is also a promise to Israel.

Gloating over the fall of God's people provokes God (vv. 3, 6; Prov 24:17-18; Obad 12).

Denying the uniqueness of God's people is denying the uniqueness of God (v. 8).

Vengeance belongs to God alone (vv. 12-17; Rom 12:19).

God's mercy reaches even into nations under judgment, as Ruth the Moabite shows (Matt 1:5).
25.examples:
One word of scorn: Aha!

A capital city turned into a camel pasture.

Nothing special about them — and a God who says, you will know that I am the LORD.

A brother nation settling an old score.

Hatred handed down like an inheritance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Aha, the Gate of the Peoples Is Broken
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tyre rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall: Aha, the gate of the peoples is broken... I shall be replenished, now that she is laid waste (vv. 1-2). So God will bring many nations against Tyre like waves of the sea, scrape her down to a bare rock, a place for drying fishermen's nets (vv. 3-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who see another's ruin as their business opportunity will find God against them.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eleventh year, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, because Tyre said concerning Jerusalem, 'Aha, the gate of the peoples is broken; it has swung open to me. I shall be replenished, now that she is laid waste,' therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and will bring up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves. They shall destroy the walls of Tyre and break down her towers, and I will scrape her soil from her and make her a bare rock. She shall be in the midst of the sea a place for the spreading of nets, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. And she shall become plunder for the nations, and her daughters on the mainland shall be killed by the sword. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapters 26-28 are given to Tyre, the great Phoenician port on the Mediterranean coast north of Israel. Tyre was a trading empire built on ships and money, with its main city on an island just off the shore. It was rich, beautiful and apparently untouchable.

"Son of man, because Tyre said concerning Jerusalem, 'Aha, the gate of the peoples is broken; it has swung open to me. I shall be replenished, now that she is laid waste,'

Tyre's reaction to Jerusalem's fall was pure business. The gate of the peoples is broken — Jerusalem had controlled trade routes. Now that it is gone, it has swung open to me. I shall be replenished. Another city's ruin was Tyre's opportunity for profit.

That attitude is not ancient. Markets can profit from disaster, and people can see a neighbour's collapse as their chance to get ahead. God sees it and names it.

therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and will bring up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves.

Tyre lived by the sea. God will bring nations against it as the sea brings up its waves — not one attack, but wave after wave.

They shall destroy the walls of Tyre and break down her towers, and I will scrape her soil from her and make her a bare rock. She shall be in the midst of the sea a place for the spreading of nets, for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD. And she shall become plunder for the nations, and her daughters on the mainland shall be killed by the sword. Then they will know that I am the LORD.

A bare rock... a place for the spreading of nets. The glittering city will become a place where fishermen dry their nets in the sun. Isaiah had said the same of Tyre: The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pompous pride of all glory (Isa 23:9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will bring Nebuchadnezzar, king of kings, against Tyre with horses, chariots, siege walls and battering rams (vv. 7-11). Her wealth will be plundered, her stones and timber thrown into the sea, her music silenced (vv. 12-13). I will make you a bare rock... You shall never be rebuilt, for I am the LORD; I have spoken (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: No wealth or fortification can stand when God sends judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, with horses and chariots, and with horsemen and a host of many soldiers. He will kill with the sword your daughters on the mainland. He will set up a siege wall against you and throw up a mound against you, and raise a roof of shields against you. He will direct the shock of his battering rams against your walls, and with his axes he will break down your towers. His horses will be so many that their dust will cover you. Your walls will shake at the noise of the horsemen and wagons and chariots, when he enters your gates as men enter a city that has been breached. With the hoofs of his horses he will trample all your streets. He will kill your people with the sword, and your mighty pillars will fall to the ground. They will plunder your riches and loot your merchandise. They will break down your walls and destroy your pleasant houses. Your stones and timber and soil they will cast into the midst of the waters. And I will stop the music of your songs, and the sound of your lyres shall be heard no more. I will make you a bare rock. You shall be a place for the spreading of nets. You shall never be rebuilt, for I am the LORD; I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will bring against Tyre from the north Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, with horses and chariots, and with horsemen and a host of many soldiers.

The first wave has a name: Nebuchadnezzar (the ESV notes that the Hebrew spells it "Nebuchadrezzar" throughout Ezekiel). He is called king of kings — the greatest human ruler of his day. Daniel addressed him the same way, and added the crucial point: the God of heaven has given the kingdom to him (Dan 2:37). Even the king of kings is a servant of the LORD.

He will kill with the sword your daughters on the mainland. He will set up a siege wall against you... He will direct the shock of his battering rams against your walls... His horses will be so many that their dust will cover you... With the hoofs of his horses he will trample all your streets.

The description is of a full siege: siege walls, battering rams, cavalry, dust, noise, trampling hoofs. Nebuchadnezzar did besiege Tyre, for many years. Ezekiel later records that his army laboured hard, yet neither he nor his army got anything from Tyre to pay for the labor that he had performed against her (29:18). God's word was not finished with Tyre.

They will plunder your riches and loot your merchandise. They will break down your walls and destroy your pleasant houses. Your stones and timber and soil they will cast into the midst of the waters.

Notice that the subject changes from he to they. The waves of nations keep coming. Centuries later, Alexander the Great besieged the island city; his army built a causeway out to it using the rubble of the mainland, and the city fell. Its stones and timber and soil were literally thrown into the sea.

And I will stop the music of your songs, and the sound of your lyres shall be heard no more.

Silenced music is a sad sign of a dead city. John uses the same picture for the final Babylon: the sound of harpists and musicians... will be heard in you no more (Rev 18:22).

I will make you a bare rock. You shall be a place for the spreading of nets. You shall never be rebuilt, for I am the LORD; I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD.

Tyre trusted in its island walls and its wealth. Tyre has built herself a rampart and heaped up silver like dust... But behold, the Lord will strip her of her possessions (Zech 9:3-4). Security built on money and walls is a bare rock waiting to happen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The princes of the sea will step down from their thrones, sit on the ground trembling and lament Tyre's fall (vv. 15-18). God will cover her with the deep and send her down to the pit with the people of old; though you be sought for, you will never be found again (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The fall of a great commercial power shakes all who trusted in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD to Tyre: Will not the coastlands shake at the sound of your fall, when the wounded groan, when slaughter is made in your midst? Then all the princes of the sea will step down from their thrones and remove their robes and strip off their embroidered garments. They will clothe themselves with trembling; they will sit on the ground and tremble every moment and be appalled at you. And they will raise a lamentation over you and say to you, "'How you have perished, you who were inhabited from the seas, O city renowned, who was mighty on the sea; she and her inhabitants imposed their terror on all her inhabitants! Now the coastlands tremble on the day of your fall, and the coastlands that are on the sea are dismayed at your passing.' "For thus says the Lord GOD: When I make you a city laid waste, like the cities that are not inhabited, when I bring up the deep over you, and the great waters cover you, then I will make you go down with those who go down to the pit, to the people of old, and I will make you to dwell in the world below, among ruins from of old, with those who go down to the pit, so that you will not be inhabited; but I will set beauty in the land of the living. I will bring you to a dreadful end, and you shall be no more. Though you be sought for, you will never be found again, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the Lord GOD to Tyre: Will not the coastlands shake at the sound of your fall, when the wounded groan, when slaughter is made in your midst?

Then all the princes of the sea will step down from their thrones and remove their robes and strip off their embroidered garments. They will clothe themselves with trembling; they will sit on the ground and tremble every moment and be appalled at you.

Tyre's fall sends shock waves through every port that traded with it. The rulers of the coastlands take off their royal robes and sit on the ground in mourning — not only out of sympathy, but out of fear. If Tyre can fall, who is safe?

And they will raise a lamentation over you and say to you, "'How you have perished, you who were inhabited from the seas, O city renowned, who was mighty on the sea; she and her inhabitants imposed their terror on all her inhabitants! Now the coastlands tremble on the day of your fall, and the coastlands that are on the sea are dismayed at your passing.'

The lament begins How, like the book of Lamentations. O city renowned, who was mighty on the sea. Those who depended on the system grieve its collapse most bitterly. John saw the same scene at the fall of the final Babylon: the merchants of the earth weep and mourn for her, since no one buys their cargo anymore (Rev 18:11).

"For thus says the Lord GOD: When I make you a city laid waste... when I bring up the deep over you, and the great waters cover you, then I will make you go down with those who go down to the pit, to the people of old... but I will set beauty in the land of the living.

Tyre, which ruled the sea, will be swallowed by it, and go down to the pit — the place of the dead. And set against that: I will set beauty in the land of the living. While proud Tyre sinks, God will give glory to his own land and people.

I will bring you to a dreadful end, and you shall be no more. Though you be sought for, you will never be found again, declares the Lord GOD."

Though you be sought for, you will never be found. The old island city that was the wonder of the seas has vanished. The lesson is not only about Tyre. The world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever (1 John 2:17).

And yet even Tyre was not beyond grace. Jesus said that if his mighty works had been done there, they would have repented long ago (Luke 10:13). He went to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Gentile mother begged for her daughter and received his mercy (Mark 7:24-30). And when Paul later landed at Tyre, he found a church there (Acts 21:3-4). The city of merchants fell; the kingdom of Christ reached its people.

26.title: Tyre, the Bare Rock
26.overview:
Tyre, the great sea-trading city, rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall as an opportunity for profit. So God declares that he is against Tyre and will bring many nations against it like the waves of the sea, scraping it down to a bare rock where fishermen spread their nets (vv. 1-6).

God will bring Nebuchadnezzar, king of kings, against Tyre with a vast army, siege works and battering rams. Its wealth will be plundered, its stones and timber thrown into the sea, and its music silenced. It will become a bare rock and never be rebuilt (vv. 7-14).

The coastlands will tremble at Tyre's fall. The princes of the sea will leave their thrones, sit on the ground and lament the renowned city that was mighty on the sea. God will cover Tyre with the deep, send it down to the pit with the dead, and it will never be found again, while he sets beauty in the land of the living (vv. 15-21).
26.theology:
God judges those who profit from the ruin of others (v. 2).

Wealth, commerce and fortifications cannot protect a proud city from God's judgment (vv. 4-14; Isa 23:8-9; Zech 9:3-4).

The greatest rulers are servants of God's purposes (v. 7; Dan 2:37).

God's word is fulfilled over time, wave upon wave (vv. 3, 12; 29:18).

The fall of worldly powers shakes all who trusted in them, as the final Babylon will (vv. 15-18; Rev 18:9-19, 22).

Christ's mercy reached the region of Tyre, and a church grew there (Mark 7:24-30; Acts 21:3-4).
26.examples:
Seeing a neighbour's ruin as a business opportunity.

Wave after wave of armies.

A city's rubble thrown into the sea.

A place for fishermen to dry their nets.

Kings stepping off their thrones to sit on the ground.

Music that stops.
