verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — I Am Perfect in Beauty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel raises a lament for Tyre, who said, I am perfect in beauty (vv. 1-3). She is pictured as a magnificent ship: planks from Senir, a cedar mast from Lebanon, oars of Bashan oak, a deck inlaid with ivory, a sail of Egyptian linen, crews and craftsmen from the finest cities (vv. 4-9), and soldiers from distant lands hanging their shields on her walls (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Beauty and splendour gathered by human effort breed a pride that says, I am perfect.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Now you, son of man, raise a lamentation over Tyre, and say to Tyre, who dwells at the entrances to the sea, merchant of the peoples to many coastlands, thus says the Lord GOD: "O Tyre, you have said, 'I am perfect in beauty.' Your borders are in the heart of the seas; your builders made perfect your beauty. They made all your planks of fir trees from Senir; they took a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you. Of oaks of Bashan they made your oars; they made your deck of pines from the coasts of Cyprus, inlaid with ivory. Of fine embroidered linen from Egypt was your sail, serving as your banner; blue and purple from the coasts of Elishah was your awning. The inhabitants of Sidon and Arvad were your rowers; your skilled men, O Tyre, were in you; they were your pilots. The elders of Gebal and her skilled men were in you, caulking your seams; all the ships of the sea with their mariners were in you to barter for your wares. "Persia and Lud and Put were in your army as your men of war. They hung the shield and helmet in you; they gave you splendor. Men of Arvad and Helech were on your walls all around, and men of Gamad were in your towers. They hung their shields on your walls all around; they made perfect your beauty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 27 is a funeral song for Tyre, and a vivid one. Tyre is pictured as a great merchant ship, magnificently built, loaded with the world's wealth — and then wrecked in the open sea.

and say to Tyre, who dwells at the entrances to the sea, merchant of the peoples to many coastlands, thus says the Lord GOD: "O Tyre, you have said, 'I am perfect in beauty.'

Here is Tyre's heart in four words: I am perfect in beauty. Not "God has blessed me", but "I am perfect". That is the pride that goes before a fall.

Your borders are in the heart of the seas; your builders made perfect your beauty. They made all your planks of fir trees from Senir; they took a cedar from Lebanon to make a mast for you. Of oaks of Bashan they made your oars; they made your deck of pines from the coasts of Cyprus, inlaid with ivory.

The shipbuilding is lavish: the best wood from every mountain, a mast of Lebanon cedar, a deck inlaid with ivory. Of fine embroidered linen from Egypt was your sail (v. 7), with awnings of blue and purple.

And the crew is the best in the world: rowers from Sidon and Arvad, skilled pilots, expert caulkers from Gebal (vv. 8-9). Soldiers from Persia, Lud and Put hung the shield and helmet in you; they gave you splendor (v. 10), and men from Arvad and Gamad lined the walls (v. 11).

Notice how everything in the description is borrowed. Wood from Senir and Lebanon, linen from Egypt, sailors from Sidon, soldiers from Persia. Tyre's perfect beauty was assembled from the whole world. Nothing was hers. It is a picture of every human glory: impressive, and entirely on loan. What do you have that you did not receive? (1 Cor 4:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A long list of trading partners follows — Tarshish, Javan, Tubal and Meshech, Dedan, Syria, Judah and Israel, Damascus, Arabia, Sheba, Asshur and more — exchanging metals, horses, ivory, jewels, food, spices, cloth, and even human beings (vv. 12-24). So you were filled and heavily laden in the heart of the seas (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: A global economy can be dazzling and still be built partly on the trade in human lives.

verseByVerse.quote: "Tarshish did business with you because of your great wealth of every kind; silver, iron, tin, and lead they exchanged for your wares. Javan, Tubal, and Meshech traded with you; they exchanged human beings and vessels of bronze for your merchandise. From Beth-togarmah they exchanged horses, war horses, and mules for your wares. The men of Dedan traded with you. Many coastlands were your own special markets; they brought you in payment ivory tusks and ebony. Syria did business with you because of your abundant goods; they exchanged for your wares emeralds, purple, embroidered work, fine linen, coral, and ruby. Judah and the land of Israel traded with you; they exchanged for your merchandise wheat of Minnith, meal, honey, oil, and balm. Damascus did business with you for your abundant goods, because of your great wealth of every kind; wine of Helbon and wool of Sahar and casks of wine from Uzal they exchanged for your wares; wrought iron, cassia, and calamus were bartered for your merchandise. Dedan traded with you in saddlecloths for riding. Arabia and all the princes of Kedar were your favored dealers in lambs, rams, and goats; in these they did business with you. The traders of Sheba and Raamah traded with you; they exchanged for your wares the best of all kinds of spices and all precious stones and gold. Haran, Canneh, Eden, traders of Sheba, Asshur, and Chilmad traded with you. In your market these traded with you in choice garments, in clothes of blue and embroidered work, and in carpets of colored material, bound with cords and made secure. The ships of Tarshish traveled for you with your merchandise. So you were filled and heavily laden in the heart of the seas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Tarshish did business with you because of your great wealth of every kind; silver, iron, tin, and lead they exchanged for your wares.

Now comes a long, crowded trade list. From the far west (Tarshish) to Arabia, from Syria to the lands of the north, goods poured into Tyre: metals (v. 12), horses and mules (v. 14), ivory and ebony (v. 15), emeralds, purple, fine linen, coral and ruby (v. 16), wine and wool (v. 18), spices and precious stones and gold (v. 22), fine garments and carpets (v. 24).

Judah and the land of Israel traded with you; they exchanged for your merchandise wheat of Minnith, meal, honey, oil, and balm.

Even God's own people were part of Tyre's market (v. 17), selling their grain and oil. Nobody stands outside the world economy.

Javan, Tubal, and Meshech traded with you; they exchanged human beings and vessels of bronze for your merchandise.

And there, casually, in the middle of the list: human beings, traded alongside bronze pots. The glittering economy of Tyre included slaves. John's description of the final Babylon's cargo ends the same way: horses and chariots, and slaves, that is, human souls (Rev 18:13).

Every age must ask what its prosperity is built on. A dazzling market can hide exploitation — people treated as merchandise. God reads the whole list, including the line everyone else skims past.

The ships of Tarshish traveled for you with your merchandise. So you were filled and heavily laden in the heart of the seas.

Filled and heavily laden. The ship is loaded to the waterline with wealth. It looks like success. It is also exactly the condition in which a ship is most likely to sink.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–36 — Wrecked in the Heart of the Seas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ship is rowed out into the high seas, and The east wind has wrecked you in the heart of the seas (v. 26). Everything and everyone sinks (v. 27). Sailors on shore weep, throw dust on their heads and lament: Who is like Tyre, like one destroyed in the midst of the sea? (vv. 28-32). She once enriched the kings of the earth; now she is wrecked, and the merchants hiss (vv. 33-36).
verseByVerse.theology: Wealth that fills a ship to the waterline can sink it in a single storm.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your rowers have brought you out into the high seas. The east wind has wrecked you in the heart of the seas. Your riches, your wares, your merchandise, your mariners and your pilots, your caulkers, your dealers in merchandise, and all your men of war who are in you, with all your crew that is in your midst, sink into the heart of the seas on the day of your fall. At the sound of the cry of your pilots the countryside shakes, and down from their ships come all who handle the oar. The mariners and all the pilots of the sea stand on the land and shout aloud over you and cry out bitterly. They cast dust on their heads and wallow in ashes; they make themselves bald for you and put sackcloth on their waist, and they weep over you in bitterness of soul, with bitter mourning. In their wailing they raise a lamentation for you and lament over you: 'Who is like Tyre, like one destroyed in the midst of the sea? When your wares came from the seas, you satisfied many peoples; with your abundant wealth and merchandise you enriched the kings of the earth. Now you are wrecked by the seas, in the depths of the waters; your merchandise and all your crew in your midst have sunk with you. All the inhabitants of the coastlands are appalled at you, and the hair of their kings bristles with horror; their faces are convulsed. The merchants among the peoples hiss at you; you have come to a dreadful end and shall be no more forever.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Your rowers have brought you out into the high seas. The east wind has wrecked you in the heart of the seas.

The ship sails proudly into deep water. And then, in one line, the east wind — the storm God sends — wrecks it. A psalm had sung, By the east wind you shattered the ships of Tarshish (Ps 48:7). All that beauty and skill, all those expert pilots, could not steer through God's storm.

Your riches, your wares, your merchandise, your mariners and your pilots, your caulkers, your dealers in merchandise, and all your men of war who are in you, with all your crew that is in your midst, sink into the heart of the seas on the day of your fall.

The list of verse 27 reverses the list of verses 5-11. Everything that made the ship great goes down with it: the riches and the people. That is the rich fool's story on a national scale. He said, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years, but God said, Fool! This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:19-20).

At the sound of the cry of your pilots the countryside shakes, and down from their ships come all who handle the oar. The mariners and all the pilots of the sea stand on the land and shout aloud over you and cry out bitterly. They cast dust on their heads and wallow in ashes; they make themselves bald for you and put sackcloth on their waist, and they weep over you in bitterness of soul, with bitter mourning.

On shore, sailors of every nation watch and mourn. Dust on heads, shaved scalps, sackcloth. Their livelihood sank with Tyre.

And notice that they mourn for what they lost, not for what Tyre did. There is no repentance in their grief, only regret. The world can weep bitterly over a collapse without ever asking what God was saying through it.

In their wailing they raise a lamentation for you and lament over you: 'Who is like Tyre, like one destroyed in the midst of the sea? When your wares came from the seas, you satisfied many peoples; with your abundant wealth and merchandise you enriched the kings of the earth.

Now you are wrecked by the seas, in the depths of the waters; your merchandise and all your crew in your midst have sunk with you. All the inhabitants of the coastlands are appalled at you, and the hair of their kings bristles with horror; their faces are convulsed. The merchants among the peoples hiss at you; you have come to a dreadful end and shall be no more forever.'"

Who is like Tyre? That question was once asked in admiration. Now it is asked in horror. And the merchants who got rich through Tyre now hiss at her. The world is loyal to success, not to people.

Notice what the mourners say Tyre did for them: you satisfied many peoples; with your abundant wealth and merchandise you enriched the kings of the earth. Whole nations had built their prosperity on Tyre. When she sank, their fortunes sank with her, and the hair of their kings bristles with horror. It is the panic of a financial collapse spreading from one centre to every market that depended on it. John describes the same web of dependence around the final Babylon: the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living (Rev 18:3).

John saw this scene again at the end of history, when the great city Babylon falls. All shipmasters and seafaring men, sailors and all whose trade is on the sea, stood far off and cried out as they saw the smoke of her burning, "What city was like the great city?" And they threw dust on their heads (Rev 18:17-19). Ezekiel 27 is a preview of the collapse of every proud, godless system of wealth and power.

The question for us is where our security is anchored. Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted (Jas 5:1-2). What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? (Matt 16:26). The only treasure that does not sink is treasure in heaven.

27.title: The Wreck of the Great Ship
27.overview:
Ezekiel raises a lament for Tyre, the merchant of the peoples, who boasted that she was perfect in beauty. Tyre is pictured as a magnificent ship built from the finest materials of many lands — cypress planks, a cedar mast, oak oars, an ivory-inlaid deck, an embroidered linen sail — crewed by skilled men from other cities and defended by soldiers from distant nations (vv. 1-11).

A long list follows of the nations that traded with Tyre, including Judah and Israel, bringing metals, horses, ivory, jewels, grain, oil, wine, spices, fine cloth, and even human beings. Tyre was filled and heavily laden in the heart of the seas (vv. 12-25).

Then the east wind wrecks the ship in the high seas, and all its riches and crew sink. Sailors on shore mourn with dust, ashes and sackcloth, lamenting that Tyre, who enriched the kings of the earth, is now destroyed in the depths; the kings are horrified and the merchants hiss at her dreadful end (vv. 26-36).
27.theology:
Pride says, I am perfect in beauty, though every glory is borrowed (v. 3; 1 Cor 4:7).

Global prosperity can include the trade in human lives, and God sees it (v. 13; Rev 18:13).

Wealth that fills a life to the brim cannot survive the storm God sends (vv. 25-27; Luke 12:19-20; Jas 5:1-3).

The world's admiration turns to horror and contempt when success collapses (vv. 32-36).

Tyre's wreck previews the fall of the final Babylon and every godless system of wealth and power (Rev 18:9-19).
27.examples:
A ship built from the best wood of every mountain.

A sail of embroidered linen from Egypt.

Human beings listed between bronze pots.

Loaded to the waterline.

One east wind.

Who is like Tyre? — asked first in envy, then in horror.

28.text: <sup>1</sup>The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Because your heart is proud, and you have said, 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods, in the heart of the seas,' yet you are but a man, and no god, though you make your heart like the heart of a god—<sup>3</sup>you are indeed wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you;<sup>4</sup>by your wisdom and your understanding you have made wealth for yourself, and have gathered gold and silver into your treasuries;<sup>5</sup>by your great wisdom in your trade you have increased your wealth, and your heart has become proud in your wealth—<sup>6</sup>therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you make your heart like the heart of a god,<sup>7</sup>therefore, behold, I will bring foreigners upon you, the most ruthless of the nations; and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom and defile your splendor.<sup>8</sup>They shall thrust you down into the pit, and you shall die the death of the slain in the heart of the seas.<sup>9</sup>Will you still say, 'I am a god,' in the presence of those who kill you, though you are but a man, and no god, in the hands of those who slay you?<sup>10</sup>You shall die the death of the uncircumcised by the hand of foreigners; for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD."<sup>11</sup>Moreover, the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>12</sup>"Son of man, raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre, and say to him, Thus says the Lord GOD: "You were the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.<sup>13</sup>You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering, sardius, topaz, and diamond, beryl, onyx, and jasper, sapphire, emerald, and carbuncle; and crafted in gold were your settings and your engravings. On the day that you were created they were prepared.<sup>14</sup>You were an anointed guardian cherub. I placed you; you were on the holy mountain of God; in the midst of the stones of fire you walked.<sup>15</sup>You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you.<sup>16</sup>In the abundance of your trade you were filled with violence in your midst, and you sinned; so I cast you as a profane thing from the mountain of God, and I destroyed you, O guardian cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire.<sup>17</sup>Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor. I cast you to the ground; I exposed you before kings, to feast their eyes on you.<sup>18</sup>By the multitude of your iniquities, in the unrighteousness of your trade you profaned your sanctuaries; so I brought fire out from your midst; it consumed you, and I turned you to ashes on the earth in the sight of all who saw you.<sup>19</sup>All who know you among the peoples are appalled at you; you have come to a dreadful end and shall be no more forever."<sup>20</sup>The word of the LORD came to me:<sup>21</sup>"Son of man, set your face toward Sidon, and prophesy against her<sup>22</sup>and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I am against you, O Sidon, and I will manifest my glory in your midst. And they shall know that I am the LORD when I execute judgments in her and manifest my holiness in her;<sup>23</sup>for I will send pestilence into her, and blood into her streets; and the slain shall fall in her midst, by the sword that is against her on every side. Then they will know that I am the LORD.<sup>24</sup>"And for the house of Israel there shall be no more a brier to prick or a thorn to hurt them among all their neighbors who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.<sup>25</sup>"Thus says the Lord GOD: When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they are scattered, and manifest my holiness in them in the sight of the nations, then they shall dwell in their own land that I gave to my servant Jacob.<sup>26</sup>And they shall dwell securely in it, and they shall build houses and plant vineyards. They shall dwell securely, when I execute judgments upon all their neighbors who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the LORD their God."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prince of Tyre says in his proud heart, I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods, in the heart of the seas — yet you are but a man, and no god (v. 2). He is wiser than Daniel and has used his wisdom to gather wealth, and his heart has grown proud in it (vv. 3-5). So God will bring the most ruthless of nations against him (vv. 6-7). He will die in the heart of the seas: Will you still say, 'I am a god,' in the presence of those who kill you? (vv. 8-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Pride that makes itself a god will be exposed as mortal flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Because your heart is proud, and you have said, 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods, in the heart of the seas,' yet you are but a man, and no god, though you make your heart like the heart of a god—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to me:

"Son of man, say to the prince of Tyre, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Because your heart is proud, and you have said, 'I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods, in the heart of the seas,' yet you are but a man, and no god, though you make your heart like the heart of a god—

After two chapters on the city of Tyre, God addresses its ruler. And he goes straight to the heart: Because your heart is proud.

The king's boast is breathtaking: I am a god, I sit in the seat of the gods. From his island fortress in the heart of the seas, untouched by armies and rich beyond measure, he began to think of himself as divine.

And God's reply is five words: yet you are but a man. That is the answer to every human being who puts himself in God's place. It is the oldest temptation in the world: you will be like God (Gen 3:5). It led the people to shout of Herod, The voice of a god, and not of a man! — and an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory (Acts 12:22-23). And Paul warns of the man of lawlessness who will take his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God (2 Thess 2:3-4).

Few people say out loud, "I am a god." But the heart can say it in quieter ways: I am the master of my life. I decide what is right. I need no one. I control my future. Every one of those is the prince of Tyre's claim in modern dress.

Set it against Christ. The prince of Tyre was a man who made himself a god. Jesus was God who made himself a man: though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant (Phil 2:6-7). Tyre's king climbed up and was thrown down. Christ came down and was lifted up.

verseByVerse.quote: you are indeed wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you; by your wisdom and your understanding you have made wealth for yourself, and have gathered gold and silver into your treasuries; by your great wisdom in your trade you have increased your wealth, and your heart has become proud in your wealth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
you are indeed wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you;

This may be irony, and it may be sincere; either way it is striking. Daniel, taken to Babylon as a young man, was famous for wisdom. Nebuchadnezzar found him and his friends ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters (Dan 1:20). The king of Tyre may have been brilliant too. But wisdom without the fear of God is exactly what makes a person proud.

by your wisdom and your understanding you have made wealth for yourself, and have gathered gold and silver into your treasuries;

by your great wisdom in your trade you have increased your wealth, and your heart has become proud in your wealth—

Watch the sequence: wisdom → trade → wealth → pride. Each step looks good. Skill is good. Business is good. Wealth can be good. But your heart has become proud in your wealth. Success can be dangerous for the human heart, because it tempts us to credit ourselves. You have made wealth for yourself. Not God — yourself.

Moses warned Israel about exactly this: lest you say in your heart, my power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth (Deut 8:17). It is a warning for gifted, successful people everywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you make your heart like the heart of a god, therefore, behold, I will bring foreigners upon you, the most ruthless of the nations; and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom and defile your splendor. They shall thrust you down into the pit, and you shall die the death of the slain in the heart of the seas. Will you still say, 'I am a god,' in the presence of those who kill you, though you are but a man, and no god, in the hands of those who slay you? You shall die the death of the uncircumcised by the hand of foreigners; for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because you make your heart like the heart of a god,

therefore, behold, I will bring foreigners upon you, the most ruthless of the nations; and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of your wisdom and defile your splendor.

Swords against the beauty of your wisdom. All the brilliance and splendour he was proud of will be hacked down. Wisdom cannot argue with a sword.

They shall thrust you down into the pit, and you shall die the death of the slain in the heart of the seas.

Will you still say, 'I am a god,' in the presence of those who kill you, though you are but a man, and no god, in the hands of those who slay you?

Here is a searching question. Will you still say, 'I am a god,' in the presence of those who kill you? Death exposes every pretension. The self-made god dies like any man. A psalm says the same of rulers who thought themselves gods: nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince (Ps 82:7).

You shall die the death of the uncircumcised by the hand of foreigners; for I have spoken, declares the Lord GOD."

The death of the uncircumcised — a shameful death, outside God's people, without honour. The one who claimed to sit with the gods dies among the despised. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — Lament for the King of Tyre
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A lament: You were the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. You were in Eden, the garden of God, covered with precious stones (vv. 12-13). You were an anointed guardian cherub on the holy mountain of God (v. 14), blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you (v. 15). Through trade and violence he sinned, and God cast him out (v. 16). Your heart was proud because of your beauty (v. 17), so God brought fire out from within him and turned him to ashes (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Whether in the heavenly realm, in Eden or in a king's palace, pride corrupts the glory God gave and brings it down.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre, and say to him, Thus says the Lord GOD: "You were the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering, sardius, topaz, and diamond, beryl, onyx, and jasper, sapphire, emerald, and carbuncle; and crafted in gold were your settings and your engravings. On the day that you were created they were prepared.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moreover, the word of the LORD came to me:

"Son of man, raise a lamentation over the king of Tyre, and say to him, Thus says the Lord GOD: "You were the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.

Now comes a much-debated passage. It is a funeral lament over the king of Tyre, but the language soars far beyond any ordinary king. (The ESV notes that the meaning of the signet of perfection is uncertain.)

You were in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone was your covering, sardius, topaz, and diamond, beryl, onyx, and jasper, sapphire, emerald, and carbuncle; and crafted in gold were your settings and your engravings. On the day that you were created they were prepared.

You were in Eden, the garden of God. The king is described as if he had lived in paradise, covered with jewels. (The ESV notes that sapphire may be "lapis lazuli", and that the meaning of settings and... engravings is uncertain.) All nine stones named here appear, in the ESV, among the twelve stones on the breastpiece of Israel's high priest (Exod 28:17-20). The picture is of someone clothed in priestly and royal glory, in the very presence of God.

How should this be read? Faithful readers have understood it in two main ways. Some see the human king of Tyre described in the language of Eden, as if he were a new Adam: placed in glory, perfect in beauty, and then fallen through pride. Others see, behind the earthly king, a glimpse of a greater fall — the fall of Satan, the created being who was glorious and fell through pride, often read alongside Isaiah's How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star (Isa 14:12). Paul speaks of the condemnation of the devil as the fate of someone puffed up with conceit (1 Tim 3:6).

Both readings see the same pattern, and that pattern is the point: a creature given magnificent gifts, who turned those gifts into grounds for pride, and fell. That is the story of the devil, of Adam, of Tyre's king, and of every proud heart.

verseByVerse.quote: You were an anointed guardian cherub. I placed you; you were on the holy mountain of God; in the midst of the stones of fire you walked. You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You were an anointed guardian cherub. I placed you; you were on the holy mountain of God; in the midst of the stones of fire you walked.

An anointed guardian cherub (the ESV notes that the meaning of the phrase is uncertain). Cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life in Eden (Gen 3:24) and covered the ark in God's sanctuary. This figure had the highest place of honour: on the holy mountain of God, walking among the stones of fire. And note: I placed you. Everything he had, God gave.

You were blameless in your ways from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you.

Here is a key line in the lament. Blameless... from the day you were created, till unrighteousness was found in you. God did not create him evil. He was made good. The evil arose within him. That is how Scripture always describes the origin of sin: not a flaw in God's work, but a creature's own turning away from the Creator.

And the word found is striking. Sin was found in you, as if God searched and discovered it. Nothing escapes his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: In the abundance of your trade you were filled with violence in your midst, and you sinned; so I cast you as a profane thing from the mountain of God, and I destroyed you, O guardian cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire. Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor. I cast you to the ground; I exposed you before kings, to feast their eyes on you. By the multitude of your iniquities, in the unrighteousness of your trade you profaned your sanctuaries; so I brought fire out from your midst; it consumed you, and I turned you to ashes on the earth in the sight of all who saw you. All who know you among the peoples are appalled at you; you have come to a dreadful end and shall be no more forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the abundance of your trade you were filled with violence in your midst, and you sinned; so I cast you as a profane thing from the mountain of God, and I destroyed you, O guardian cherub, from the midst of the stones of fire.

Now the language comes back to Tyre's business. In the abundance of your trade you were filled with violence. Commerce, pursued with a proud heart, turned into exploitation and cruelty. So God cast him out (the ESV notes, perhaps "banished") as a profane thing — thrown out of the holy place like something unclean.

Your heart was proud because of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor. I cast you to the ground; I exposed you before kings, to feast their eyes on you.

Here is the root, stated plainly: Your heart was proud because of your beauty. And pride did something to his wisdom: you corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor. Pride does not only lead to sin; it corrupts the mind. Brilliant people make foolish choices when their image matters more than truth.

Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall (Prov 16:18). He is thrown to the ground and put on display before other kings.

By the multitude of your iniquities, in the unrighteousness of your trade you profaned your sanctuaries; so I brought fire out from your midst; it consumed you, and I turned you to ashes on the earth in the sight of all who saw you.

I brought fire out from your midst. The destruction came from within. Pride is a fire that burns its owner from the inside.

All who know you among the peoples are appalled at you; you have come to a dreadful end and shall be no more forever."

The lament ends like the lament for the city (27:36): a dreadful end... no more forever.

And there is a beautiful reversal in the Bible's last pages. The precious stones that covered the proud king — jasper, sapphire, emerald, onyx, beryl, topaz — reappear as the foundations of the new Jerusalem: The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of jewel. The first was jasper, the second sapphire (Rev 21:19). The glory that pride lost, grace gives to the humble people of God. The one who taught us to say, I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt 11:29), shares his glory with those who come to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sidon, Tyre's neighbour, is also judged: God will manifest his glory and holiness in her through pestilence and sword, Then they will know that I am the LORD (vv. 20-23).
verseByVerse.theology: God shows his holiness among the nations in judgment as well as in mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face toward Sidon, and prophesy against her and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I am against you, O Sidon, and I will manifest my glory in your midst. And they shall know that I am the LORD when I execute judgments in her and manifest my holiness in her; for I will send pestilence into her, and blood into her streets; and the slain shall fall in her midst, by the sword that is against her on every side. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to me:

"Son of man, set your face toward Sidon, and prophesy against her

Sidon was Tyre's older sister city along the coast, also a centre of trade — and the home of Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, who brought Baal worship into Israel (1 Kgs 16:31).

and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I am against you, O Sidon, and I will manifest my glory in your midst. And they shall know that I am the LORD when I execute judgments in her and manifest my holiness in her;

for I will send pestilence into her, and blood into her streets; and the slain shall fall in her midst, by the sword that is against her on every side. Then they will know that I am the LORD.

I will manifest my glory... manifest my holiness. God's glory is shown not only in blessing but in judgment. When God judges evil, his holiness is displayed. The world may not like that, but a God who never judged would not be holy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No more will a brier or thorn hurt Israel from her contemptuous neighbours (v. 24). God will gather his scattered people and show his holiness in them before the nations; they shall build houses and plant vineyards. They shall dwell securely (vv. 25-26).
verseByVerse.theology: God's judgments on the nations serve his purpose to gather and settle his people in safety.

verseByVerse.quote: "And for the house of Israel there shall be no more a brier to prick or a thorn to hurt them among all their neighbors who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD. "Thus says the Lord GOD: When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they are scattered, and manifest my holiness in them in the sight of the nations, then they shall dwell in their own land that I gave to my servant Jacob. And they shall dwell securely in it, and they shall build houses and plant vineyards. They shall dwell securely, when I execute judgments upon all their neighbors who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the LORD their God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And for the house of Israel there shall be no more a brier to prick or a thorn to hurt them among all their neighbors who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.

Now the purpose of all the oracles against the nations is revealed. They are good news for Israel. The neighbours who treated God's people with contempt, like thorns in their side, will trouble them no more.

"Thus says the Lord GOD: When I gather the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they are scattered, and manifest my holiness in them in the sight of the nations, then they shall dwell in their own land that I gave to my servant Jacob.

In verse 22 God manifested his holiness in Sidon through judgment. Here he manifests his holiness in Israel through restoration. Same holiness, two outcomes: fire for the proud, gathering for his people.

And they shall dwell securely in it, and they shall build houses and plant vineyards. They shall dwell securely, when I execute judgments upon all their neighbors who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the LORD their God."

They shall dwell securely... build houses and plant vineyards. Ordinary life, lived in peace. Isaiah described God's new creation in the same homely terms: They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit (Isa 65:21).

Twice: dwell securely. That is what the proud king of Tyre thought he had in his island fortress, and lost. It is what God gives to his people as a gift. And the chapter's last words are tender: the LORD their God. The security Tyre sought in wealth and walls, God's people find in belonging to him.

28.title: I Am a God
28.overview:
The prince of Tyre has a proud heart and says he is a god, seated in the heart of the seas, though he is only a man. He is wiser than Daniel and has used his wisdom in trade to build great wealth, and his heart has grown proud in it. So God will bring the most ruthless of nations against him; he will die a shameful death in the heart of the seas, and will not be able to call himself a god in front of those who kill him (vv. 1-10).

Ezekiel raises a lament over the king of Tyre. He was the signet of perfection, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; he was in Eden, the garden of God, covered with precious stones; he was an anointed guardian cherub on the holy mountain of God, blameless from the day he was created until unrighteousness was found in him. Through his trade he was filled with violence and sinned, and God cast him out. His heart was proud because of his beauty and he corrupted his wisdom for the sake of his splendour, so God cast him down, brought fire out from within him and turned him to ashes (vv. 11-19).

God declares judgment on Sidon, manifesting his glory and holiness through pestilence and sword (vv. 20-23). Then Israel will no longer be troubled by contemptuous neighbours. God will gather his scattered people, show his holiness in them before the nations, and they will live securely in their land, building houses and planting vineyards, and know that he is the LORD their God (vv. 24-26).
28.theology:
The root of sin is the proud desire to be like God; every human who claims divinity is only a man (vv. 2, 9; Gen 3:5; Acts 12:21-23; 2 Thess 2:3-4; Ps 82:6-7).

Wisdom and success tempt the heart to pride by crediting ourselves with what God gave (vv. 3-5).

Created beings were made good; sin arose within them through pride (v. 15). The lament of vv. 11-19 is read either as the king of Tyre in Eden language or as a glimpse of Satan's fall behind him; both show pride corrupting God-given glory (Isa 14:12-15; 1 Tim 3:6; Prov 16:18).

Pride corrupts wisdom and destroys from within (vv. 17-18).

God displays his holiness both in judging the proud and in restoring his people (vv. 22, 25).

The security the proud seek in wealth, God gives to his people as a gift (vv. 25-26; Isa 65:21-22).

Christ, who was God, humbled himself as a man, and the glory pride lost adorns the city of God's humble people (Phil 2:5-8; Rev 21:19-20).
28.examples:
A man on an island saying, I am a god.

Wisdom, trade, wealth, pride — each step looking good.

Will you still say it to the ones who kill you?

Blameless until unrighteousness was found.

A fire that started inside.

The jewels of the proud king set in the foundations of the city of God.

Building houses and planting vineyards in safety.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — My Nile Is My Own
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the tenth year God speaks against Pharaoh, the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams, that says, 'My Nile is my own; I made it for myself' (vv. 1-3). God will hook him like a river monster and fling him into the wilderness for the birds (vv. 4-5). Egypt has been a staff of reed to the house of Israel that broke and wounded whoever leaned on it (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Whoever claims to have made what God made, and whoever leans on such a power, will be broken.

verseByVerse.quote: In the tenth year, in the tenth month, on the twelfth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, set your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and prophesy against him and against all Egypt; speak, and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams, that says, 'My Nile is my own; I made it for myself.' I will put hooks in your jaws, and make the fish of your streams stick to your scales; and I will draw you up out of the midst of your streams, with all the fish of your streams that stick to your scales. And I will cast you out into the wilderness, you and all the fish of your streams; you shall fall on the open field, and not be brought together or gathered. To the beasts of the earth and to the birds of the heavens I give you as food. Then all the inhabitants of Egypt shall know that I am the LORD. "Because you have been a staff of reed to the house of Israel, when they grasped you with the hand, you broke and tore all their shoulders; and when they leaned on you, you broke and made all their loins to shake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapters 29-32 contain seven oracles against Egypt, more than against any other single nation in Ezekiel. Egypt was the power Judah kept running to for help against Babylon, and God wanted his people to see it for what it was.

speak, and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams, that says, 'My Nile is my own; I made it for myself.'

Pharaoh is pictured as a great dragon sprawled in the channels of the Nile, like a monstrous crocodile basking in its own river. And his boast is the heart of the matter: My Nile is my own; I made it for myself.

Egypt's entire life depended on the Nile, and Pharaoh claimed it as his own creation. It is the same pride as the prince of Tyre's: taking credit for what God made. An earlier Pharaoh had said, Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice? (Exod 5:2). This one has the same heart.

I will put hooks in your jaws, and make the fish of your streams stick to your scales; and I will draw you up out of the midst of your streams... And I will cast you out into the wilderness... To the beasts of the earth and to the birds of the heavens I give you as food.

The monster that thought itself untouchable in its river is dragged out with hooks, like a crocodile on a line, and left to rot in the desert. God asked Job, Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook...? Can you... pierce his jaw with a hook? (Job 41:1-2). No man can. God can. Scripture often pictures God's victory over proud powers as the defeat of the sea monster: Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the dragon? (Isa 51:9).

Then all the inhabitants of Egypt shall know that I am the LORD. "Because you have been a staff of reed to the house of Israel, when they grasped you with the hand, you broke and tore all their shoulders; and when they leaned on you, you broke and made all their loins to shake.

Here is why this matters for Israel. Egypt was a staff of reed. A reed looks like a walking stick, but lean your weight on it and it snaps — and the splintered end tears into you. A century earlier the Assyrian commander had mocked Judah with the same picture: you are trusting in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it (Isa 36:6).

Everyone leans on something. Money, a career, a relationship, a government, our own strength. Many of them look like staffs. Only one support will hold the full weight of a life. Everything else is reed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will bring a sword on Egypt and make it desolate from Migdol to Syene for forty years, scattering its people (vv. 8-12). Then he will gather them back, but Egypt will be the most lowly of the kingdoms, never again ruling the nations, and never again the thing Israel relies on (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: God humbles proud powers so that his people will stop trusting them.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and will cut off from you man and beast, and the land of Egypt shall be a desolation and a waste. Then they will know that I am the LORD. "Because you said, 'The Nile is mine, and I made it,' therefore, behold, I am against you and against your streams, and I will make the land of Egypt an utter waste and desolation, from Migdol to Syene, as far as the border of Cush. No foot of man shall pass through it, and no foot of beast shall pass through it; it shall be uninhabited forty years. And I will make the land of Egypt a desolation in the midst of desolated countries, and her cities shall be a desolation forty years among cities that are laid waste. I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and disperse them through the countries. "For thus says the Lord GOD: At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the peoples among whom they were scattered, and I will restore the fortunes of Egypt and bring them back to the land of Pathros, the land of their origin, and there they shall be a lowly kingdom. It shall be the most lowly of the kingdoms, and never again exalt itself above the nations. And I will make them so small that they will never again rule over the nations. And it shall never again be the reliance of the house of Israel, recalling their iniquity, when they turn to them for aid. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and will cut off from you man and beast, and the land of Egypt shall be a desolation and a waste... from Migdol to Syene, as far as the border of Cush.

From Migdol in the north to Syene in the far south: the whole length of Egypt. And again the charge is repeated: Because you said, 'The Nile is mine, and I made it' (v. 9). God judges pride precisely at the point of the boast. The river he claimed will not save him.

it shall be uninhabited forty years... I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and disperse them through the countries.

Forty years is the Bible's familiar period of discipline — the length of Israel's wilderness wandering. Egypt will taste scattering, as Israel did.

"For thus says the Lord GOD: At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the peoples among whom they were scattered, and I will restore the fortunes of Egypt... and there they shall be a lowly kingdom.

Remarkably, there is restoration for Egypt too. God will gather them back. But Egypt will be a lowly kingdom — the most lowly of the kingdoms, never again ruling over nations. The superpower will become small.

And it shall never again be the reliance of the house of Israel, recalling their iniquity, when they turn to them for aid. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD."

And the purpose is for Israel: Egypt shall never again be the reliance of the house of Israel. Every time Israel looked to Egypt, it was recalling their iniquity — a reminder of their failure to trust God. God humbles Egypt so that his people will stop leaning on it.

Sometimes God breaks the things we trust, not to punish us, but to free us from them.

And there is more grace for Egypt than this chapter says. Isaiah foresaw a day when the Egyptians will know the LORD, and God would say, Blessed be Egypt my people (Isa 19:21, 25). At Pentecost, visitors from Egypt heard the gospel in their own language (Acts 2:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the twenty-seventh year God says that Nebuchadnezzar's army laboured hard against Tyre and got nothing for it (vv. 17-18). So God gives him Egypt as his wages, because they worked for me (vv. 19-20). On that day I will cause a horn to spring up for the house of Israel, and I will open your lips among them (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Even pagan kings work for God and receive their wages from him; and he raises up strength for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-seventh year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army labor hard against Tyre. Every head was made bald, and every shoulder was rubbed bare, yet neither he nor his army got anything from Tyre to pay for the labor that he had performed against her. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon; and he shall carry off its wealth and despoil it and plunder it; and it shall be the wages for his army. I have given him the land of Egypt as his payment for which he labored, because they worked for me, declares the Lord GOD. "On that day I will cause a horn to spring up for the house of Israel, and I will open your lips among them. Then they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the twenty-seventh year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me:

This is the latest date given anywhere in Ezekiel — some sixteen years after the prophecy against Tyre in chapter 26. It has been placed here because it concerns Egypt. It shows God's word still unfolding long after it was first spoken.

"Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army labor hard against Tyre. Every head was made bald, and every shoulder was rubbed bare, yet neither he nor his army got anything from Tyre to pay for the labor that he had performed against her.

A vivid picture of a long siege: soldiers' heads rubbed bald from helmets, shoulders rubbed raw from carrying earth and timber for siege works. Years of hard labour against Tyre, and no plunder to pay the army.

Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon; and he shall carry off its wealth and despoil it and plunder it; and it shall be the wages for his army. I have given him the land of Egypt as his payment for which he labored, because they worked for me, declares the Lord GOD.

Here is an astonishing statement: because they worked for me. Nebuchadnezzar did not know it, but he was God's employee. His campaigns carried out God's judgments. And God, who is no one's debtor, paid his wages — with Egypt.

That is a remarkable picture of God's sovereignty over history. Kings, armies and empires, even pagan ones, are workers in his service. They receive what he gives them and nothing more.

"On that day I will cause a horn to spring up for the house of Israel, and I will open your lips among them. Then they will know that I am the LORD."

And in the middle of all this judgment on the nations, a promise to Israel. A horn is a symbol of strength — like the horn of a wild ox. God will make strength spring up for his people. The psalm promised, There I will make a horn to sprout for David (Ps 132:17), and Zechariah, filled with the Spirit at the birth of John the Baptist, sang that God has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69). That horn is Christ.

And I will open your lips among them. Ezekiel's voice, silenced for years, will speak again — and when it does, it will speak of restoration.

29.title: Egypt, the Broken Reed
29.overview:
In the tenth year God declares himself against Pharaoh, the great dragon lying in the Nile who claims to have made the river for himself. God will drag him out with hooks and leave him in the wilderness for the birds and beasts. Egypt has been a staff of reed to Israel, breaking and wounding everyone who leaned on it (vv. 1-7).

God will bring the sword on Egypt and make it desolate from north to south for forty years, scattering its people. Then he will gather them back, but Egypt will be the lowliest of kingdoms, never again ruling the nations, and never again the thing Israel trusts, which only reminded Israel of its sin (vv. 8-16).

In the twenty-seventh year God says that Nebuchadnezzar's army worked hard against Tyre and got nothing for its labour, so God gives him Egypt as wages, because they worked for God. On that day God will make a horn spring up for Israel and open Ezekiel's lips among them (vv. 17-21).
29.theology:
Pride claims to have made what God made, and God humbles it at the very point of its boast (vv. 3, 9; Exod 5:2).

God triumphs over every proud power pictured as a monster (vv. 3-5; Job 41:1-2; Isa 51:9; Ps 74:13-14).

Everything but God is a broken reed that wounds those who lean on it (vv. 6-7; Isa 36:6).

God sometimes breaks what his people trust in order to free them from it (v. 16).

Pagan rulers are unknowing servants of God and receive their wages from him (vv. 18-20).

God raises up a horn of strength for his people, fulfilled in Christ (v. 21; Ps 132:17; Luke 1:69).

God's mercy reaches Egypt too (Isa 19:21-25; Acts 2:10).
29.examples:
A crocodile king saying, My river, I made it.

A monster dragged out with hooks.

A walking stick that snaps and cuts your hand.

A superpower made small.

Bald heads and raw shoulders, and no pay.

They worked for me.
