verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wail, 'Alas for the day!' For the day is near, the day of the LORD is near (vv. 2-3). A sword will fall on Egypt and on Cush, Put, Lud, Arabia and Libya, all her allies (vv. 4-5). Those who support Egypt will fall, and her proud might will come down (vv. 6-8); messengers will terrify distant Cush (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The day of the LORD comes on the proud and on all who stand with them.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, prophesy, and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Wail, 'Alas for the day!' For the day is near, the day of the LORD is near; it will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations. A sword shall come upon Egypt, and anguish shall be in Cush, when the slain fall in Egypt, and her wealth is carried away, and her foundations are torn down. Cush, and Put, and Lud, and all Arabia, and Libya, and the people of the land that is in league, shall fall with them by the sword. "Thus says the LORD: Those who support Egypt shall fall, and her proud might shall come down; from Migdol to Syene they shall fall within her by the sword, declares the Lord GOD. And they shall be desolated in the midst of desolated countries, and their cities shall be in the midst of cities that are laid waste. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have set fire to Egypt, and all her helpers are broken. "On that day messengers shall go out from me in ships to terrify the unsuspecting people of Cush, and anguish shall come upon them on the day of Egypt's doom; for, behold, it comes!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Son of man, prophesy, and say, Thus says the Lord GOD: "Wail, 'Alas for the day!' For the day is near, the day of the LORD is near; it will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations.

The day of the LORD is the prophets' phrase for the day when God steps into history to judge. It had fallen on Israel. Now it comes for Egypt and the nations. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks doom for.) Zephaniah described it: A day of wrath is that day, a day of distress and anguish... a day of clouds and thick darkness (Zeph 1:15).

A sword shall come upon Egypt, and anguish shall be in Cush, when the slain fall in Egypt, and her wealth is carried away, and her foundations are torn down. Cush, and Put, and Lud, and all Arabia, and Libya, and the people of the land that is in league, shall fall with them by the sword.

Egypt did not stand alone. Its allies to the south and west — Cush, Put, Lud, Libya — and the people of the land that is in league (the ESV notes, literally "the sons of the land of the covenant") will fall with it. When you tie yourself to a falling power, you fall with it.

"Thus says the LORD: Those who support Egypt shall fall, and her proud might shall come down; from Migdol to Syene they shall fall within her by the sword... Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have set fire to Egypt, and all her helpers are broken.

Her proud might shall come down. All her helpers are broken. Egypt was the great helper others looked to, and its helpers will be broken too. Human support systems collapse together.

"On that day messengers shall go out from me in ships to terrify the unsuspecting people of Cush, and anguish shall come upon them on the day of Egypt's doom; for, behold, it comes!

Even distant Cush, far up the Nile, living carelessly, will hear the news and tremble. Behold, it comes! The day of the LORD always arrives on people who thought they were safe.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will end Egypt's wealth by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (vv. 10-11). He will dry up the Nile (v. 12), destroy the idols of Memphis, and bring fire and judgment on Pathros, Zoan, Thebes, Pelusium, On, Pi-beseth and Tehaphnehes, where the day shall be dark (vv. 13-18). Thus I will execute judgments on Egypt. Then they will know that I am the LORD (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: No city, idol or river can shelter a nation from the LORD's judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the Lord GOD: "I will put an end to the wealth of Egypt, by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He and his people with him, the most ruthless of nations, shall be brought in to destroy the land, and they shall draw their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain. And I will dry up the Nile and will sell the land into the hand of evildoers; I will bring desolation upon the land and everything in it, by the hand of foreigners; I am the LORD; I have spoken. "Thus says the Lord GOD: "I will destroy the idols and put an end to the images in Memphis; there shall no longer be a prince from the land of Egypt; so I will put fear in the land of Egypt. I will make Pathros a desolation and will set fire to Zoan and will execute judgments on Thebes. And I will pour out my wrath on Pelusium, the stronghold of Egypt, and cut off the multitude of Thebes. And I will set fire to Egypt; Pelusium shall be in great agony; Thebes shall be breached, and Memphis shall face enemies by day. The young men of On and of Pi-beseth shall fall by the sword, and the women shall go into captivity. At Tehaphnehes the day shall be dark, when I break there the yoke bars of Egypt, and her proud might shall come to an end in her; she shall be covered by a cloud, and her daughters shall go into captivity. Thus I will execute judgments on Egypt. Then they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the Lord GOD: "I will put an end to the wealth of Egypt, by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He and his people with him, the most ruthless of nations, shall be brought in to destroy the land, and they shall draw their swords against Egypt and fill the land with the slain.

The instrument is named: Nebuchadnezzar. But the subject of the sentence is God: I will put an end to the wealth of Egypt. The king of Babylon is the hand; God is the one acting.

And I will dry up the Nile and will sell the land into the hand of evildoers; I will bring desolation upon the land and everything in it, by the hand of foreigners; I am the LORD; I have spoken.

I will dry up the Nile. The river Pharaoh claimed to have made (29:3) is in God's hand. The thing a nation depends on most can be dried up by the word of God.

"Thus says the Lord GOD: "I will destroy the idols and put an end to the images in Memphis; there shall no longer be a prince from the land of Egypt; so I will put fear in the land of Egypt.

The judgment strikes Egypt's gods first. Jeremiah said the same: I am bringing punishment upon Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh and Egypt and her gods (Jer 46:25). As at the exodus, the plagues fall on the gods of Egypt as much as on its people.

I will make Pathros a desolation and will set fire to Zoan and will execute judgments on Thebes. And I will pour out my wrath on Pelusium, the stronghold of Egypt... Thebes shall be breached, and Memphis shall face enemies by day. The young men of On and of Pi-beseth shall fall by the sword... At Tehaphnehes the day shall be dark, when I break there the yoke bars of Egypt, and her proud might shall come to an end in her.

The list of cities marches through the whole country: the south (Pathros), the great capitals (Memphis, Thebes), the stronghold of Pelusium, On and Pi-beseth, and Tehaphnehes, where Judean refugees had fled against God's word (Jer 43:7 calls it Tahpanhes). Not one place is safe. The day shall be dark.

For the Judeans who had run to Egypt for safety, this was a direct warning: the refuge you chose instead of God is under judgment too.

Thus I will execute judgments on Egypt. Then they will know that I am the LORD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the eleventh year God says, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and it has not been bound up (vv. 20-21). He will break both arms and strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, putting my sword in his hand (vv. 22-25), and scatter the Egyptians, Then they will know that I am the LORD (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: God breaks the arm of flesh that people trust and strengthens whom he will.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eleventh year, in the first month, on the seventh day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and behold, it has not been bound up, to heal it by binding it with a bandage, so that it may become strong to wield the sword. Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt and will break his arms, both the strong arm and the one that was broken, and I will make the sword fall from his hand. I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them through the countries. And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon and put my sword in his hand, but I will break the arms of Pharaoh, and he will groan before him like a man mortally wounded. I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, but the arms of Pharaoh shall fall. Then they shall know that I am the LORD, when I put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon and he stretches it out against the land of Egypt. And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them throughout the countries. Then they will know that I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the eleventh year, in the first month, on the seventh day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me:

"Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and behold, it has not been bound up, to heal it by binding it with a bandage, so that it may become strong to wield the sword.

This oracle is dated during the siege of Jerusalem. It likely looks back to the time when Pharaoh's army marched out to relieve Jerusalem and then withdrew (Jer 37:5-7). God says: I have broken the arm of Pharaoh. The arm that held the sword is already broken, and no bandage will fix it.

Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt and will break his arms, both the strong arm and the one that was broken, and I will make the sword fall from his hand.

And I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon and put my sword in his hand, but I will break the arms of Pharaoh, and he will groan before him like a man mortally wounded.

Two kings, four arms. God breaks Pharaoh's and strengthens Nebuchadnezzar's. And the sword in Babylon's hand is my sword. Military power belongs to God and he gives or withdraws it.

The people of Judah trusted Pharaoh's arm. Hezekiah had once said of an invading king, With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God (2 Chr 32:8). Jeremiah warned, Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength (Jer 17:5).

And the Bible's answer to every broken human arm is the arm of the LORD. Isaiah asked, to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? (Isa 53:1), and then described the suffering Servant. God's mighty arm was revealed not in a Pharaoh or a Nebuchadnezzar, but in a Saviour pierced for our transgressions. That is the arm that does not break.

I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, but the arms of Pharaoh shall fall. Then they shall know that I am the LORD, when I put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon and he stretches it out against the land of Egypt. And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them throughout the countries. Then they will know that I am the LORD."

30.title: The Day of Egypt
30.overview:
God calls for wailing, because the day of the LORD is near. A sword will come on Egypt and its allies — Cush, Put, Lud, Arabia, Libya and those in league with it. Egypt's proud might and all her helpers will fall, and even distant Cush will tremble (vv. 1-9).

God will end Egypt's wealth through Nebuchadnezzar and the most ruthless of nations. He will dry up the Nile, destroy the idols of Memphis, and bring fire and judgment on city after city — Pathros, Zoan, Thebes, Pelusium, On, Pi-beseth and Tehaphnehes — until Egypt's proud might ends and its people go into captivity (vv. 10-19).

In the eleventh year God declares that he has broken Pharaoh's arm and it will not heal. He will break both his arms and make the sword fall from his hand, while strengthening the arms of the king of Babylon and putting God's own sword in his hand. The Egyptians will be scattered, and they will know that he is the LORD (vv. 20-26).
30.theology:
The day of the LORD falls on the proud nations and on all who ally themselves with them (vv. 2-8; Zeph 1:14-15).

God judges the gods of the nations along with the nations (v. 13; Jer 46:25).

No refuge chosen instead of God is safe from his judgment (vv. 14-18).

God breaks and strengthens human arms as he wills; the sword in any ruler's hand is his (vv. 21-25; 2 Chr 32:8; Jer 17:5).

The arm of the LORD that never breaks is revealed in the suffering Servant, Christ (Isa 53:1).
30.examples:
Alas for the day!

Allies falling like dominoes.

A river dried up by a word.

A refugee city with the lights going out.

A broken arm no bandage can fix.

God's sword in a pagan king's hand.

31.text: <sup>1</sup>In the eleventh year, in the third month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>2</sup>"Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude: "Whom are you like in your greatness?<sup>3</sup>Behold, Assyria was a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches and forest shade, and of towering height, its top among the clouds.<sup>4</sup>The waters nourished it; the deep made it grow tall, making its rivers flow around the place of its planting, sending forth its streams to all the trees of the field.<sup>5</sup>So it towered high above all the trees of the field; its boughs grew large and its branches long from abundant water in its shoots.<sup>6</sup>All the birds of the heavens made their nests in its boughs; under its branches all the beasts of the field gave birth to their young, and under its shadow lived all great nations.<sup>7</sup>It was beautiful in its greatness, in the length of its branches; for its roots went down to abundant waters.<sup>8</sup>The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it, nor the fir trees equal its boughs; neither were the plane trees like its branches; no tree in the garden of God was its equal in beauty.<sup>9</sup>I made it beautiful in the mass of its branches, and all the trees of Eden envied it, that were in the garden of God.<sup>10</sup>"Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because it towered high and set its top among the clouds, and its heart was proud of its height,<sup>11</sup>I will give it into the hand of a mighty one of the nations. He shall surely deal with it as its wickedness deserves. I have cast it out.<sup>12</sup>Foreigners, the most ruthless of nations, have cut it down and left it. On the mountains and in all the valleys its branches have fallen, and its boughs have been broken in all the ravines of the land, and all the peoples of the earth have gone away from its shadow and left it.<sup>13</sup>On its fallen trunk dwell all the birds of the heavens, and on its branches are all the beasts of the field.<sup>14</sup>All this is in order that no trees by the waters may grow to towering height or set their tops among the clouds, and that no trees that drink water may reach up to them in height. For they are all given over to death, to the world below, among the children of man, with those who go down to the pit.<sup>15</sup>"Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day the cedar went down to Sheol I caused mourning; I closed the deep over it, and restrained its rivers, and many waters were stopped. I clothed Lebanon in gloom for it, and all the trees of the field fainted because of it.<sup>16</sup>I made the nations quake at the sound of its fall, when I cast it down to Sheol with those who go down to the pit. And all the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, all that drink water, were comforted in the world below.<sup>17</sup>They also went down to Sheol with it, to those who are slain by the sword; yes, those who were its arm, who lived under its shadow among the nations.<sup>18</sup>"Whom are you thus like in glory and in greatness among the trees of Eden? You shall be brought down with the trees of Eden to the world below. You shall lie among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword. "This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God asks Pharaoh, Whom are you like in your greatness? (v. 2). Look at Assyria: a cedar of Lebanon, towering to the clouds, watered by the deep, sheltering birds, beasts and all great nations (vv. 3-7). No tree in the garden of God could rival it; I made it beautiful, and the trees of Eden envied it (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The greatest earthly power is a tree God planted and watered.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eleventh year, in the third month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude: "Whom are you like in your greatness? Behold, Assyria was a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches and forest shade, and of towering height, its top among the clouds. The waters nourished it; the deep made it grow tall, making its rivers flow around the place of its planting, sending forth its streams to all the trees of the field. So it towered high above all the trees of the field; its boughs grew large and its branches long from abundant water in its shoots. All the birds of the heavens made their nests in its boughs; under its branches all the beasts of the field gave birth to their young, and under its shadow lived all great nations. It was beautiful in its greatness, in the length of its branches; for its roots went down to abundant waters. The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it, nor the fir trees equal its boughs; neither were the plane trees like its branches; no tree in the garden of God was its equal in beauty. I made it beautiful in the mass of its branches, and all the trees of Eden envied it, that were in the garden of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the eleventh year, in the third month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, say to Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude: "Whom are you like in your greatness?

God asks Pharaoh a question: Whom are you like in your greatness? Who do you compare yourself to? And then he tells him a story about someone greater — so that Pharaoh can learn from how it ended.

Behold, Assyria was a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches and forest shade, and of towering height, its top among the clouds.

Assyria had been the superpower before Babylon — the empire that destroyed Samaria and dominated the ancient world for generations. It is pictured as the most magnificent cedar in Lebanon, its top among the clouds (the ESV notes, perhaps "through the thick boughs").

The waters nourished it; the deep made it grow tall... So it towered high above all the trees of the field... All the birds of the heavens made their nests in its boughs; under its branches all the beasts of the field gave birth to their young, and under its shadow lived all great nations.

This tree was a blessing to many. Birds nested, animals sheltered, nations lived in its shade. Great empires do bring order and protection. Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of himself as exactly such a tree: a tree in the midst of the earth, and its height was great (Dan 4:10).

It was beautiful in its greatness, in the length of its branches; for its roots went down to abundant waters. The cedars in the garden of God could not rival it... no tree in the garden of God was its equal in beauty. I made it beautiful in the mass of its branches, and all the trees of Eden envied it, that were in the garden of God.

The praise is lavish. Not even the trees of Eden could match it. But notice the key phrase: I made it beautiful. Its height, its water, its beauty — all were gifts from God. Its roots went down to waters it did not create. Every great power stands on what God provides.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because it towered high and set its top among the clouds, and its heart was proud of its height, God handed it to the most ruthless of nations, who cut it down (vv. 10-12). Birds now perch on its fallen trunk (v. 13). This is so that no tree will exalt itself; all go down to death (v. 14). When it went down to Sheol, God darkened Lebanon and the nations quaked (vv. 15-17). This is Pharaoh and all his multitude (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Pride of height leads to the pit; learn from the fall of those who were greater than you.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because it towered high and set its top among the clouds, and its heart was proud of its height, I will give it into the hand of a mighty one of the nations. He shall surely deal with it as its wickedness deserves. I have cast it out. Foreigners, the most ruthless of nations, have cut it down and left it. On the mountains and in all the valleys its branches have fallen, and its boughs have been broken in all the ravines of the land, and all the peoples of the earth have gone away from its shadow and left it. On its fallen trunk dwell all the birds of the heavens, and on its branches are all the beasts of the field. All this is in order that no trees by the waters may grow to towering height or set their tops among the clouds, and that no trees that drink water may reach up to them in height. For they are all given over to death, to the world below, among the children of man, with those who go down to the pit. "Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day the cedar went down to Sheol I caused mourning; I closed the deep over it, and restrained its rivers, and many waters were stopped. I clothed Lebanon in gloom for it, and all the trees of the field fainted because of it. I made the nations quake at the sound of its fall, when I cast it down to Sheol with those who go down to the pit. And all the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, all that drink water, were comforted in the world below. They also went down to Sheol with it, to those who are slain by the sword; yes, those who were its arm, who lived under its shadow among the nations. "Whom are you thus like in glory and in greatness among the trees of Eden? You shall be brought down with the trees of Eden to the world below. You shall lie among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword. "This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: Because it towered high and set its top among the clouds, and its heart was proud of its height,

And here is the turn: its heart was proud of its height. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads "you" for it, as if the words slide from Assyria to Pharaoh himself.) The tree forgot who made it beautiful and took pride in its own greatness. It is Nebuchadnezzar's boast in another form: Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power (Dan 4:30).

I will give it into the hand of a mighty one of the nations. He shall surely deal with it as its wickedness deserves. I have cast it out. Foreigners, the most ruthless of nations, have cut it down and left it. On the mountains and in all the valleys its branches have fallen... and all the peoples of the earth have gone away from its shadow and left it.

The great cedar is felled. Its branches lie scattered over mountains and valleys. And the nations who once sheltered in its shade simply walk away. The world's loyalty lasts as long as your power does.

On its fallen trunk dwell all the birds of the heavens, and on its branches are all the beasts of the field.

A sad irony: birds still perch on it — but now on a fallen log.

All this is in order that no trees by the waters may grow to towering height or set their tops among the clouds, and that no trees that drink water may reach up to them in height. For they are all given over to death, to the world below, among the children of man, with those who go down to the pit.

Here is the lesson for every nation and every person: they are all given over to death. However tall the tree, it goes down to the pit among the children of man (the ESV notes, perhaps "of Adam"). Death is the great leveller. For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him (Ps 49:17).

"Thus says the Lord GOD: On the day the cedar went down to Sheol I caused mourning; I closed the deep over it, and restrained its rivers... I clothed Lebanon in gloom for it, and all the trees of the field fainted because of it. I made the nations quake at the sound of its fall... And all the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, all that drink water, were comforted in the world below.

Creation itself mourns. And in the world below, the other fallen trees — the great powers that fell before — are comforted, a grim comfort: at least the mighty Assyria has come down to join them.

They also went down to Sheol with it... those who were its arm, who lived under its shadow among the nations. "Whom are you thus like in glory and in greatness among the trees of Eden? You shall be brought down with the trees of Eden to the world below. You shall lie among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword. "This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD."

And the question comes back: Whom are you thus like? Pharaoh, you think you are like the great cedar? You are. And you will fall like it. This is Pharaoh.

The answer to the pride of height is not merely to fear the fall. It is to find the one tree God himself plants. Ezekiel has already heard of it: a tender sprig planted by God on a high mountain, in whose shade birds of every sort will nest (17:23). Jesus said his kingdom is like that — a small seed that becomes a tree where the birds nest (Mark 4:32). The empires of pride fall. The kingdom of the humble King grows. Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11).

31.title: The Fall of the Great Cedar
31.overview:
God asks Pharaoh whom he resembles in his greatness, and points him to Assyria. Assyria was like a magnificent cedar of Lebanon, towering to the clouds, watered by the deep, sheltering birds, animals and great nations in its shade. No tree in the garden of God could rival it; God made it beautiful, and the trees of Eden envied it (vv. 1-9).

But because it towered high and its heart was proud of its height, God handed it to the most ruthless of nations, who cut it down and left it; its branches fell across the land and the nations left its shade. This is so that no tree will exalt itself, for all are given over to death. When it went down to Sheol, God brought mourning, darkened Lebanon and made the nations quake, while the fallen trees below were comforted. Pharaoh will be brought down the same way: this is Pharaoh and all his multitude (vv. 10-18).
31.theology:
All the greatness of earthly powers is God's gift; he makes them beautiful and waters their roots (vv. 4, 9).

Pride in one's height brings a certain fall (vv. 10-12; Dan 4:30-32; Luke 14:11).

Death levels every great power and person (v. 14; Ps 49:16-17).

God teaches the proud through the fall of those greater than they (vv. 2, 18).

The empires of pride fall, but the kingdom God plants in humility grows to shelter the nations (17:22-24; Mark 4:32).
31.examples:
Whom are you like in your greatness?

A cedar that even the trees of Eden envied.

Nations sheltering in its shade, then walking away.

Birds perching on a fallen trunk.

This is Pharaoh.

They shall tremble every moment, every one for his own life, on the day of your downfall.<sup>11</sup>"For thus says the Lord GOD: The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon you.<sup>12</sup>I will cause your multitude to fall by the swords of mighty ones, all of them most ruthless of nations. "They shall bring to ruin the pride of Egypt, and all its multitude shall perish.<sup>13</sup>I will destroy all its beasts from beside many waters; and no foot of man shall trouble them anymore, nor shall the hoofs of beasts trouble them.<sup>14</sup>Then I will make their waters clear, and cause their rivers to run like oil, declares the Lord GOD.<sup>15</sup>When I make the land of Egypt desolate, and when the land is desolate of all that fills it, when I strike down all who dwell in it, then they will know that I am the LORD.<sup>16</sup>This is a lamentation that shall be chanted; the daughters of the nations shall chant it; over Egypt, and over all her multitude, shall they chant it, declares the Lord GOD."<sup>17</sup>In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me:<sup>18</sup>"Son of man, wail over the multitude of Egypt, and send them down, her and the daughters of majestic nations, to the world below, to those who have gone down to the pit:<sup>19</sup>'Whom do you surpass in beauty? Go down and be laid to rest with the uncircumcised.'<sup>20</sup>They shall fall amid those who are slain by the sword. Egypt is delivered to the sword; drag her away, and all her multitudes.<sup>21</sup>The mighty chiefs shall speak of them, with their helpers, out of the midst of Sheol: 'They have come down, they lie still, the uncircumcised, slain by the sword.'<sup>22</sup>"Assyria is there, and all her company, its graves all around it, all of them slain, fallen by the sword,<sup>23</sup>whose graves are set in the uttermost parts of the pit; and her company is all around her grave, all of them slain, fallen by the sword, who spread terror in the land of the living.<sup>24</sup>"Elam is there, and all her multitude around her grave; all of them slain, fallen by the sword, who went down uncircumcised into the world below, who spread their terror in the land of the living; and they bear their shame with those who go down to the pit.<sup>25</sup>They have made her a bed among the slain with all her multitude, her graves all around it, all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword; for terror of them was spread in the land of the living, and they bear their shame with those who go down to the pit; they are placed among the slain.<sup>26</sup>"Meshech-Tubal is there, and all her multitude, her graves all around it, all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword; for they spread their terror in the land of the living.<sup>27</sup>And they do not lie with the mighty, the fallen from among the uncircumcised, who went down to Sheol with their weapons of war, whose swords were laid under their heads, and whose iniquities are upon their bones; for the terror of the mighty men was in the land of the living.<sup>28</sup>But as for you, you shall be broken and lie among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword.<sup>29</sup>"Edom is there, her kings and all her princes, who for all their might are laid with those who are killed by the sword; and he shall be laid to rest among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A lament for Pharaoh: he thinks himself a lion of the nations, but he is like a dragon in the seas, fouling the rivers (vv. 1-2). God will net him, fling him on the land and feed the birds and beasts with him (vv. 3-6). When I blot you out, I will cover the heavens and make their stars dark (vv. 7-8), and the nations will tremble at his fall (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The proud ruler who troubles the nations will be hauled out by God, and heaven itself darkens at his fall.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, raise a lamentation over Pharaoh king of Egypt and say to him: "You consider yourself a lion of the nations, but you are like a dragon in the seas; you burst forth in your rivers, trouble the waters with your feet, and foul their rivers. Thus says the Lord GOD: I will throw my net over you with a host of many peoples, and they will haul you up in my dragnet. And I will cast you on the ground; on the open field I will fling you, and will cause all the birds of the heavens to settle on you, and I will gorge the beasts of the whole earth with you. I will strew your flesh upon the mountains and fill the valleys with your carcass. I will drench the land even to the mountains with your flowing blood, and the ravines will be full of you. When I blot you out, I will cover the heavens and make their stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of heaven will I make dark over you, and put darkness on your land, declares the Lord GOD. "I will trouble the hearts of many peoples, when I bring your destruction among the nations, into the countries that you have not known. I will make many peoples appalled at you, and the hair of their kings shall bristle with horror because of you, when I brandish my sword before them. They shall tremble every moment, every one for his own life, on the day of your downfall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, raise a lamentation over Pharaoh king of Egypt and say to him: "You consider yourself a lion of the nations, but you are like a dragon in the seas; you burst forth in your rivers, trouble the waters with your feet, and foul their rivers.

This lament is dated after Jerusalem had fallen. Pharaoh sees himself as a lion of the nations — noble, majestic, a king of beasts. God sees a dragon in the seas, a thrashing water monster that muddies every river it moves in. What Pharaoh called leadership, God calls fouling the waters for everyone else.

Leaders often see themselves as lions. God sees the effect of their power on others.

Thus says the Lord GOD: I will throw my net over you with a host of many peoples, and they will haul you up in my dragnet. And I will cast you on the ground; on the open field I will fling you... I will strew your flesh upon the mountains and fill the valleys with your carcass. I will drench the land even to the mountains with your flowing blood.

As in chapter 29, the monster is caught — this time in my dragnet — hauled out and left on the land. The imagery is grisly because the fall of a violent empire is grisly.

When I blot you out, I will cover the heavens and make their stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of heaven will I make dark over you, and put darkness on your land, declares the Lord GOD.

Sun, moon and stars go dark. This is the language the prophets use for the day of the LORD — when a world order collapses under God's judgment, it is as if the lights of heaven go out. Isaiah used it for the fall of Babylon: the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light (Isa 13:10). And Jesus used it for the end of the age: the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light (Matt 24:29). Every such judgment in history is a rehearsal for the last.

"I will trouble the hearts of many peoples, when I bring your destruction among the nations... I will make many peoples appalled at you, and the hair of their kings shall bristle with horror because of you, when I brandish my sword before them. They shall tremble every moment, every one for his own life, on the day of your downfall.

When the mighty fall, the other kings tremble every one for his own life. If Egypt can go, so can they.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon you (v. 11). The most ruthless of nations will ruin Egypt's pride and its multitude (v. 12). The muddied waters will run clear again when no foot troubles them (vv. 13-14). Egypt will be desolate, and the daughters of the nations will chant this lament (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: When God brings down the proud, even the troubled waters are stilled.

verseByVerse.quote: "For thus says the Lord GOD: The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon you. I will cause your multitude to fall by the swords of mighty ones, all of them most ruthless of nations. "They shall bring to ruin the pride of Egypt, and all its multitude shall perish. I will destroy all its beasts from beside many waters; and no foot of man shall trouble them anymore, nor shall the hoofs of beasts trouble them. Then I will make their waters clear, and cause their rivers to run like oil, declares the Lord GOD. When I make the land of Egypt desolate, and when the land is desolate of all that fills it, when I strike down all who dwell in it, then they will know that I am the LORD. This is a lamentation that shall be chanted; the daughters of the nations shall chant it; over Egypt, and over all her multitude, shall they chant it, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus says the Lord GOD: The sword of the king of Babylon shall come upon you. I will cause your multitude to fall by the swords of mighty ones, all of them most ruthless of nations. "They shall bring to ruin the pride of Egypt, and all its multitude shall perish.

The metaphor becomes plain history: The sword of the king of Babylon. And the target is named: the pride of Egypt. God's judgment aims at pride.

I will destroy all its beasts from beside many waters; and no foot of man shall trouble them anymore, nor shall the hoofs of beasts trouble them. Then I will make their waters clear, and cause their rivers to run like oil, declares the Lord GOD.

A striking detail. The dragon had fouled the rivers (v. 2). Once it is gone, I will make their waters clear, and the rivers run smooth like oil. The removal of a violent power brings a kind of peace. The world is quieter when the proud are gone.

When I make the land of Egypt desolate... then they will know that I am the LORD. This is a lamentation that shall be chanted; the daughters of the nations shall chant it; over Egypt, and over all her multitude, shall they chant it, declares the Lord GOD."

Professional mourning women among the nations will sing this dirge. Egypt, which caused so much weeping, will be wept over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–32 — With Those Who Go Down to the Pit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel is to wail over Egypt and send her down to the world below (vv. 17-18): Whom do you surpass in beauty? Go down and be laid to rest with the uncircumcised (v. 19). There already lie Assyria, Elam, Meshech-Tubal, Edom, the princes of the north and the Sidonians — all slain, all who spread terror in the land of the living, all bearing their shame (vv. 20-30). Pharaoh will be grimly comforted to find them there, and will lie among them (vv. 31-32).
verseByVerse.theology: Every power that spread terror on earth ends in the same shameful grave, unless it finds the one who holds the keys of death.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, wail over the multitude of Egypt, and send them down, her and the daughters of majestic nations, to the world below, to those who have gone down to the pit: 'Whom do you surpass in beauty? Go down and be laid to rest with the uncircumcised.' They shall fall amid those who are slain by the sword. Egypt is delivered to the sword; drag her away, and all her multitudes. The mighty chiefs shall speak of them, with their helpers, out of the midst of Sheol: 'They have come down, they lie still, the uncircumcised, slain by the sword.' "Assyria is there, and all her company, its graves all around it, all of them slain, fallen by the sword, whose graves are set in the uttermost parts of the pit; and her company is all around her grave, all of them slain, fallen by the sword, who spread terror in the land of the living. "Elam is there, and all her multitude around her grave; all of them slain, fallen by the sword, who went down uncircumcised into the world below, who spread their terror in the land of the living; and they bear their shame with those who go down to the pit. They have made her a bed among the slain with all her multitude, her graves all around it, all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword; for terror of them was spread in the land of the living, and they bear their shame with those who go down to the pit; they are placed among the slain. "Meshech-Tubal is there, and all her multitude, her graves all around it, all of them uncircumcised, slain by the sword; for they spread their terror in the land of the living. And they do not lie with the mighty, the fallen from among the uncircumcised, who went down to Sheol with their weapons of war, whose swords were laid under their heads, and whose iniquities are upon their bones; for the terror of the mighty men was in the land of the living. But as for you, you shall be broken and lie among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword. "Edom is there, her kings and all her princes, who for all their might are laid with those who are killed by the sword; they lie with the uncircumcised, with those who go down to the pit. "The princes of the north are there, all of them, and all the Sidonians, who have gone down in shame with the slain, for all the terror that they caused by their might; they lie uncircumcised with those who are slain by the sword, and bear their shame with those who go down to the pit. "When Pharaoh sees them, he will be comforted for all his multitude, Pharaoh and all his army, slain by the sword, declares the Lord GOD. For I spread terror in the land of the living; and he shall be laid to rest among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the twelfth year, in the twelfth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to me:

Two weeks later comes the last oracle against the nations, and a haunting one. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks in the twelfth month.) Ezekiel is told to escort Egypt, in words, down into the grave, and to show her who is already there.

"Son of man, wail over the multitude of Egypt, and send them down... to those who have gone down to the pit: 'Whom do you surpass in beauty? Go down and be laid to rest with the uncircumcised.'

Whom do you surpass in beauty? In death, nobody surpasses anybody. All beauty and rank are left at the door.

The mighty chiefs shall speak of them, with their helpers, out of the midst of Sheol: 'They have come down, they lie still, the uncircumcised, slain by the sword.'

The dead rulers greet the new arrivals, just as Isaiah pictured the kings of the underworld rising to greet the fallen king of Babylon: You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us! (Isa 14:10).

Then comes a roll call of the fallen empires. Assyria is there, and all her company, its graves all around it, all of them slain... who spread terror in the land of the living (vv. 22-23). Elam is there (v. 24). Meshech-Tubal is there (v. 26). Edom is there, her kings and all her princes (v. 29). The princes of the north are there, all of them, and all the Sidonians (v. 30).

Listen to the refrain repeated for each: who spread terror in the land of the living. Every one of these powers terrified the world. And every one now bears their shame with those who go down to the pit. The terror they spread on earth becomes the shame they carry below. The mighty who were feared are now helpless.

Verse 27 adds a detail about the fallen warriors, whose swords were laid under their heads, and whose iniquities are upon their bones. They were buried with their weapons as heroes. But what lies on their bones is not glory; it is iniquity.

"When Pharaoh sees them, he will be comforted for all his multitude, Pharaoh and all his army, slain by the sword, declares the Lord GOD. For I spread terror in the land of the living; and he shall be laid to rest among the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword, Pharaoh and all his multitude, declares the Lord GOD."

Pharaoh's only comfort is the bleak comfort of company: he is not the only one. And the last word goes to God: For I spread terror in the land of the living. The nations thought they were the terror of the earth. God is the one whose judgment is to be feared.

This chapter confronts everyone with the grave. It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Heb 9:27). Power, beauty and fame do not go down after us (Ps 49:17).

But the Bible does not leave the pit with the last word. One went down into death who had spread no terror, only mercy — and he came back. The risen Christ says, I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades (Rev 1:18). Because of him, Paul can taunt the grave: O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?... thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor 15:55, 57).

And the nations in the pit are not beyond the reach of the gospel's call. On the day of Pentecost, among those who heard the mighty works of God in their own tongues were Elamites and visitors from Egypt (Acts 2:9-10). The empires went down. Their peoples were invited up.

32.title: Down to the Pit
32.overview:
Ezekiel laments over Pharaoh, who thinks himself a lion of the nations but is like a dragon thrashing in the rivers and fouling them. God will catch him in his net with many peoples, fling him on the land and feed the birds and beasts with his body. When God blots him out, he will darken the sun, moon and stars, and the nations and their kings will tremble at his fall (vv. 1-10).

The sword of the king of Babylon will come and ruin Egypt's pride; its beasts will be destroyed, and its muddied waters will run clear. The daughters of the nations will chant this lament over Egypt (vv. 11-16).

Two weeks later Ezekiel is told to wail over Egypt and send her down to the world below. There, among the uncircumcised slain, already lie Assyria, Elam, Meshech-Tubal, Edom, the princes of the north and the Sidonians — all who spread terror in the land of the living and now bear their shame in the pit. Pharaoh will be comforted only to find them there, and he and his multitude will lie among them (vv. 17-32).
32.theology:
God sees the true effect of proud power: not a noble lion but a dragon fouling the waters (v. 2).

Cosmic darkening is the prophetic language of God's judgment on world powers, previewing the last day (vv. 7-8; Isa 13:10; Matt 24:29).

God aims his judgment at pride (v. 12).

Death levels all powers; those who spread terror on earth bear shame in the grave (vv. 18-32; Isa 14:9-11; Heb 9:27; Ps 49:17).

Christ holds the keys of death and gives victory over the grave; the gospel calls the peoples of the fallen empires (Rev 1:18; 1 Cor 15:54-57; Acts 2:9-10).
32.examples:
A self-styled lion who is really a monster muddying the river.

The lights of heaven going out over a fallen empire.

Waters running clear again.

A roll call of empires in the grave.

Swords under their heads, iniquity on their bones.

The comfort of company in the pit.

The one who holds the keys.

shall you then possess the land?<sup>27</sup>Say this to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: As I live, surely those who are in the waste places shall fall by the sword, and whoever is in the open field I will give to the beasts to be devoured, and those who are in strongholds and in caves shall die by pestilence.<sup>28</sup>And I will make the land a desolation and a waste, and her proud might shall come to an end, and the mountains of Israel shall be so desolate that none will pass through.<sup>29</sup>Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have made the land a desolation and a waste because of all their abominations that they have committed.<sup>30</sup>"As for you, son of man, your people who talk together about you by the walls and at the doors of the houses say to one another, each to his brother, 'Come, and hear what the word is that comes from the LORD.'<sup>31</sup>And they come to you as people come, and they sit before you as my people, and they hear what you say but they will not do it; for with lustful talk in their mouths they act; their heart is set on their gain.<sup>32</sup>And behold, you are to them like one who sings lustful songs with a beautiful voice and plays well on an instrument, for they hear what you say, but they will not do it.<sup>33</sup>When this comes—and come it will!— then they will know that a prophet has been among them."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God repeats Ezekiel's commission. When a watchman sees the sword coming and blows the trumpet, anyone who ignores it is responsible for his own death (vv. 2-5); if the watchman stays silent, their blood is on his hands (v. 6). So you, son of man, I have made a watchman for the house of Israel (v. 7), responsible to warn the wicked, whether they turn or not (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The messenger must warn, and the hearer must heed.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, speak to your people and say to them, If I bring the sword upon a land, and the people of the land take a man from among them, and make him their watchman, and if he sees the sword coming upon the land and blows the trumpet and warns the people, then if anyone who hears the sound of the trumpet does not take warning, and the sword comes and takes him away, his blood shall be upon his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet and did not take warning; his blood shall be upon himself. But if he had taken warning, he would have saved his life. But if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, so that the people are not warned, and the sword comes and takes any one of them, that person is taken away in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to me:

Chapter 33 is a hinge in the book of Ezekiel. Before it, chapters 1-24 warned Jerusalem, and chapters 25-32 judged the nations. Now the news of Jerusalem's fall is about to arrive (v. 21), and a new phase of ministry will begin. God starts it by renewing Ezekiel's call, just as he did at the beginning (3:16-21).

"Son of man, speak to your people and say to them, If I bring the sword upon a land, and the people of the land take a man from among them, and make him their watchman,

and if he sees the sword coming upon the land and blows the trumpet and warns the people,

then if anyone who hears the sound of the trumpet does not take warning, and the sword comes and takes him away, his blood shall be upon his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet and did not take warning; his blood shall be upon himself. But if he had taken warning, he would have saved his life.

This time the picture starts with the people's side. Everyone understood how a watchman worked. If he blew the trumpet and you stayed in bed, your death was your own fault. He heard the sound of the trumpet and did not take warning.

And the tragic line: But if he had taken warning, he would have saved his life. The warning was the offer of life. Ignoring it was choosing death.

But if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, so that the people are not warned, and the sword comes and takes any one of them, that person is taken away in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand.

And the other side: a silent watchman is guilty. Both the preacher and the hearer carry responsibility. See that you do not refuse him who is speaking (Heb 12:25).

verseByVerse.quote: "So you, son of man, I have made a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me. If I say to the wicked, O wicked one, you shall surely die, and you do not speak to warn the wicked to turn from his way, that wicked person shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand. But if you warn the wicked to turn from his way, and he does not turn from his way, that person shall die in his iniquity, but you will have delivered your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So you, son of man, I have made a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me.

If I say to the wicked, O wicked one, you shall surely die, and you do not speak to warn the wicked to turn from his way, that wicked person shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand.

But if you warn the wicked to turn from his way, and he does not turn from his way, that person shall die in his iniquity, but you will have delivered your soul.

These verses repeat almost word for word what God said at the start (3:17-19). Why repeat it? Because after the fall of Jerusalem, Ezekiel's message will change from warning to hope, and it would be easy to think the watchman's job was over. It is not. Even a message of hope must include the warning that people must turn. Grace that never calls anyone to repent is not the grace of the Bible.

For every pastor and every Christian who shares the gospel: the watchman's trumpet is not only bad news. It sounds so that people can be saved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — How Then Can We Live?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The exiles now say, Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live? (v. 10). God answers, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn back, turn back (v. 11). Past righteousness will not save a person who turns to sin, and past sin will not condemn a wicked person who turns and makes restitution; none of his sins will be remembered (vv. 12-16). God's way is just; he judges each by his ways (vv. 17-20).
verseByVerse.theology: Despair over sin is answered by God's plea to turn and live, and by the promise that the repentant sinner's sins are not remembered.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, son of man, say to the house of Israel, Thus have you said: 'Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?' Say to them, As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And you, son of man, say to the house of Israel, Thus have you said: 'Surely our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?'

Listen to how the exiles are now talking. For years they denied their guilt: it was their fathers' fault (18:2), or God was unjust (18:25). Now they have swung to the opposite extreme: our transgressions and our sins are upon us, and we rot away because of them. How then can we live?

From denial to despair. That is a common path. First we insist we are not that bad. Then, when the truth sinks in, we conclude it is hopeless. My iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me (Ps 38:4). Both denial and despair keep a person away from God.

Say to them, As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?

And God's answer to despair is the same as his answer to denial: turn back, turn back. With an oath — As I live — he declares that he takes no pleasure in anyone's death. He wants them to live.

If you feel crushed by your sins, that weight is not meant to drive you away from God but to him. If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness (Ps 130:3-4). Jesus says, Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28). The question "How can we live?" has an answer: by turning to the God who does not want you to die.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, son of man, say to your people, The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him when he transgresses, and as for the wickedness of the wicked, he shall not fall by it when he turns from his wickedness, and the righteous shall not be able to live by his righteousness when he sins. Though I say to the righteous that he shall surely live, yet if he trusts in his righteousness and does injustice, none of his righteous deeds shall be remembered, but in his injustice that he has done he shall die. Again, though I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' yet if he turns from his sin and does what is just and right, if the wicked restores the pledge, gives back what he has taken by robbery, and walks in the statutes of life, not doing injustice, he shall surely live; he shall not die. None of the sins that he has committed shall be remembered against him. He has done what is just and right; he shall surely live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And you, son of man, say to your people, The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him when he transgresses, and as for the wickedness of the wicked, he shall not fall by it when he turns from his wickedness, and the righteous shall not be able to live by his righteousness when he sins.

The principle of chapter 18 is restated. The past does not decide the future. A good record is no insurance for someone who turns away; a bad record is no prison for someone who turns back. (The ESV notes that by his righteousness is literally "by it".)

Though I say to the righteous that he shall surely live, yet if he trusts in his righteousness and does injustice, none of his righteous deeds shall be remembered, but in his injustice that he has done he shall die.

Notice the phrase if he trusts in his righteousness. The danger is not only turning to sin but trusting in one's own goodness as a licence. The person who thinks, "I've been faithful for years; a little compromise won't matter," has already stopped trusting God.

Again, though I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' yet if he turns from his sin and does what is just and right, if the wicked restores the pledge, gives back what he has taken by robbery, and walks in the statutes of life, not doing injustice, he shall surely live; he shall not die.

Real repentance is practical. It restores the pledge and gives back what he has taken by robbery. When Zacchaeus met Jesus, he said, if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold (Luke 19:8). Turning to God includes making things right with people, wherever that can be done.

And the phrase the statutes of life is beautiful. God's commands are not a cage but a way of life.

None of the sins that he has committed shall be remembered against him. He has done what is just and right; he shall surely live.

None of the sins... shall be remembered. That is the answer to our sins are upon us (v. 10). The sins that were crushing them can be lifted and forgotten by God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet your people say, 'The way of the Lord is not just,' when it is their own way that is not just. When the righteous turns from his righteousness and does injustice, he shall die for it. And when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does what is just and right, he shall live by this. Yet you say, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' O house of Israel, I will judge each of you according to his ways."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Yet your people say, 'The way of the Lord is not just,' when it is their own way that is not just.

When the righteous turns from his righteousness and does injustice, he shall die for it. And when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does what is just and right, he shall live by this.

Yet you say, 'The way of the Lord is not just.' O house of Israel, I will judge each of you according to his ways."

The complaint of chapter 18 is still around: The way of the Lord is not just. People object that it is unfair for God to forgive a wicked person who turns, or to condemn someone who had lived well and then turned away.

But God's way is simply this: he looks at where a person is heading and whom they are trusting. I will judge each of you according to his ways. That is perfectly just. What would be unjust is a God who condemned the repentant or excused the rebellious. The ones who complain are usually the ones who do not want to repent.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–22 — The City Has Been Struck Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the twelfth year of the exile a survivor arrives: The city has been struck down (v. 21). The evening before, God had opened Ezekiel's mouth, and I was no longer mute (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: When God's word is fulfilled, his messenger's mouth is opened to speak hope.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twelfth year of our exile, in the tenth month, on the fifth day of the month, a fugitive from Jerusalem came to me and said, "The city has been struck down." Now the hand of the LORD had been upon me the evening before the fugitive came; and he had opened my mouth by the time the man came to me in the morning, so my mouth was opened, and I was no longer mute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the twelfth year of our exile, in the tenth month, on the fifth day of the month, a fugitive from Jerusalem came to me and said, "The city has been struck down."

Here is the moment the whole first half of the book has been leading to. A survivor, exhausted from the long journey, stumbles into the exile settlement with five words: The city has been struck down.

The walls had been breached months before (Jer 39:2), and the news had only now reached Babylon. Everything Ezekiel had acted out — the brick, the siege, the shaved hair, the baggage through the wall — had come true. The unthinkable had happened. Jerusalem was gone.

Imagine the scene among the exiles. The hopes of a quick return, the promises of the false prophets, the confidence that God would never let his temple fall — all collapsed in a single sentence.

Now the hand of the LORD had been upon me the evening before the fugitive came; and he had opened my mouth by the time the man came to me in the morning, so my mouth was opened, and I was no longer mute.

And at exactly that moment, Ezekiel's long silence ends (3:26-27; 24:27). God opened his mouth the night before the news arrived, so that when the people were ready to listen, the prophet was ready to speak.

And what will he speak? Not more judgment on the city. That word has been fulfilled. From here on, Ezekiel's message will turn to hope: a true shepherd (ch. 34), a new heart (ch. 36), dry bones living (ch. 37), a new temple (chs. 40-48). The prophet who was silent while the people were proud will speak comfort now that they are broken. It is the same pattern as Isaiah: after the judgment, Comfort, comfort my people (Isa 40:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — Abraham Was Only One Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The survivors in the ruined land reason, Abraham was only one man, yet he got possession of the land; but we are many (v. 24). God answers: you eat blood, worship idols, shed blood, rely on the sword and commit adultery — shall you then possess the land? (vv. 25-26). Sword, beasts and pestilence will reach them, and the land will be desolate (vv. 27-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Claiming the promises of God while living in rebellion against him is presumption, not faith.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, the inhabitants of these waste places in the land of Israel keep saying, 'Abraham was only one man, yet he got possession of the land; but we are many; the land is surely given us to possess.' Therefore say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: You eat flesh with the blood and lift up your eyes to your idols and shed blood; shall you then possess the land? You rely on the sword, you commit abominations, and each of you defiles his neighbor's wife; shall you then possess the land?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD came to me: "Son of man, the inhabitants of these waste places in the land of Israel keep saying, 'Abraham was only one man, yet he got possession of the land; but we are many; the land is surely given us to possess.'

Even after the catastrophe, some people have not learned. The survivors left in the ruins of Judah have a new argument: Abraham was only one man, yet he got possession of the land; but we are many. If God gave the land to one man, surely he will give it to all of us. We are the heirs of the promise.

It sounds like faith. It is presumption. They claim Abraham's promise without Abraham's faith. John the Baptist confronted the same attitude: do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father' (Matt 3:9). Jesus said, If you were Abraham's children, you would be doing the works Abraham did (John 8:39).

Therefore say to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: You eat flesh with the blood and lift up your eyes to your idols and shed blood; shall you then possess the land?

You rely on the sword, you commit abominations, and each of you defiles his neighbor's wife; shall you then possess the land?

Twice: shall you then possess the land? They broke the food laws, worshipped idols, murdered, trusted violence and committed adultery — and still expected God's blessing.

That is always the danger of claiming God's promises without living under his lordship. The New Testament says the true children of Abraham are those of faith (Gal 3:7), and the promise comes through the righteousness of faith (Rom 4:13). Faith that is real shows itself in turning from sin. A promise claimed by people who despise the Promiser is not faith but presumption.

verseByVerse.quote: Say this to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: As I live, surely those who are in the waste places shall fall by the sword, and whoever is in the open field I will give to the beasts to be devoured, and those who are in strongholds and in caves shall die by pestilence. And I will make the land a desolation and a waste, and her proud might shall come to an end, and the mountains of Israel shall be so desolate that none will pass through. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have made the land a desolation and a waste because of all their abominations that they have committed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Say this to them, Thus says the Lord GOD: As I live, surely those who are in the waste places shall fall by the sword, and whoever is in the open field I will give to the beasts to be devoured, and those who are in strongholds and in caves shall die by pestilence.

Wherever they hide — in the ruins, in the open country, in caves and strongholds — judgment will find them. The survivors who presumed on God's promise will not inherit it.

And I will make the land a desolation and a waste, and her proud might shall come to an end, and the mountains of Israel shall be so desolate that none will pass through. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have made the land a desolation and a waste because of all their abominations that they have committed.

Her proud might shall come to an end. The same words were used of Egypt (30:18); now they are used of Israel. God's people who behave like the nations will be judged like the nations.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: People talk about Ezekiel in doorways and invite one another to come and hear the word of the LORD (v. 30). They sit before him and listen, but they do not do what he says; their hearts are set on gain (v. 31). You are to them like one who sings lustful songs with a beautiful voice and plays well on an instrument, for they hear what you say, but they will not do it (v. 32). When this comes—and come it will!— then they will know that a prophet has been among them (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: Enjoying the preaching of God's word without obeying it is a dangerous self-deception.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, son of man, your people who talk together about you by the walls and at the doors of the houses say to one another, each to his brother, 'Come, and hear what the word is that comes from the LORD.' And they come to you as people come, and they sit before you as my people, and they hear what you say but they will not do it; for with lustful talk in their mouths they act; their heart is set on their gain. And behold, you are to them like one who sings lustful songs with a beautiful voice and plays well on an instrument, for they hear what you say, but they will not do it. When this comes—and come it will!— then they will know that a prophet has been among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As for you, son of man, your people who talk together about you by the walls and at the doors of the houses say to one another, each to his brother, 'Come, and hear what the word is that comes from the LORD.'

Now that Ezekiel has been proved right, he has become popular. People talk about him in the street and on their doorsteps. Come, and hear what the word is that comes from the LORD. It sounds like revival.

And they come to you as people come, and they sit before you as my people, and they hear what you say but they will not do it; for with lustful talk in their mouths they act; their heart is set on their gain.

But God sees beneath the surface. They come... they sit... they hear... but they will not do it. Their mouths are full of the language of desire, and their heart is set on their gain. They come to hear God's word, and leave unchanged.

And behold, you are to them like one who sings lustful songs with a beautiful voice and plays well on an instrument, for they hear what you say, but they will not do it.

Here is a painfully honest picture of how preaching can be received. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is literally "like the singing of lustful songs with a beautiful voice". To the people, Ezekiel is entertainment — a talented performer with a beautiful voice. They enjoy the sermon the way they enjoy a love song. They admire the delivery. And they go home and do nothing.

Herod was like that with John the Baptist: When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly (Mark 6:20) — and he still had him killed. Felix listened to Paul speak about judgment, was alarmed, and said, Go away for the present (Acts 24:25).

This is a sharp warning for church-going people. It is possible to love good preaching and never obey it. Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves (Jas 1:22). Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and not do what I tell you? (Luke 6:46). The question to ask after every sermon is not "Did I enjoy that?" but "What must I do?"

When this comes—and come it will!— then they will know that a prophet has been among them."

And the chapter closes with the words of Ezekiel's first commission: they will know that a prophet has been among them (2:5). One day, what he said will come to pass, and they will realise too late that it was not a song. It was the word of God.

33.title: Hearers but Not Doers
33.overview:
God renews Ezekiel's calling as a watchman. A watchman who blows the trumpet is innocent if people ignore him; one who stays silent is guilty of their blood. So Ezekiel must warn the wicked, whether or not they turn (vv. 1-9).

The exiles, now overwhelmed by their sins, ask how they can live. God swears he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked and calls them to turn back and live. A righteous person who trusts in his righteousness and turns to sin will not be saved by his past; a wicked person who turns, restores what he has taken and walks in the statutes of life will live, and none of his sins will be remembered. When they say God's way is not just, he answers that it is their way that is unjust; he will judge each by his ways (vv. 10-20).

In the twelfth year of the exile a fugitive from Jerusalem arrives with the news that the city has been struck down. God had opened Ezekiel's mouth the evening before, and he is no longer mute (vv. 21-22).

The survivors in the ruined land claim that since Abraham, one man, possessed the land, they, being many, will surely possess it. But they eat blood, worship idols, shed blood, rely on the sword and commit adultery; they will not possess the land, and it will be made desolate (vv. 23-29).

The exiles now talk about Ezekiel and come to hear the word of the LORD, but they do not do it; their hearts are set on gain. To them he is like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice. When his words come true, they will know that a prophet has been among them (vv. 30-33).
33.theology:
The messenger is responsible to warn and the hearer to heed; even a message of hope must call people to turn (vv. 1-9; Heb 12:25).

Both denial of sin and despair over sin keep people from God; his answer to both is to turn and live (vv. 10-11; Ps 130:3-4; Matt 11:28).

Real repentance is practical and includes restitution; God does not remember the sins of the repentant (vv. 14-16; Luke 19:8).

God judges each person justly by the direction of his life (vv. 17-20).

God's word is fulfilled, and he opens his servant's mouth to speak hope at the right time (vv. 21-22; 3:26-27; 24:27).

Claiming God's promises while living in rebellion is presumption; Abraham's true children share his faith (vv. 24-26; Matt 3:9; John 8:39; Gal 3:7).

Enjoying preaching without obeying it is self-deception (vv. 30-32; Jas 1:22-25; Luke 6:46; Mark 6:20).
33.examples:
A trumpet blown, and a man who stayed in bed.

From 'we're not that bad' to 'there's no hope'.

A thief giving back what he stole.

Five words from a fugitive: the city has been struck down.

A mouth opened the night before the news arrived.

We are Abraham's heirs — with idols in our hands.

A congregation that loves the preacher's voice and goes home unchanged.

Should not shepherds feed the sheep?<sup>3</sup>You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones, but you do not feed the sheep.<sup>4</sup>The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up, the strayed you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and with force and harshness you have ruled them.<sup>5</sup>So they were scattered, because there was no shepherd, and they became food for all the wild beasts. My sheep were scattered;<sup>6</sup>they wandered over all the mountains and on every high hill. I am the LORD; I have spoken.<sup>25</sup>"I will make with them a covenant of peace and banish wild beasts from the land, so that they may dwell securely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods.<sup>26</sup>And I will make them and the places all around my hill a blessing, and I will send down the showers in their season; they shall be showers of blessing.<sup>27</sup>And the trees of the field shall yield their fruit, and the earth shall yield its increase, and they shall be secure in their land.
