verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — On a Very High Mountain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Fourteen years after Jerusalem fell, God brings Ezekiel in visions of God to a very high mountain in the land of Israel, where there is something like a city (vv. 1-2). A man like bronze, holding a linen cord and a measuring reed, stands in the gateway (v. 3) and tells him: look with your eyes, and hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you... Declare all that you see to the house of Israel (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: After the ruin, God gives his people a vision of his dwelling restored in perfect order.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-fifth year of our exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month, in the fourteenth year after the city was struck down, on that very day, the hand of the LORD was upon me, and he brought me to the city. In visions of God he brought me to the land of Israel, and set me down on a very high mountain, on which was a structure like a city to the south. When he brought me there, behold, there was a man whose appearance was like bronze, with a linen cord and a measuring reed in his hand. And he was standing in the gateway. And the man said to me, "Son of man, look with your eyes, and hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you, for you were brought here in order that I might show it to you. Declare all that you see to the house of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the twenty-fifth year of our exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month, in the fourteenth year after the city was struck down, on that very day, the hand of the LORD was upon me, and he brought me to the city.

The last nine chapters of Ezekiel are one long vision. Fourteen years after Jerusalem was destroyed — when the temple had lain in ashes for well over a decade — God shows Ezekiel a new temple, a restored land and a holy city. The book that began with the glory of God in Babylon ends with the glory of God coming home.

These chapters are full of measurements, and they are rarely read. But they matter. Ezekiel was a priest who had watched the glory leave a defiled temple. Now God shows him a perfect one.

How should they be read? Faithful Christians have understood them in different ways. Some believe they describe a literal temple still to be built in the future. Others think they gave a plan for the returning exiles that was never carried out. Many, especially in the Reformed tradition, read them as a symbolic vision, in the language of temple and priesthood that Ezekiel knew, of God dwelling in perfect holiness with a purified people — fulfilled in Christ, who called his body the temple (John 2:21), in the church, a dwelling place for God by the Spirit (Eph 2:22), and finally in the new creation, where John saw a city measured by an angel with a river of life flowing from the throne (Rev 21-22). Whatever the reading, the heart of the vision is the same: a holy God living among his people forever.

In visions of God he brought me to the land of Israel, and set me down on a very high mountain, on which was a structure like a city to the south.

A very high mountain. Isaiah had foreseen that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established as the highest of the mountains (Isa 2:2). And John was carried in the Spirit to a great, high mountain and shown the holy city Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God (Rev 21:10).

When he brought me there, behold, there was a man whose appearance was like bronze, with a linen cord and a measuring reed in his hand. And he was standing in the gateway.

A heavenly guide, gleaming like bronze, with measuring tools. In the Bible, measuring something often means claiming it, protecting it and setting it apart for God. Zechariah saw a man with a measuring line in his hand measuring Jerusalem, and God said, I will be to her a wall of fire all around... and I will be the glory in her midst (Zech 2:1, 5). John was told, Rise and measure the temple of God (Rev 11:1).

And the man said to me, "Son of man, look with your eyes, and hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you, for you were brought here in order that I might show it to you. Declare all that you see to the house of Israel."

Three commands: look... hear... set your heart. This is not dry architecture. It is to be received with the heart. And it is for the people: Declare all that you see to the house of Israel. Exiles who had lost everything needed to see that God's dwelling with them had a future.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A wall surrounds the temple area (v. 5). The man measures the east gate: its steps, threshold, side rooms for guards, vestibule, jambs, windows and palm tree decorations (vv. 6-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The way into God's presence is guarded, ordered and beautiful.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, there was a wall all around the outside of the temple area, and the length of the measuring reed in the man's hand was six long cubits, each being a cubit and a handbreadth in length. So he measured the thickness of the wall, one reed; and the height, one reed. Then he went into the gateway facing east, going up its steps, and measured the threshold of the gate, one reed deep. And the side rooms, one reed long and one reed broad; and the space between the side rooms, five cubits; and the threshold of the gate by the vestibule of the gate at the inner end, one reed. Then he measured the vestibule of the gateway, on the inside, one reed. Then he measured the vestibule of the gateway, eight cubits; and its jambs, two cubits; and the vestibule of the gate was at the inner end. And there were three side rooms on either side of the east gate. The three were of the same size, and the jambs on either side were of the same size. Then he measured the width of the opening of the gateway, ten cubits; and the length of the gateway, thirteen cubits. There was a barrier before the side rooms, one cubit on either side. And the side rooms were six cubits on either side. Then he measured the gate from the ceiling of the one side room to the ceiling of the other, a breadth of twenty-five cubits; the openings faced each other. He measured also the vestibule, sixty cubits. And around the vestibule of the gateway was the court. From the front of the gate at the entrance to the front of the inner vestibule of the gate was fifty cubits. And the gateway had windows all around, narrowing inwards toward the side rooms and toward their jambs, and likewise the vestibule had windows all around inside, and on the jambs were palm trees.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, there was a wall all around the outside of the temple area, and the length of the measuring reed in the man's hand was six long cubits, each being a cubit and a handbreadth in length. So he measured the thickness of the wall, one reed; and the height, one reed.

The first thing Ezekiel sees is a wall. Using the ESV's note, a cubit was about eighteen inches and a handbreadth about three, so the reed of six long cubits was roughly ten feet. The wall is as thick as it is high.

Why start with a wall? Because the problem with the old temple was that there was no real separation between the holy and the common. Idols stood at the altar gate; men worshipped the sun in the inner court (ch. 8). This wall marks a clear boundary. Holiness is not casual.

Then the man measures the east gate in detail (vv. 6-16): steps up to it, a threshold, three guard rooms on each side, a vestibule, jambs, and windows all around. And on the jambs were palm trees (v. 16).

Palm trees were carved in Solomon's temple too, with cherubim and flowers (1 Kgs 6:29). They recall a garden. God's house is decorated like Eden, the first place where God walked with people. The way into God's presence is guarded, but it leads into paradise.

The east gate is measured first because it faces the rising sun and the Mount of Olives — the direction from which the glory left (11:23) and the direction from which it will return (43:1-2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — The Outer Court and Its Gates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the outer court are chambers and a pavement (vv. 17-18). The north and south gates match the east gate exactly, each with seven steps (vv. 19-27).
verseByVerse.theology: God's house is built with perfect symmetry, open on every side yet entered with care.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me into the outer court. And behold, there were chambers and a pavement, all around the court. Thirty chambers faced the pavement. And the pavement ran along the side of the gates, corresponding to the length of the gates. This was the lower pavement. Then he measured the distance from the inner front of the lower gate to the outer front of the inner court, a hundred cubits on the east side and on the north side. As for the gate that faced toward the north, belonging to the outer court, he measured its length and its breadth. Its side rooms, three on either side, and its jambs and its vestibule were of the same size as those of the first gate. Its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth twenty-five cubits. And its windows, its vestibule, and its palm trees were of the same size as those of the gate that faced toward the east. And by seven steps people would go up to it, and find its vestibule before them. And opposite the gate on the north, as on the east, was a gate to the inner court. And he measured from gate to gate, a hundred cubits. And he led me toward the south, and behold, there was a gate on the south. And he measured its jambs and its vestibule; they had the same size as the others. Both it and its vestibule had windows all around, like the windows of the others. Its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth twenty-five cubits. And there were seven steps leading up to it, and its vestibule was before them, and it had palm trees on its jambs, one on either side. And there was a gate on the south of the inner court. And he measured from gate to gate toward the south, a hundred cubits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he brought me into the outer court. And behold, there were chambers and a pavement, all around the court. Thirty chambers faced the pavement.

Inside the wall is the outer court, with a paved area and thirty rooms around it — perhaps for worshippers to gather and eat their sacrificial meals.

Then the man measures the north gate and the south gate (vv. 20-27), and they are exactly the same as the east gate: the same side rooms, the same vestibule, the same windows, the same palm trees, the same fifty by twenty-five cubits. And by seven steps people would go up to it (v. 22).

The repetition is deliberate. Every gate is identical. There is order, symmetry and balance in God's house. Nothing is haphazard. The chaos and corruption of the old temple are replaced by perfect proportion.

And there are gates on every side (except the west, where the temple building itself stands). God's people come from every direction. John saw the same in the new Jerusalem: on the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates (Rev 21:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The inner court has matching gates on the south, east and north, each reached by eight steps and decorated with palm trees (vv. 28-37).
verseByVerse.theology: Drawing nearer to God means going higher, step by step.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me to the inner court through the south gate, and he measured the south gate. It was of the same size as the others. Its side rooms, its jambs, and its vestibule were of the same size as the others, and both it and its vestibule had windows all around. Its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth twenty-five cubits. And there were vestibules all around, twenty-five cubits long and five cubits broad. Its vestibule faced the outer court, and palm trees were on its jambs, and its stairway had eight steps. Then he brought me to the inner court on the east side, and he measured the gate. It was of the same size as the others. Its side rooms, its jambs, and its vestibule were of the same size as the others, and both it and its vestibule had windows all around. Its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth twenty-five cubits. Its vestibule faced the outer court, and it had palm trees on its jambs, on either side, and its stairway had eight steps. Then he brought me to the north gate, and he measured it. It had the same size as the others. Its side rooms, its jambs, and its vestibule were of the same size as the others, and it had windows all around. Its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth twenty-five cubits. Its vestibule faced the outer court, and it had palm trees on its jambs, on either side, and its stairway had eight steps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he brought me to the inner court through the south gate, and he measured the south gate. It was of the same size as the others.

Now into the inner court, through a second set of gates on the south, east and north, each matching the outer gates. Its stairway had eight steps (vv. 31, 34, 37).

Notice the steps. Seven steps up to the outer gates; eight more up to the inner gates; later, ten steps up to the temple itself (v. 49). The whole complex rises in levels. To come nearer to God is to go higher.

That is how worshippers have always felt. Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart (Ps 24:3-4). The question those steps raise is: who can climb them? No one, by his own purity. Only one has clean hands and a pure heart, and he takes his people with him. I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved (John 10:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38–49 — Tables for Sacrifice, Rooms for Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the inner gate are tables for slaughtering burnt, sin and guilt offerings (vv. 38-43). Rooms are set aside for the priests who keep the temple and the altar, the sons of Zadok, who alone among the sons of Levi may come near to the LORD to minister to him (vv. 44-46). The inner court is a perfect square, with the altar before the temple, whose vestibule is reached by ten steps (vv. 47-49).
verseByVerse.theology: Access to God is by sacrifice and through appointed priests — a pattern fulfilled in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a chamber with its door in the vestibule of the gate, where the burnt offering was to be washed. And in the vestibule of the gate were two tables on either side, on which the burnt offering and the sin offering and the guilt offering were to be slaughtered. And off to the side, on the outside as one goes up to the entrance of the north gate, were two tables; and off to the other side of the vestibule of the gate were two tables. Four tables were on either side of the gate, eight tables, on which to slaughter. And there were four tables of hewn stone for the burnt offering, a cubit and a half long, and a cubit and a half broad, and one cubit high, on which the instruments were to be laid with which the burnt offerings and the sacrifices were slaughtered. And hooks, a handbreadth long, were fastened all around within. And on the tables the flesh of the offering was to be laid. On the outside of the inner gateway there were two chambers in the inner court, one at the side of the north gate facing south, the other at the side of the south gate facing north. And he said to me, "This chamber that faces south is for the priests who have charge of the temple, and the chamber that faces north is for the priests who have charge of the altar. These are the sons of Zadok, who alone among the sons of Levi may come near to the LORD to minister to him." And he measured the court, a hundred cubits long and a hundred cubits broad, a square. And the altar was in front of the temple. Then he brought me to the vestibule of the temple and measured the jambs of the vestibule, five cubits on either side. And the breadth of the gate was fourteen cubits, and the sidewalls of the gate were three cubits on either side. The length of the vestibule was twenty cubits, and the breadth twelve cubits, and people would go up to it by ten steps. And there were pillars beside the jambs, one on either side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a chamber with its door in the vestibule of the gate, where the burnt offering was to be washed. And in the vestibule of the gate were two tables on either side, on which the burnt offering and the sin offering and the guilt offering were to be slaughtered.

At the inner gate are rooms for washing the sacrifices and stone tables for slaughtering them: burnt offerings, sin offerings, guilt offerings (vv. 38-43). The way to the altar goes past the place of sacrifice.

This is one of the places where readers of Ezekiel ask hard questions. If Christ has come, why does the vision include sacrifices? Those who expect a literal future temple often understand these as memorials looking back to the cross. Those who read the vision symbolically understand Ezekiel to be describing true worship in the only terms he and his hearers knew — terms that the New Testament shows are fulfilled in Christ. On any reading, Hebrews is clear: when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, and Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin (Heb 10:12, 18). The tables of Ezekiel 40 point to the one sacrifice that makes all others unnecessary.

On the outside of the inner gateway there were two chambers in the inner court... And he said to me, "This chamber that faces south is for the priests who have charge of the temple, and the chamber that faces north is for the priests who have charge of the altar. These are the sons of Zadok, who alone among the sons of Levi may come near to the LORD to minister to him."

Rooms for the priests (the ESV notes that the Hebrew reads "chambers for singers" where it follows the Septuagint). And a special place for the sons of Zadok, the priestly family Solomon installed (1 Kgs 2:35) that had remained faithful. Chapter 44 will explain why. Faithfulness matters to God, and he remembers it.

And he measured the court, a hundred cubits long and a hundred cubits broad, a square. And the altar was in front of the temple.

A perfect square, and at its centre the altar. Everything in the vision is ordered around the place of sacrifice, just in front of the house of God.

Then he brought me to the vestibule of the temple... The length of the vestibule was twenty cubits, and the breadth twelve cubits, and people would go up to it by ten steps. And there were pillars beside the jambs, one on either side.

And finally the entrance to the temple building itself, up ten more steps, with pillars on either side.

For the exiles sitting by the canals of Babylon, with the real temple a burnt ruin, every measurement said something: God has not finished with his dwelling place. For Christians it says more. Something greater than the temple is here, Jesus said (Matt 12:6). He is the true temple, his people are being built into God's house, and one day we will live in the city where its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev 21:22).

40.title: The Measured Temple
40.overview:
In the twenty-fifth year of the exile, fourteen years after Jerusalem fell, God brings Ezekiel in visions to a very high mountain in the land of Israel, where there is a structure like a city. A man shining like bronze, with a measuring line and reed, tells him to look, listen and pay close attention, and to declare everything he sees to Israel (vv. 1-4).

The man measures the wall around the temple area and the east gate with its steps, guard rooms, vestibule, windows and palm tree carvings (vv. 5-16). He shows Ezekiel the outer court with its chambers and pavement, and measures the north and south gates, which match the east gate exactly (vv. 17-27). He measures the three gates of the inner court, each reached by eight steps (vv. 28-37).

At the inner gate are tables for slaughtering burnt, sin and guilt offerings. Rooms are set aside for the priests who keep the temple and the altar, the sons of Zadok, who alone may come near to minister to the LORD. The inner court is a perfect square with the altar before the temple, and the temple's vestibule is reached by ten steps (vv. 38-49).

Chapters 40-48 have been read as a future literal temple, as a plan for the returning exiles, or as a symbolic vision of God's perfect dwelling with a purified people fulfilled in Christ, the church and the new creation. All readings share the vision's heart: a holy God dwelling among his people.
40.theology:
After judgment God gives his people a vision of his dwelling restored in perfect holiness and order (vv. 1-4).

Measuring marks God's ownership and protection of what is his (vv. 3, 5; Zech 2:1-5; Rev 11:1; 21:15-17).

God's holiness requires clear boundaries between the holy and the common (v. 5).

Nearness to God is pictured as ascent, open to those with clean hands and a pure heart, which Christ alone provides (vv. 22, 31, 49; Ps 24:3-4; John 10:9).

The sacrifices of the vision point to the single sacrifice of Christ, after which no offering for sin remains (vv. 38-43; Heb 10:11-14, 18).

The temple vision finds its fulfilment in Christ the true temple, the church as God's dwelling, and the new creation (John 2:19-21; Eph 2:19-22; Rev 21:10-22).
40.examples:
A temple shown to a priest whose temple was ashes.

A man of bronze holding a measuring reed.

A wall as thick as it is high.

Gates exactly alike, on every side.

Palm trees carved on the doorposts, like a garden.

Seven steps, then eight, then ten.

Tables for sacrifice at the gate to the altar.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — This Is the Most Holy Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The guide measures the entrance and the nave (vv. 1-2), then goes alone into the inner room and measures it, twenty cubits by twenty: This is the Most Holy Place (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: At the centre of God's house is the place of his holy presence, where no one may come casually.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought me to the nave and measured the jambs. On each side six cubits was the breadth of the jambs. And the breadth of the entrance was ten cubits, and the sidewalls of the entrance were five cubits on either side. And he measured the length of the nave, forty cubits, and its breadth, twenty cubits. Then he went into the inner room and measured the jambs of the entrance, two cubits; and the entrance, six cubits; and the sidewalls on either side of the entrance, seven cubits. And he measured the length of the room, twenty cubits, and its breadth, twenty cubits, across the nave. And he said to me, "This is the Most Holy Place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he brought me to the nave and measured the jambs. On each side six cubits was the breadth of the jambs.

Having measured the courts and gates, the guide now brings Ezekiel into the temple building itself — first the main hall, the nave (vv. 1-2), forty cubits long and twenty wide. (The ESV notes that a long cubit was about twenty-one inches.)

Then he went into the inner room and measured the jambs of the entrance, two cubits; and the entrance, six cubits; and the sidewalls on either side of the entrance, seven cubits.

Notice a small but significant detail: he went into the inner room. The guide goes in. Ezekiel, a priest but not the high priest, is not said to follow. The inner room was the place no ordinary priest could enter. Into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year (Heb 9:7).

And he measured the length of the room, twenty cubits, and its breadth, twenty cubits, across the nave. And he said to me, "This is the Most Holy Place."

This is the Most Holy Place. Twenty cubits by twenty — the same size as the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 6:20). A perfect square, at the heart of the whole vision. This is the place where God's presence dwells.

For the exiles, this was a promise that God's presence would again be at the centre of his people's life. For Christians, it speaks of something even greater. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Matt 27:51). Now we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb 10:19-20). The room Ezekiel could not enter is open to every believer in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The temple's thick walls are surrounded by side chambers in three stories, thirty on each level, rising and widening as they go up (vv. 5-7), on a raised platform with open space all around (vv. 8-11), and a large building stands to the west (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's house is solid, spacious and set apart.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he measured the wall of the temple, six cubits thick, and the breadth of the side chambers, four cubits, all around the temple. And the side chambers were in three stories, one over another, thirty in each story. There were offsets all around the wall of the temple to serve as supports for the side chambers, so that they should not be supported by the wall of the temple. And it became broader as it wound upward to the side chambers, because the temple was enclosed upward all around the temple. Thus the temple had a broad area upward, and so one went up from the lowest story to the top story through the middle story. I saw also that the temple had a raised platform all around; the foundations of the side chambers measured a full reed of six long cubits. The thickness of the outer wall of the side chambers was five cubits. The free space between the side chambers of the temple and the other chambers was a breadth of twenty cubits all around the temple on every side. And the doors of the side chambers opened on the free space, one door toward the north, and another door toward the south. And the breadth of the free space was five cubits all around. The building that was facing the separate yard on the west side was seventy cubits broad, and the wall of the building was five cubits thick all around, and its length ninety cubits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he measured the wall of the temple, six cubits thick, and the breadth of the side chambers, four cubits, all around the temple.

The temple walls are thick — six cubits. Around them runs a structure of side chambers, in three stories, one over another, thirty in each story (v. 6), much like the side rooms around Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 6:5-6). They were probably used for storage of offerings and temple equipment.

The chambers widen as they go up (v. 7), resting on ledges so they do not press on the temple wall itself (v. 6). The whole building stands on a raised platform all around (v. 8), with open space around it (vv. 9-11), and a large separate building stands to the west (v. 12).

What do all these details say? That God's house is solid, well-built and orderly. It is not a flimsy tent pitched in a hurry. It is permanent. And it is surrounded by space — separated from everything around it. God's presence among his people is both secure and holy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole complex measures a hundred cubits each way (vv. 13-15). Inside, the walls are panelled in wood and carved all over with cherubim and palm trees, a palm tree between cherub and cherub, each cherub with a human face and a lion's face (vv. 16-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The temple is a picture of Eden, where God dwells with his people again.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he measured the temple, a hundred cubits long; and the yard and the building with its walls, a hundred cubits long; also the breadth of the east front of the temple and the yard, a hundred cubits. Then he measured the length of the building facing the yard that was at the back and its galleries on either side, a hundred cubits. The inside of the nave and the vestibules of the court, the thresholds and the narrow windows and the galleries all around the three of them, opposite the threshold, were paneled with wood all around, from the floor up to the windows (now the windows were covered), to the space above the door, even to the inner room, and on the outside. And on all the walls all around, inside and outside, was a measured pattern. It was carved of cherubim and palm trees, a palm tree between cherub and cherub. Every cherub had two faces: a human face toward the palm tree on the one side, and the face of a young lion toward the palm tree on the other side. They were carved on the whole temple all around. From the floor to above the door, cherubim and palm trees were carved; similarly the wall of the nave.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he measured the temple, a hundred cubits long; and the yard and the building with its walls, a hundred cubits long; also the breadth of the east front of the temple and the yard, a hundred cubits.

A hundred cubits each way (vv. 13-15). Again and again the vision uses round, balanced numbers and squares. Nothing is out of proportion. The old temple had been corrupted by idols and chaos; this one is perfectly ordered.

Then the guide shows the interior: walls and thresholds panelled with wood from floor to window, narrow windows and galleries (vv. 15-17; the ESV notes that some of these terms are uncertain). And on all the walls all around, inside and outside, was a measured pattern (v. 17).

It was carved of cherubim and palm trees, a palm tree between cherub and cherub. Every cherub had two faces: a human face toward the palm tree on the one side, and the face of a young lion toward the palm tree on the other side. They were carved on the whole temple all around.

Every wall is carved with the same design: cherub, palm tree, cherub, palm tree. Each cherub has two faces, one human and one like a young lion, looking toward the trees on either side.

Cherubim and trees take us back to the beginning. After Adam and Eve sinned, God placed the cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life (Gen 3:24). The temple was always meant to be a picture of Eden, the garden where God dwelt with people. In Ezekiel's vision the cherubim stand beside the palm trees on every wall of the house where God will live among his people. What was lost in Eden is being given back.

The Bible ends in that garden restored: No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face (Rev 22:3-4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–26 — The Table Before the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the Holy Place stands a wooden altar-like table: This is the table that is before the LORD (vv. 21-22). The nave and the Holy Place have double doors carved with cherubim and palm trees (vv. 23-26).
verseByVerse.theology: God sets a table in his presence for fellowship with his people.

verseByVerse.quote: The doorposts of the nave were squared, and in front of the Holy Place was something resembling an altar of wood, three cubits high, two cubits long, and two cubits broad. Its corners, its base, and its walls were of wood. He said to me, "This is the table that is before the LORD." The nave and the Holy Place had each a double door. The double doors had two leaves apiece, two swinging leaves for each door. And on the doors of the nave were carved cherubim and palm trees, such as were carved on the walls. And there was a canopy of wood in front of the vestibule outside. And there were narrow windows and palm trees on either side, on the sidewalls of the vestibule, the side chambers of the temple, and the canopies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The doorposts of the nave were squared, and in front of the Holy Place was something resembling an altar of wood, three cubits high, two cubits long, and two cubits broad. Its corners, its base, and its walls were of wood. He said to me, "This is the table that is before the LORD."

In front of the Holy Place stands a wooden object that looks like an altar, and the guide names it: This is the table that is before the LORD. This recalls the table in the tabernacle, where the priests set the bread of the Presence on the table before me regularly (Exod 25:30) — twelve loaves, set out afresh every Sabbath (Lev 24:5-8).

It is the only piece of furniture in the building that the guide explains, and it is a table. God's house is not only a place of awe but a place of fellowship. The God before whom priests bowed also sets a table in his presence.

That table points to Christ. I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever (John 6:51). And the risen Lord still says to his people, If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Rev 3:20).

The nave and the Holy Place had each a double door. The double doors had two leaves apiece, two swinging leaves for each door. And on the doors of the nave were carved cherubim and palm trees, such as were carved on the walls. And there was a canopy of wood in front of the vestibule outside. And there were narrow windows and palm trees on either side...

Double doors with swinging leaves, carved with the same cherubim and palms. (The ESV notes that the meaning of the word canopy is uncertain.) Doors are made to open. The house of God is not a fortress sealed shut, but a house with doors that swing wide for those whom God welcomes.

41.title: The Most Holy Place
41.overview:
The guide brings Ezekiel into the nave of the temple and measures it, then enters the inner room alone and measures it at twenty cubits square, declaring that it is the Most Holy Place (vv. 1-4).

He measures the thick temple walls and the side chambers built around them in three stories, widening as they rise, the raised platform, the open space around the building and the large building to the west (vv. 5-12).

The whole temple complex measures a hundred cubits each way. Its interior is panelled with wood and carved all around with cherubim and palm trees, each cherub having a human face and a lion's face (vv. 13-20).

In front of the Holy Place is a wooden altar-like table, which the guide calls the table that is before the LORD. The nave and the Holy Place have carved double doors (vv. 21-26).
41.theology:
At the centre of God's dwelling is the Most Holy Place, where no one may enter casually (vv. 3-4; Heb 9:7-8).

In Christ the way into God's holy presence has been opened to all believers (Matt 27:51; Heb 10:19-22).

God's house is solid, ordered and set apart (vv. 5-17).

The cherubim and palm trees picture Eden restored, where God dwells with his people and nothing accursed remains (vv. 18-20; Gen 3:24; Rev 22:3-4).

God sets a table before him for fellowship, fulfilled in Christ the bread of life (v. 22; Exod 25:30; John 6:48-51; Rev 3:20).
41.examples:
A guide who goes into a room the prophet cannot enter.

A square room at the heart of everything.

Walls carved like a garden: cherub, palm, cherub, palm.

A table in God's house.

Double doors made to swing open.

42.text: <sup>1</sup>Then he led me out into the outer court, toward the north, and he brought me to the chambers that were opposite the separate yard and opposite the building on the north.<sup>2</sup>The length of the building whose door faced north was a hundred cubits, and the breadth fifty cubits.<sup>3</sup>Facing the twenty cubits that belonged to the inner court, and facing the pavement that belonged to the outer court, was gallery against gallery in three stories.<sup>4</sup>And before the chambers was a passage inward, ten cubits wide and a hundred cubits long, and their doors were on the north.<sup>5</sup>Now the upper chambers were narrower, for the galleries took more away from them than from the lower and middle chambers of the building.<sup>6</sup>For they were in three stories, and they had no pillars like the pillars of the courts. Thus the upper chambers were set back from the ground more than the lower and the middle ones.<sup>7</sup>And there was a wall outside parallel to the chambers, toward the outer court, opposite the chambers, fifty cubits long.<sup>8</sup>For the chambers on the outer court were fifty cubits long, while those opposite the nave were a hundred cubits long.<sup>9</sup>Below these chambers was an entrance on the east side, as one enters them from the outer court.<sup>10</sup>In the thickness of the wall of the court, on the south also, opposite the yard and opposite the building, there were chambers<sup>11</sup>with a passage in front of them. They were similar to the chambers on the north, of the same length and breadth, with the same exits and arrangements and doors,<sup>12</sup>as were the entrances of the chambers on the south. There was an entrance at the beginning of the passage, the passage before the corresponding wall on the east as one enters them.<sup>13</sup>Then he said to me, "The north chambers and the south chambers opposite the yard are the holy chambers, where the priests who approach the LORD shall eat the most holy offerings. There they shall put the most holy offerings— the grain offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering—for the place is holy.<sup>14</sup>When the priests enter the Holy Place, they shall not go out of it into the outer court without laying there the garments in which they minister, for these are holy. They shall put on other garments before they go near to that which is for the people."<sup>15</sup>Now when he had finished measuring the interior of the temple area, he led me out by the gate that faced east, and measured the temple area all around.<sup>16</sup>He measured the east side with the measuring reed, 500 cubits by the measuring reed all around.<sup>17</sup>He measured the north side, 500 cubits by the measuring reed all around.<sup>18</sup>He measured the south side, 500 cubits by the measuring reed.<sup>19</sup>Then he turned to the west side and measured, 500 cubits by the measuring reed.<sup>20</sup>He measured it on the four sides. It had a wall around it, 500 cubits long and 500 cubits broad, to make a separation between the holy and the common.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The guide shows Ezekiel two long buildings of chambers, north and south of the temple, three stories high, with passages and entrances (vv. 1-12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's house provides a place for those who serve him to live out their holy calling.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he led me out into the outer court, toward the north, and he brought me to the chambers that were opposite the separate yard and opposite the building on the north. The length of the building whose door faced north was a hundred cubits, and the breadth fifty cubits. Facing the twenty cubits that belonged to the inner court, and facing the pavement that belonged to the outer court, was gallery against gallery in three stories. And before the chambers was a passage inward, ten cubits wide and a hundred cubits long, and their doors were on the north. Now the upper chambers were narrower, for the galleries took more away from them than from the lower and middle chambers of the building. For they were in three stories, and they had no pillars like the pillars of the courts. Thus the upper chambers were set back from the ground more than the lower and the middle ones. And there was a wall outside parallel to the chambers, toward the outer court, opposite the chambers, fifty cubits long. For the chambers on the outer court were fifty cubits long, while those opposite the nave were a hundred cubits long. Below these chambers was an entrance on the east side, as one enters them from the outer court. In the thickness of the wall of the court, on the south also, opposite the yard and opposite the building, there were chambers with a passage in front of them. They were similar to the chambers on the north, of the same length and breadth, with the same exits and arrangements and doors, as were the entrances of the chambers on the south. There was an entrance at the beginning of the passage, the passage before the corresponding wall on the east as one enters them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he led me out into the outer court, toward the north, and he brought me to the chambers that were opposite the separate yard and opposite the building on the north.

The guide leads Ezekiel back out to see two blocks of rooms, one on the north side of the temple and one on the south. The description is detailed: a building a hundred cubits long and fifty wide (v. 2), gallery against gallery in three stories (v. 3), a passage in front (v. 4), upper floors set back because of the galleries (vv. 5-6), a wall outside (vv. 7-8), and entrances from the east (v. 9). The south block matches the north exactly (vv. 10-12). (The ESV notes that some words, and verse 12 as a whole, are uncertain in meaning.)

Why so much detail about rooms? Because the next verses explain their purpose, and that purpose tells us something important about God. These are not storerooms. They are holy rooms for holy use.

For readers today, the long descriptions are a reminder that God cares about the whole of his house, not only its dramatic centre. The side rooms, the passages, the places where ordinary work gets done — all are part of his dwelling and all are measured by him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–14 — Holy Food and Holy Garments
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The north chambers and the south chambers... are the holy chambers, where the priests who approach the LORD shall eat the most holy offerings (v. 13). When the priests leave the Holy Place, they must lay aside their holy garments and put on others before they go near to that which is for the people (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: What belongs to God must be treated as holy, and his servants must honour the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to me, "The north chambers and the south chambers opposite the yard are the holy chambers, where the priests who approach the LORD shall eat the most holy offerings. There they shall put the most holy offerings— the grain offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering—for the place is holy. When the priests enter the Holy Place, they shall not go out of it into the outer court without laying there the garments in which they minister, for these are holy. They shall put on other garments before they go near to that which is for the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said to me, "The north chambers and the south chambers opposite the yard are the holy chambers, where the priests who approach the LORD shall eat the most holy offerings. There they shall put the most holy offerings— the grain offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering—for the place is holy.

The rooms are where the priests eat their portion of the most holy offerings. The law required it: the priest who offered a sin offering shall eat it. In a holy place it shall be eaten (Lev 6:26). Things given to God were not to be handled casually or eaten just anywhere.

That may seem remote. But the principle is not. What is given to God belongs to him. The time, money and gifts we dedicate to him are not ours to treat as ordinary.

When the priests enter the Holy Place, they shall not go out of it into the outer court without laying there the garments in which they minister, for these are holy. They shall put on other garments before they go near to that which is for the people."

The priests must change clothes. The garments they wore in the Holy Place stay there; they put on ordinary clothes before going out among the people. On the Day of Atonement Aaron did the same: take off the linen garments that he put on when he went into the Holy Place and shall leave them there (Lev 16:23).

The point is that holiness is not a costume to wear casually wherever you go. It marks a real difference between God's presence and ordinary life.

And the gospel speaks of garments too. Zechariah saw the high priest standing in filthy clothes, and God said, Remove the filthy garments from him... Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments (Zech 3:4). Believers are those who have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Rev 7:14). And now every day we are told to Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience (Col 3:12). In Christ, the holy garments go with us into ordinary life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–20 — A Separation Between the Holy and the Common
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The guide measures the whole temple area from outside: five hundred cubits on each side, a perfect square with a wall around it, to make a separation between the holy and the common (vv. 15-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole temple vision teaches that God is holy and must be approached as holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he had finished measuring the interior of the temple area, he led me out by the gate that faced east, and measured the temple area all around. He measured the east side with the measuring reed, 500 cubits by the measuring reed all around. He measured the north side, 500 cubits by the measuring reed all around. He measured the south side, 500 cubits by the measuring reed. Then he turned to the west side and measured, 500 cubits by the measuring reed. He measured it on the four sides. It had a wall around it, 500 cubits long and 500 cubits broad, to make a separation between the holy and the common.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when he had finished measuring the interior of the temple area, he led me out by the gate that faced east, and measured the temple area all around.

He measured the east side with the measuring reed, 500 cubits by the measuring reed all around. He measured the north side, 500 cubits... He measured the south side, 500 cubits... Then he turned to the west side and measured, 500 cubits by the measuring reed.

The guide walks round the outside of the whole complex: east, north, south, west. Five hundred cubits each side. A perfect square. John saw the new Jerusalem the same way: The city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width (Rev 21:16).

He measured it on the four sides. It had a wall around it, 500 cubits long and 500 cubits broad, to make a separation between the holy and the common.

And here, at the end of three chapters of measurement, is the purpose of it all: to make a separation between the holy and the common.

That sentence explains everything that went wrong before. Ezekiel had charged Jerusalem's priests: They have made no distinction between the holy and the common (22:26). God had told Aaron's sons from the start, You are to distinguish between the holy and the common (Lev 10:10). Idolatry had crept into God's house because the line had been erased. In the new temple, the line is built in stone.

Christians do not worship in a walled temple. But the principle stands. As he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (1 Pet 1:15-16). The wall now runs through the heart and life of God's people: go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you (2 Cor 6:17).

And yet the wall has a gate on the east, and in the next chapter the glory of God will come through it. Holiness is not meant to keep God away from his people. It is what makes it possible for him to come and live among them.

42.title: Between the Holy and the Common
42.overview:
The guide leads Ezekiel into the outer court to two buildings of chambers on the north and south sides of the temple, each three stories high with galleries, passages and entrances (vv. 1-12).

These are the holy chambers where the priests who approach the LORD eat the most holy offerings — the grain, sin and guilt offerings. When the priests leave the Holy Place they must leave their holy garments there and put on other clothes before going among the people (vv. 13-14).

When he has finished measuring the inside, the guide measures the whole temple area from outside: five hundred cubits on each of its four sides, with a wall around it to separate the holy from the common (vv. 15-20).
42.theology:
What is given to God is holy and must not be treated as ordinary (v. 13; Lev 6:26).

Holiness marks a real difference between God's presence and common life (v. 14; Lev 16:23-24).

In Christ believers are given clean garments and called to put on holiness in all of life (Zech 3:3-5; Rev 7:14; Col 3:12).

The purpose of the temple vision is to separate the holy from the common, reversing the failure that brought judgment (v. 20; 22:26; Lev 10:10).

God's people are called to be holy as he is holy, and holiness is what allows God to dwell among them (1 Pet 1:15-16; 2 Cor 6:17).
42.examples:
Three storeys of rooms measured as carefully as the altar.

Holy food eaten in a holy place.

Priests changing clothes before going back among the people.

A square wall, 500 cubits each way.

A line between holy and common, built in stone.

43.text: <sup>1</sup>Then he led me to the gate, the gate facing east.<sup>2</sup>And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east. And the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his glory.<sup>3</sup>And the vision I saw was just like the vision that I had seen when he came to destroy the city, and just like the vision that I had seen by the Chebar canal. And I fell on my face.<sup>4</sup>As the glory of the LORD entered the temple by the gate facing east,<sup>5</sup>the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple.<sup>6</sup>While the man was standing beside me, I heard one speaking to me out of the temple,<sup>7</sup>and he said to me, "Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever. They have defiled my holy name by their abominations that they have committed, so I have consumed them in my anger.<sup>9</sup>Now let them put away their whoring and the dead bodies of their kings far from me, and I will dwell in their midst forever.<sup>10</sup>"As for you, son of man, describe to the house of Israel the temple, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities; and they shall measure the plan.<sup>11</sup>And if they are ashamed of all that they have done, make known to them the design of the temple, its arrangement, its exits and its entrances, that is, its whole design; and make known to them as well all its statutes and its whole design and all its laws, and write it down in their sight, so that they may observe all its laws and all its statutes and carry them out.<sup>12</sup>This is the law of the temple: the whole territory on the top of the mountain all around shall be most holy. Behold, this is the law of the temple.<sup>13</sup>"These are the measurements of the altar by cubits (the cubit being a cubit and a handbreadth): its base shall be one cubit high and one cubit broad, with a rim of one span around its edge. And this shall be the height of the altar:<sup>14</sup>from the base on the ground to the lower ledge, two cubits, with a breadth of one cubit; and from the smaller ledge to the larger ledge, four cubits, with a breadth of one cubit;<sup>15</sup>and the altar hearth, four cubits; and from the altar hearth projecting upward, four horns.<sup>16</sup>The altar hearth shall be square, twelve cubits long by twelve broad.<sup>17</sup>The ledge also shall be square, fourteen cubits long by fourteen broad, with a rim around it half a cubit broad, and its base one cubit all around. The steps of the altar shall face east."<sup>18</sup>And he said to me, "Son of man, thus says the Lord GOD: These are the ordinances for the altar: On the day when it is erected for offering burnt offerings upon it and for throwing blood against it,<sup>19</sup>you shall give to the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok, who draw near to me to minister to me, declares the Lord GOD, a bull from the herd for a sin offering.<sup>20</sup>And you shall take some of its blood and put it on the four horns of the altar and on the four corners of the ledge and upon the rim all around. Thus you shall purify the altar and make atonement for it.<sup>21</sup>You shall also take the bull of the sin offering, and it shall be burned in the appointed place belonging to the temple, outside the sacred area.<sup>22</sup>And on the second day you shall offer a male goat without blemish for a sin offering; and the altar shall be purified, as it was purified with the bull.<sup>23</sup>When you have finished purifying it, you shall offer a bull from the herd without blemish and a ram from the flock without blemish.<sup>24</sup>You shall present them before the LORD, and the priests shall sprinkle salt on them and offer them up as a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>25</sup>For seven days you shall provide daily a male goat for a sin offering; also, a bull from the herd and a ram from the flock, without blemish, shall be provided.<sup>26</sup>Seven days shall they make atonement for the altar and cleanse it, and so consecrate it.<sup>27</sup>And when they have completed these days, then from the eighth day onward the priests shall offer on the altar your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, and I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Glory of the LORD Filled the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezekiel is brought to the east gate, and behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east, with a sound like many waters (vv. 1-2). It is the same vision he saw by the Chebar canal and when the glory left the city, and he falls on his face (v. 3). The glory enters by the east gate, the Spirit lifts Ezekiel into the inner court, and behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who left his defiled house in judgment comes back to dwell with his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he led me to the gate, the gate facing east. And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east. And the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his glory. And the vision I saw was just like the vision that I had seen when he came to destroy the city, and just like the vision that I had seen by the Chebar canal. And I fell on my face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he led me to the gate, the gate facing east. And behold, the glory of the God of Israel was coming from the east. And the sound of his coming was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his glory.

This is the moment the whole book has been waiting for. Nineteen years earlier Ezekiel had watched the glory of God leave the temple. It rose from the cherubim, paused at the entrance of the east gate (10:19), and then stood on the mountain that is on the east side of the city (11:23). Then it was gone. God had abandoned his defiled house to the Babylonians.

Now, in the vision, Ezekiel stands at that same east gate — and the glory is coming back, from the same direction it left. The sound is like the sound of many waters, the thunder of a great river or the sea. When John saw the risen Christ, his voice was like the roar of many waters (Rev 1:15). The earth shone with his glory: this is not a private light in one building, but a glory that lights up the whole land.

And the vision I saw was just like the vision that I had seen when he came to destroy the city, and just like the vision that I had seen by the Chebar canal. And I fell on my face.

Ezekiel makes sure we connect the three visions. The glory by the Chebar canal (ch. 1) came to call him. The glory in chapters 8-11 came to destroy the city. Now the same glory comes to dwell. It is one and the same God, holy in judgment and holy in mercy. And Ezekiel responds exactly as before: I fell on my face. Returning grace does not make God less awesome.

verseByVerse.quote: As the glory of the LORD entered the temple by the gate facing east, the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the glory of the LORD entered the temple by the gate facing east, the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and behold, the glory of the LORD filled the temple.

The glory of the LORD filled the temple. The words echo the great days of Israel's worship. When Moses finished the tabernacle, the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (Exod 40:34). When Solomon dedicated the temple, the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD (1 Kgs 8:11). Now, after the disaster of the exile, it happens again.

For the exiles sitting in Babylon, this was the answer to their deepest fear: that God had left them for good. He had not. He would come back.

And he did, in a way beyond Ezekiel's sight. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). Jesus pointed to his own body and called it this temple (John 2:19-21). The glory that filled Ezekiel's temple came to live among us in a person.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Place of My Throne
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks from the temple: this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever (v. 7). Israel and its kings will no longer defile his name (vv. 7-9). Ezekiel must describe the temple so that the people will be ashamed of their sins and keep its laws (vv. 10-11). This is the law of the temple: the whole territory on the top of the mountain all around shall be most holy (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's presence among his people is forever, and it makes everything around it holy.

verseByVerse.quote: While the man was standing beside me, I heard one speaking to me out of the temple, and he said to me, "Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever. And the house of Israel shall no more defile my holy name, neither they, nor their kings, by their whoring and by the dead bodies of their kings at their high places, by setting their threshold by my threshold and their doorposts beside my doorposts, with only a wall between me and them. They have defiled my holy name by their abominations that they have committed, so I have consumed them in my anger. Now let them put away their whoring and the dead bodies of their kings far from me, and I will dwell in their midst forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the man was standing beside me, I heard one speaking to me out of the temple, and he said to me, "Son of man, this is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever.

Now God himself speaks from inside the house. This is the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet. The temple is the place where the King of heaven sets his feet on earth. And the promise is not for a season: I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever. The Bible ends with that promise kept: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people (Rev 21:3).

And the house of Israel shall no more defile my holy name, neither they, nor their kings, by their whoring and by the dead bodies of their kings at their high places, by setting their threshold by my threshold and their doorposts beside my doorposts, with only a wall between me and them.

What went wrong before? God names two things. First, idolatry — their whoring, the book's blunt word for spiritual unfaithfulness. Second, the kings. (The ESV notes that dead bodies may be "monuments" and at their high places may be "at their deaths".) Whatever the precise practice, the kings had treated God's house as an annex to their own. Solomon's palace stood right beside the temple (1 Kgs 7:1-8) — with only a wall between me and them. Manasseh even built altars in the house of the LORD to other gods (2 Kgs 21:4-5).

The picture is a warning for every age. The danger is not only open idolatry but crowding God: building our own house right up against his, treating him as a neighbour whose property we can use. God will not share his throne.

They have defiled my holy name by their abominations that they have committed, so I have consumed them in my anger. Now let them put away their whoring and the dead bodies of their kings far from me, and I will dwell in their midst forever.

The order matters: put away... and I will dwell in their midst forever. God's presence and idolatry cannot live in the same place. Paul applies the same truth to the church: What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God (2 Cor 6:16).

verseByVerse.quote: "As for you, son of man, describe to the house of Israel the temple, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities; and they shall measure the plan. And if they are ashamed of all that they have done, make known to them the design of the temple, its arrangement, its exits and its entrances, that is, its whole design; and make known to them as well all its statutes and its whole design and all its laws, and write it down in their sight, so that they may observe all its laws and all its statutes and carry them out. This is the law of the temple: the whole territory on the top of the mountain all around shall be most holy. Behold, this is the law of the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As for you, son of man, describe to the house of Israel the temple, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities; and they shall measure the plan.

Why did God show Ezekiel all those measurements in chapters 40-42? Here is the answer: that they may be ashamed of their iniquities. When the exiles saw the beauty and holiness of the house God intended, they would see how far they had fallen.

This is how grace works on the heart. God does not first demand that his people become worthy and then show them his plans. He shows them what he is going to do, and the sight of his goodness makes them ashamed. Ezekiel had said the same of God's covenant love: that you may remember and be confounded, and never open your mouth again because of your shame, when I atone for you for all that you have done (16:63).

And if they are ashamed of all that they have done, make known to them the design of the temple, its arrangement, its exits and its entrances, that is, its whole design; and make known to them as well all its statutes and its whole design and all its laws, and write it down in their sight, so that they may observe all its laws and all its statutes and carry them out.

Shame leads to instruction, and instruction leads to obedience. The one who is truly sorry for sin wants to know how to live. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret (2 Cor 7:10).

This is the law of the temple: the whole territory on the top of the mountain all around shall be most holy. Behold, this is the law of the temple.

The heading is stated twice, like a frame: This is the law of the temple. And its content is one sentence. Before, only the inner room was most holy. Now the whole territory on the top of the mountain all around is most holy. Holiness spreads outward from God's presence. The book of Revelation shows where this ends: a city shaped like the Most Holy Place, its length and width and height are equal (Rev 21:16; 1 Kgs 6:20), where nothing unclean will ever enter (Rev 21:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The altar is measured: a base, two ledges, a square hearth twelve cubits by twelve with four horns, and steps facing east (vv. 13-17).
verseByVerse.theology: At the centre of the court stands the altar: the way to God is by sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: "These are the measurements of the altar by cubits (the cubit being a cubit and a handbreadth): its base shall be one cubit high and one cubit broad, with a rim of one span around its edge. And this shall be the height of the altar: from the base on the ground to the lower ledge, two cubits, with a breadth of one cubit; and from the smaller ledge to the larger ledge, four cubits, with a breadth of one cubit; and the altar hearth, four cubits; and from the altar hearth projecting upward, four horns. The altar hearth shall be square, twelve cubits long by twelve broad. The ledge also shall be square, fourteen cubits long by fourteen broad, with a rim around it half a cubit broad, and its base one cubit all around. The steps of the altar shall face east."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"These are the measurements of the altar by cubits (the cubit being a cubit and a handbreadth): its base shall be one cubit high and one cubit broad, with a rim of one span around its edge. And this shall be the height of the altar:

After the temple and the law comes the altar, placed in front of the temple in the inner court (40:47). The ESV notes give the measures: a cubit about eighteen inches, a handbreadth about three inches, a span about nine inches. (It also notes that the line about the base may read "its gutter shall be one cubit deep".)

from the base on the ground to the lower ledge, two cubits, with a breadth of one cubit; and from the smaller ledge to the larger ledge, four cubits, with a breadth of one cubit; and the altar hearth, four cubits; and from the altar hearth projecting upward, four horns.

The altar rises in stages like a stepped tower — base, lower ledge, upper ledge, hearth — with four horns at the top corners. Those horns were where blood was applied for atonement (Lev 4:25).

The altar hearth shall be square, twelve cubits long by twelve broad. The ledge also shall be square, fourteen cubits long by fourteen broad, with a rim around it half a cubit broad, and its base one cubit all around. The steps of the altar shall face east."

A square hearth, a square ledge, steps on the east side. The priest climbing them would face west, toward the temple and toward the presence of God.

Why does the altar get so much attention right after the glory returns? Because a holy God can dwell among sinful people only on the basis of atonement. The glory fills the house; the altar stands before the house. Access to God has always come by the blood of sacrifice — and it comes now through the one sacrifice to which every altar pointed. We have an altar, says Hebrews (Heb 13:10) — the cross where Christ offered himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The altar is to be purified with the blood of a bull as a sin offering, its body burned outside the sacred area (vv. 18-21), then with a goat each day for seven days, with burnt offerings sprinkled with salt (vv. 22-26). From the eighth day the priests will offer the people's offerings, and I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: God provides the atonement by which he can accept his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "Son of man, thus says the Lord GOD: These are the ordinances for the altar: On the day when it is erected for offering burnt offerings upon it and for throwing blood against it, you shall give to the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok, who draw near to me to minister to me, declares the Lord GOD, a bull from the herd for a sin offering. And you shall take some of its blood and put it on the four horns of the altar and on the four corners of the ledge and upon the rim all around. Thus you shall purify the altar and make atonement for it. You shall also take the bull of the sin offering, and it shall be burned in the appointed place belonging to the temple, outside the sacred area.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to me, "Son of man, thus says the Lord GOD: These are the ordinances for the altar: On the day when it is erected for offering burnt offerings upon it and for throwing blood against it, you shall give to the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok, who draw near to me to minister to me, declares the Lord GOD, a bull from the herd for a sin offering.

Before the altar can be used, it must itself be cleansed. Even the instrument of atonement must be made clean. Ezekiel is given a part to play, like Moses at the first altar (Exod 29:36-37), and the ministry is given to the family of Zadok, the priestly line that had stayed faithful (44:15).

And you shall take some of its blood and put it on the four horns of the altar and on the four corners of the ledge and upon the rim all around. Thus you shall purify the altar and make atonement for it.

Blood on every horn, every corner, the whole rim. Nothing in the service of God is clean by nature. Everything must be purified by blood. Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins (Heb 9:22).

You shall also take the bull of the sin offering, and it shall be burned in the appointed place belonging to the temple, outside the sacred area.

Outside the sacred area. The body of the sin offering, carrying the uncleanness, is taken out and burned. Hebrews sees Christ in exactly this detail: For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb 13:11-12). Our Lord was led out of the city to die, bearing the uncleanness of his people, so that we could be brought in.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the second day you shall offer a male goat without blemish for a sin offering; and the altar shall be purified, as it was purified with the bull. When you have finished purifying it, you shall offer a bull from the herd without blemish and a ram from the flock without blemish. You shall present them before the LORD, and the priests shall sprinkle salt on them and offer them up as a burnt offering to the LORD. For seven days you shall provide daily a male goat for a sin offering; also, a bull from the herd and a ram from the flock, without blemish, shall be provided. Seven days shall they make atonement for the altar and cleanse it, and so consecrate it. And when they have completed these days, then from the eighth day onward the priests shall offer on the altar your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, and I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the second day you shall offer a male goat without blemish for a sin offering; and the altar shall be purified, as it was purified with the bull.

Day after day the cleansing continues. First a bull, then a goat without blemish. God requires a perfect offering, because only the perfect can atone for the imperfect. That requirement is met in the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet 1:19).

When you have finished purifying it, you shall offer a bull from the herd without blemish and a ram from the flock without blemish. You shall present them before the LORD, and the priests shall sprinkle salt on them and offer them up as a burnt offering to the LORD.

After the sin offering come burnt offerings, the offering of complete dedication, wholly consumed on the altar. First sin is dealt with; then the worshipper gives himself entirely to God. The salt follows the old law: with all your offerings you shall offer salt (Lev 2:13), which that verse calls the salt of the covenant with your God — a sign of a lasting bond.

For seven days you shall provide daily a male goat for a sin offering; also, a bull from the herd and a ram from the flock, without blemish, shall be provided. Seven days shall they make atonement for the altar and cleanse it, and so consecrate it.

Seven days, as at the first consecration of the altar under Moses (Exod 29:37). The ESV notes that the Hebrew behind consecrate it is "fill its hand". The altar is set apart completely for God.

And when they have completed these days, then from the eighth day onward the priests shall offer on the altar your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, and I will accept you, declares the Lord GOD."

And here is the goal of all the blood and all the days: I will accept you. Everything in the temple vision moves toward that sentence. A holy God receives a sinful people.

How should Christians read these sacrifices? Believers who expect a literal future temple often understand them as memorials pointing back to the cross. Those who read the vision symbolically understand Ezekiel to be describing true worship in the terms he knew, fulfilled in Christ. On any reading, the New Testament is clear that where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin (Heb 10:18). God's acceptance now rests on Christ's one sacrifice. And the accepted people respond with their own offering: present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship (Rom 12:1).

43.title: The Glory Comes Home
43.overview:
At the east gate Ezekiel sees the glory of the God of Israel coming from the east, with a sound like many waters, and the earth shining with his glory. It is the same vision he saw at the Chebar canal and when God came to destroy the city, and he falls on his face (vv. 1-3).

The glory enters the temple by the east gate. The Spirit lifts Ezekiel into the inner court, and the glory of the LORD fills the temple (vv. 4-5).

God speaks from the temple: this is the place of his throne, where he will dwell among Israel forever. Israel and its kings will no longer defile his name with idolatry and with their kings' dead bodies, as when their buildings stood with only a wall between them and God. If they put these things away, he will dwell among them forever (vv. 6-9).

Ezekiel must describe the temple to Israel so that they will be ashamed of their iniquities, and, if they are ashamed, make known its whole design and laws so that they may keep them. The law of the temple is that the whole territory on the mountain top is most holy (vv. 10-12).

The altar is measured: base, ledges, a hearth twelve cubits square, four horns and steps facing east (vv. 13-17).

The altar is to be consecrated over seven days. The Zadokite priests are to receive a bull for a sin offering, its blood applied to the horns, corners and rim to purify the altar, and its body burned outside the sacred area; then a goat each day, with a bull and a ram offered as burnt offerings with salt. From the eighth day the priests will offer the people's burnt offerings and peace offerings, and God will accept them (vv. 18-27).
43.theology:
The God who departed from his defiled house in judgment returns in glory to dwell with his people (vv. 1-5; 10:18-19; 11:22-23).

God's glory came to dwell among us in Jesus Christ, the true temple (John 1:14; 2:19-21).

God's presence among his people is forever, and it cannot coexist with idolatry (vv. 7-9; 2 Cor 6:16; Rev 21:3).

The sight of God's gracious purposes produces godly shame and a desire to obey (vv. 10-11; 16:63; 2 Cor 7:10).

Holiness spreads outward from God's presence until the whole mountain is most holy (v. 12; Rev 21:16, 27).

A holy God dwells with sinners only on the basis of atoning blood (vv. 13-26; Heb 9:22).

The sin offering burned outside the sacred area points to Christ, who suffered outside the gate (v. 21; Heb 13:11-12).

God's aim is acceptance: "I will accept you", now grounded in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice, to which believers respond with their lives (v. 27; Heb 10:18; Rom 12:1).
43.examples:
The glory coming back through the very gate it left by.

A sound like many waters.

A prophet falling on his face again.

A palace built with only a wall between it and God's house.

A beautiful plan that makes people ashamed.

A whole mountain made most holy.

Blood on the four horns of the altar.

A bull burned outside the sacred area.

Seven days of cleansing, then the eighth day: I will accept you.
